You can be so busy serving Jesus that you forget to be with him.

That's the trap for many committed Christians. You do things for God, so many things, good things. Meetings, service, projects, phones ringing, notifications without end. And one day you realize you haven't spent real time alone with him in weeks. You serve the Master of the house, but you never sit at his feet anymore.

Imagine a wife whose husband works all the time to give her a beautiful house, but never spends an evening with her. She would eventually say: "I don't want your gifts—I want you." God doesn't first look for exhausted servants, but for present children.

Service must flow from presence. Martha without Mary is exhaustion. Mary sitting forever without getting up is spiritual selfishness. But Mary first, then Martha—that's balance.

Today, set a specific, protected time—even if it's short—when you'll sit at Jesus' feet. Phone on airplane mode, Bible open, heart available. That's "the good part," and no one can take it from you.

Put it into practice.

One. Protected Time. Set a time each day at Jesus' feet, even if it's short: phone on airplane mode, Bible open. Put it on your calendar.

Two. Martha or Mary?. Write down what makes you "worried and troubled" in your service or life. Give it to Jesus before you keep serving.

Three. As a Family. If you're a busy parent, take five minutes with your children to read a verse and pray together. The good part can be shared as a family too.

To reflect on. Do I tend to be more like Martha or more like Mary? What protected time will I set aside to sit at Jesus' feet?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I've been so busy serving you that I forgot to be with you. I choose the good part. Teach me to sit at your feet, to listen to you, and then to serve with a heart at peace. Amen.

Key takeaway. You can be so busy serving Jesus that you forget to be with him.

Day 28. The Father Who Ran.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 15, verses 11 to 32.

He said, “A certain man had two sons. The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of your property.’ So he divided his livelihood between them. Not many days after, the younger son gathered all of this together and traveled into a far country. There he wasted his property with riotous living. When he had spent all of it, there arose a severe famine in that country, and he began to be in need. He went and joined himself to one of the citizens of that country, and he sent him into his fields to feed pigs. He wanted to fill his belly with the pods that the pigs ate, but no one gave him any. But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger! I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.”’ “He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him. The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ “But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet. Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat and celebrate; for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate. “Now his elder son was in the field. As he came near to the house, he heard music and dancing. He called one of the servants to him and asked what was going on. He said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and healthy.’ But he was angry and would not go in. Therefore his father came out and begged him. But he answered his father, ‘Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this your son came, who has devoured your living with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.’ “He said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’”

The Story.

It may be the most beautiful story ever told. A father had two sons. The younger said to him, "Father, give me the share of the property that falls to me." In the culture of that time, many commentators point out, asking for your inheritance while your father is alive was almost like saying, "I wish you were dead."

The father agrees. The son goes to a distant country and squanders everything in wild living. Then comes the famine. He ends up keeping pigs, the unclean animal par excellence for a Jew, and he even envies their food. He has hit bottom.

That's when he "comes to himself." He prepares a speech: "I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me like one of your hired servants." And he takes the road home.

What This Reveals About God.

"And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him." (Luke, chapter 15, verse 20)

"While he was still a long way off, his father saw him." That means the father was watching the road. Maybe every day. He had never stopped waiting.

And he runs. In that culture, an elderly, respected man did not run in public—he would have to lift his robe, and it was beneath his dignity. But this father doesn't care. He runs, throws his arms around his son, kisses him. The son starts his speech, but the father won't even let him finish. He calls his servants: the best robe, a ring on his finger, sandals on his feet, the fattened calf. A celebration.

The Father wasn't waiting for your speech; he was waiting for your return.

For Your Life.

But the story isn't over. There's a second son. The one who stayed, who always obeyed. When he hears the music, he gets angry and refuses to go in. "All these years I have been serving you…" He was at home, but his heart was just as far away as his brother's. He served his father like an employee, not like a son.

And the father comes out to him too: "My child," the father said to him, "you have always been with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, because this your brother was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found." (Luke, chapter 15, verses 31 to 32)

There are two ways to be far from the Father: by leaving home, or by staying at home with a hard heart. The first son loses himself in sin, the second in religion. And the Father runs toward both.

If you're the son who left, the road back is open. You don't need a perfect speech. The Father is already running toward you.

If you're the older son, ask yourself: Am I serving God with joy, like a son, or with bitterness, like an employee counting his hours? Do I rejoice when someone comes back, even if they've done anything wrong?

Today, come to yourself, no matter which son you are. And let yourself be embraced by the Father.

Put it into practice.

One. Come to Yourself. Which son are you right now—the one who left or the one who stayed with a hard heart? Tell the Father honestly.

Two. Take the Road Home. If you've wandered away, take a concrete step today: pray, go back to church, call a pastor or a Christian friend. The Father is already running toward you.

Three. Rejoice in a Return. Think of someone who is coming back to God or to church. Welcome them warmly this week, without bringing up their past.

To reflect on. Do I see myself more in the younger son or the older son? What does the Father want to say to me today?

Prayer. Father, thank you for watching the road and running toward me. I come back to you, with my faults and without a perfect speech. Clothe me with your finest robe. And deliver me from the hardness of the older son: give me to serve you with joy, as your child, and to rejoice in every return. Amen.

Key takeaway. The Father wasn't waiting for your speech; he was waiting for your return.

Day 29. Roll Away the Stone.

Today's reading : John, chapter 11, verses 17 to 44.

So when Jesus came, he found that he had been in the tomb four days already. Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away. Many of the Jews had joined the women around Martha and Mary, to console them concerning their brother. Then when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary stayed in the house. Therefore Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died. Even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.” Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.” Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.” Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies. Whoever lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” She said to him, “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Christ, God’s Son, he who comes into the world.” When she had said this, she went away and called Mary, her sister, secretly, saying, “The Teacher is here and is calling you.” When she heard this, she arose quickly and went to him. Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was in the place where Martha met him. Then the Jews who were with her in the house and were consoling her, when they saw Mary, that she rose up quickly and went out, followed her, saying, “She is going to the tomb to weep there.” Therefore when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell down at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you would have been here, my brother wouldn’t have died.” When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping who came with her, he groaned in the spirit and was troubled, and said, “Where have you laid him?” They told him, “Lord, come and see.” Jesus wept. The Jews therefore said, “See how much affection he had for him!” Some of them said, “Couldn’t this man, who opened the eyes of him who was blind, have also kept this man from dying?” Jesus therefore, again groaning in himself, came to the tomb. Now it was a cave, and a stone lay against it. Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of him who was dead, said to him, “Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days.” Jesus said to her, “Didn’t I tell you that if you believed, you would see God’s glory?” So they took away the stone from the place where the dead man was lying. Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you listened to me. I know that you always listen to me, but because of the multitude standing around I said this, that they may believe that you sent me.” When he had said this, he cried with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” He who was dead came out, bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Free him, and let him go.”

The Story.

Lazarus, the friend of Jesus, brother of Martha and Mary, is gravely ill. The sisters send a message: "Lord, the one you love is sick." And Jesus… stays where he is for two more days. When he finally arrives in Bethany, Lazarus has been dead for four days.

Martha runs toward him: "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died." Then Mary arrives, falls at his feet, and says exactly the same thing. They must have repeated it for four days: "If only you had come…"

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Jesus knew he was going to raise Lazarus. He had even announced it to his disciples. And yet, before the tomb, in the midst of weeping: "Jesus wept. So the Jews said, 'See how he loved him.'" (John, chapter 11, verses 35 to 36)

It's the shortest verse in the Bible, and one of the most profound. Jesus weeps. He's not rushed to move on to the miracle. He doesn't say, "Stop weeping, you'll see!" He enters into the grief of his friends. He weeps with those who weep.

Your sorrow is not indifferent to Jesus. He knows the end of your story, and yet he weeps with you in the middle.

Then he gives an order: "Jesus said, 'Roll away the stone.' Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, 'Lord, by this time there is a stench, for he has been dead four days.' Jesus said to her, 'Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?'" (John, chapter 11, verses 39 to 40)

Martha has a very logical objection: "He already stinks." Everyone knows that after four days, it's over. But Jesus asks her to do her part: roll away the stone. He could have done it with a word. But he wants human hands to roll it.

Then he cries out: "Lazarus, come out!" And the dead man comes out, his feet and hands wrapped with burial strips. And Jesus gives one final order to the witnesses: "Unbind him, and let him go."

For Your Life.

Jesus can raise the dead, but he asks you to roll away the stone.

Maybe there's something in your life that has been dead for "four days": a dream, a marriage, a relationship, a calling, your joy. Everyone says, "It's over, it already stinks." And maybe you repeat, "Lord, if you had been here…"

Jesus weeps with you. But he also tells you: "Roll away the stone." The stone might be bitterness, refusal to forgive, a closed door, fear of believing again. He's not asking you to raise the dead; that's his job. He's asking you to roll the stone.

And look at the last word: "Unbind him." Lazarus was alive, but still wrapped in his burial cloths. It's the role of the community: to help those whom Jesus has brought back to life to free themselves from what still wraps them.

Today, name your "stone," and dare to roll it away before Jesus.

Put it into practice.

One. Name Your Stone. Write down what's preventing God from acting in a situation that seems dead: bitterness, refusal to forgive, a closed door, fear of believing again.

Two. Roll It Away. Take a concrete step this week: forgive, make a first move, reach out again, dare to pray about this matter once more.

Three. Help Someone Be Unbound. Think of someone who has known Jesus but remains trapped by their "burial cloths" (shame, habits, wounds). Walk alongside them: listen, pray, offer concrete help.

To reflect on. What "stone" is Jesus asking me to roll away today so he can act?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for weeping with me. You know what has died in my life and what everyone thinks is lost. I roll away the stone before you: my bitterness, my doubts, my closed doors. Cry out life again. And help me to unbind others. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus can raise the dead, but he asks you to roll away the stone.

Day 30. I Must Stay at Your House.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 19, verses 1 to 10.

He entered and was passing through Jericho. There was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector, and he was rich. He was trying to see who Jesus was, and couldn’t because of the crowd, because he was short. He ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was going to pass that way. When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.” He hurried, came down, and received him joyfully. When they saw it, they all murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.” Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.” Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”

The Story.

Jericho. Zacchaeus is not just a tax collector: he is the chief tax collector, and he is rich. In other words, he has grown wealthy by collaborating with the occupier and collecting more than required. The whole city hates him.

He wants to see Jesus, but there are two problems: the crowd, and his height. He is short. So he does something very undignified for a wealthy man: he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree. Imagine a bank manager perched in a tree in a suit.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Jesus arrives at the tree. He stops, looks up, and calls him by name: "And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, 'Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.'" (Luke, chapter 19, verse 5)

Jesus knows his name. He doesn't say to him, "Come down, so I can lecture you." He says, "I must stay at your house today." "I must": as if it were the most important appointment of his journey.

The crowd murmurs, "He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner." But Jesus won't let public opinion dictate his friendships.

And yet, Jesus asks nothing of Zacchaeus. No list of conditions, no sermon on honesty. Zacchaeus himself stands up: "And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, 'Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.' And Jesus said to him, 'Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.'" (Luke, chapter 19, verses 8 to 10)

For Your Life.

Zacchaeus was seeking to see Jesus; he discovered that Jesus was seeking him.

Notice the order: first, Jesus welcomes Zacchaeus. Then, Zacchaeus changes. Change is not the condition for Jesus's love; it is the fruit of that love. No one forced Zacchaeus to give back the money. Grace did what shame and the reproach of an entire city had never been able to do.

And his repentance is concrete. He doesn't just say "I'm sorry." He gives half his possessions to the poor, and restores four times what he stole. The true encounter with Jesus always touches the wallet, relationships, and habits.

Maybe you feel small too: small because of your past, your reputation, what others say about you. Maybe the crowd is hiding Jesus from you. Do what Zacchaeus did: run ahead, climb a tree, do what it takes to see him. And you will discover that he stops under your tree, and that he knows your name.

And if Jesus comes to your house today, what needs to change? Is there something to repair, to restore, to give back? Grace doesn't ask it as a price to pay. It gives you the desire to do it.

Put it into practice.

One. Climb Your Tree. Make a concrete effort to see Jesus this week: wake up earlier, go to a prayer meeting, read an entire Gospel.

Two. What Needs to Be Repaired. If Jesus came to your house today, what would need to change? A debt to repay, an apology, a wrong to make right? Do it, with joy.

Three. Your Generosity. Zacchaeus gave to the poor. Choose a concrete gift this week, within your means: money, a meal, your time.

To reflect on. If Jesus came to my house today, what would need to change or be made right?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for stopping under my tree and calling me by my name. I receive you with joy in my house and in my life. May your grace produce true change in me. Show me what I need to repair, and give me the joy of doing it. Amen.

Key takeaway. Zacchaeus was seeking to see Jesus; he discovered that Jesus was seeking him.

Day 31. The King on a Donkey.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 19, verses 28 to 44.

Having said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. When he came near to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the mountain that is called Olivet, he sent two of his disciples, saying, “Go your way into the village on the other side, in which, as you enter, you will find a colt tied, which no man has ever sat upon. Untie it and bring it. If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ say to him: ‘The Lord needs it.’” Those who were sent went away and found things just as he had told them. As they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?” They said, “The Lord needs it.” Then they brought it to Jesus. They threw their cloaks on the colt and sat Jesus on them. As he went, they spread their cloaks on the road. As he was now getting near, at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works which they had seen, saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!” Some of the Pharisees from the multitude said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples!” He answered them, “I tell you that if these were silent, the stones would cry out.” When he came near, he saw the city and wept over it, saying, “If you, even you, had known today the things which belong to your peace! But now, they are hidden from your eyes. For the days will come on you when your enemies will throw up a barricade against you, surround you, hem you in on every side, and will dash you and your children within you to the ground. They will not leave in you one stone on another, because you didn’t know the time of your visitation.”

The Story.

Jesus arrives near Jerusalem. The city is full of pilgrims who have come for Passover. He sends two disciples to find a young donkey that no one has ever ridden. When asked why they're untying it, they must answer, "The Lord needs it."

Then Jesus enters the city riding on this donkey. The crowd spreads their clothes on the road like a red carpet for a king. The disciples burst with joy: "They said, 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!' " (Luke, chapter 19, verse 38)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

When a king entered a city in those days, he arrived on a war horse, surrounded by soldiers. Jesus arrives on a donkey. He fulfills the prophecy of Zechariah: "Behold, your King is coming to you; He is just and having salvation, lowly and riding on a donkey" (Zechariah, chapter 9, verse 9). Jesus is a king, but not the kind many were expecting. They hoped for a political liberator who would drive out the Romans. He comes to free hearts.

And then there is this moving moment. In the midst of the cries of joy, Jesus looks at the city, and: "As He drew near, He saw the city and wept over it, saying, 'If you had known, even you, especially in this your day, the things that make for your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. '" (Luke, chapter 19, verses 41 to 42)

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem. He knows that the same city crying "Hosanna" today will cry "Crucify Him" in a few days. He also knows that, having rejected Him, the city will be destroyed—which happened in 70 AD. He weeps because it "did not know the time of your visitation."

For Your Life.

Jesus is not looking for fans; He is looking for disciples.

A crowd can cheer for Jesus on Sunday and reject Him on Friday. One day's enthusiasm is not enough. Fans applaud when everything is going well; disciples follow when it costs something. The question is not "Did I shout Hosanna?" but "Do I still follow Him when He takes the path to the cross?"

Notice too the little donkey. An animal of no value, never ridden, tied up somewhere. And yet: "The Lord needs it." That day, this donkey carried the King of kings. You may feel small, insignificant, tied down. But if the Lord needs you, He will come to untie you, and you will carry His presence wherever He wants to go.

And think of Jesus' tears. He still weeps today over cities that do not recognize Him. Over your city, your neighborhood, your family.

Today, do two things. Ask yourself whether your faith is that of a fan or that of a disciple. Then pray for your city as Jesus wept over Jerusalem: that it may recognize the time of its visitation.

Put it into practice.

One. Fan or Disciple?. Write honestly what shows that you follow Jesus even when it costs something, and what shows that you follow Him only when everything is going well.

Two. The Lord Needs It. Ask God what He wants to use in you (your time, your car, your home, your talent) and say yes to Him this week.

Three. Pray for Your City. Take ten minutes to pray for your city, walking if possible: its leaders, its families, those who don't know Jesus.

To reflect on. Does my faith look more like a fan's or a disciple's? For which city or place will I pray with Jesus' heart?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, humble and victorious King, I don't want to cheer for You only when everything is going well—I want to follow You all the way. Untie me and use me to carry Your presence. And give me Your heart for my city, that it may recognize the time of Your visitation. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus is not looking for fans; He is looking for disciples.

Day 32. The King with a Towel.

Today's reading : John, chapter 13, verses 1 to 17.

Now before the feast of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his time had come that he would depart from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, the devil having already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him, Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God, arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. Then he came to Simon Peter. He said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?” Jesus answered him, “You don’t know what I am doing now, but you will understand later.” Peter said to him, “You will never wash my feet!” Jesus answered him, “If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me.” Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!” Jesus said to him, “Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean. You are clean, but not all of you.” For he knew him who would betray him; therefore he said, “You are not all clean.” So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you? You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am. If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you. Most certainly I tell you, a servant is not greater than his lord, neither is one who is sent greater than he who sent him. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.

Part 5: The Cross.

We enter the last days of Jesus before the cross. John devotes almost half his Gospel to this final week. Slow down, read carefully: this is the heart of everything.

The Story.

"Before the Feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that His hour had come that He should depart from this world to the Father, having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the end." (John, chapter 13, verse 1)

"He loved them to the end." And how? With a gesture no one expected. During the meal, Jesus rises, removes His outer garments, takes a towel, pours water into a basin, and begins to wash His disciples' feet.

In that culture, roads were dusty, people wore sandals, and feet were dirty. Washing guests' feet was the task of the lowest slave. Even a disciple was not required to wash his master's feet. That evening there was no slave, and none of the disciples offered to do it. Luke even tells us that during this meal they were arguing about who was the greatest (Luke, chapter 22, verse 24).

So while they argue over first place, Jesus takes last place.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Peter refuses: "You shall never wash my feet." He cannot accept that his Lord would humble Himself this way. But Jesus answers him: "If I do not wash you, you have no part with Me." Before serving, you must accept being served by Jesus, being washed by Him. Pride can also hide in the refusal to receive.

And there is a detail that takes your breath away: Jesus knows that Judas will betray Him (John, chapter 13, verse 2, 11). Yet He also washes his feet. He kneels before the one who will hand Him over for thirty pieces of silver, takes his feet in His hands, and washes them.

Then Jesus puts His outer garments back on and explains: "If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. For I have given you an example, that you should do as I have done to you." (John, chapter 13, verses 14 to 15)

For Your Life.

The greatest is not the one who has the most people serving him, but the one who serves the most people.

In the world, greatness is measured by how many people are under your command. In the kingdom of God, it is measured by how many people you serve. Jesus didn't say, "Blessed are you if you know these things," but "Blessed are you if you practice them" (John, chapter 13, verse 17).

Washing feet today may not be with a basin and water. It's doing the task no one wants to do. It's serving someone who can give you nothing in return. It's even serving someone who has hurt you, as Jesus did with Judas.

Today, take a towel, literally or figuratively. Find a humble, invisible service that no one will notice. And do it for Jesus.

Put it into practice.

One. Take a Towel. Find a humble and invisible service this week (dishes, cleaning at church, helping a neighbor) and do it for Jesus.

Two. Let Yourself Be Served. If you struggle to receive help, accept someone's assistance this week without making excuses. Receiving is also a form of humility.

Three. Serve the One Who Hurt You. Think of a person who has hurt you. Without putting yourself in danger, do a small act of kindness toward them, as Jesus did with Judas.

To reflect on. What humble and invisible service can I render this week? Is there someone who has hurt me whom I could serve?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, You, the Master, took the towel and washed the feet of Your disciples, even the feet of Judas. Wash me first, and cleanse my heart of all pride. Then teach me to serve as You do, without seeking first place, even those who have hurt me. Amen.

Key takeaway. While they argued over first place, Jesus took last place.

Day 33. Do This in Remembrance of Me.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 22, verses 14 to 30.

When the hour had come, he sat down with the twelve apostles. He said to them, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer, for I tell you, I will no longer by any means eat of it until it is fulfilled in God’s Kingdom.” He received a cup, and when he had given thanks, he said, “Take this and share it among yourselves, for I tell you, I will not drink at all again from the fruit of the vine, until God’s Kingdom comes.” He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me.” Likewise, he took the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you. But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. The Son of Man indeed goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man through whom he is betrayed!” They began to question among themselves which of them it was who would do this thing. A dispute also arose among them, which of them was considered to be greatest. He said to them, “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’ But not so with you. Rather, the one who is greater among you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves. For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves? Isn’t it he who sits at the table? But I am among you as one who serves. “But you are those who have continued with me in my trials. I confer on you a kingdom, even as my Father conferred on me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my Kingdom. You will sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

The Story.

It is the evening of Passover. For more than a thousand years, every Jewish family has celebrated this meal to remember the night when God freed Israel from Egypt. The blood of the lamb on the doorposts, the angel of death passing over, the exodus from slavery. Each element of the meal tells this story.

And that evening, Jesus says to His disciples a phrase full of emotion: "I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer." Then He takes the bread and the cup and gives them new meaning: "And He took bread, gave thanks and broke it, and gave it to them, saying, 'This is My body which is given for you; do this in remembrance of Me.' Likewise He also took the cup after supper, saying, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is shed for you.' " (Luke, chapter 22, verses 19 to 20)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Jesus is saying: "Tonight, a new liberation is beginning, and I am the Lamb." The broken bread is His body that will be broken on the cross. The cup is His blood that will be shed. Not for Israel alone: "for you," for all who believe.

He speaks of a "new covenant." A covenant is more than a contract. A contract says, "I'll do my part if you do yours." A covenant says, "I give myself to you." Like in a marriage. Jesus seals this covenant with His own blood.

Yet at the same table there is Judas' betrayal, and right after, an argument over who is the greatest. Jesus answers them: "Let it not be so among you; on the contrary, he who is greatest among you, let him be as the younger, and he who governs as he who serves. For who is greater, he who sits at the table, or he who serves? Is it not he who sits at the table? Yet I am among you as the One who serves." (Luke, chapter 22, verses 26 to 27)

Even on His last evening, the disciples don't understand. And Jesus doesn't reject them. He continues to love them, to teach them, to share bread with them.

For Your Life.

When you take communion, you're not just remembering—you're proclaiming a covenant.

When you take the bread and the cup, you are saying: "Jesus died for me. His body was broken in my place. His blood paid my debt. I am in the covenant." Paul adds that every time you do this, you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes (1 Corinthians, chapter 11, verse 26). This is a proclamation looking to the past, but also to the future.

It's possible to take communion out of habit, thinking about something else, as if reciting a formula. This text invites us to rediscover it as a meal of love. Jesus "eagerly desired" this moment with His disciples. He desires it also with you.

Today, even if you're not taking communion, take a moment to remember. Thank Jesus for His broken body and shed blood, given precisely for you. And the next time you share the bread and cup at church, do it with awareness: you are proclaiming the covenant.

Put it into practice.

One. Remember. Take a moment to thank Jesus for His broken body and shed blood, given precisely for you. Write a prayer of thanksgiving.

Two. Prepare Your Next Communion. The next time you take it, prepare your heart the day before: confess what weighs on you, forgive, and live it as the proclamation of the covenant.

Three. A Meal That Gathers. Organize a meal with brothers and sisters this week or with your family, and take a moment to remember what Jesus did.

To reflect on. How do I live communion: out of habit, or as the proclamation of a covenant? What could change?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for Your broken body and shed blood given for me. Thank you for this new covenant, sealed by Your love. Forgive me for the times I took this meal without thinking about it. I remember You, and I proclaim Your death until You come. Amen.

Key takeaway. Communion is not just a memory—it's the proclamation of a covenant.

Day 34. Gethsemane, the Wine Press.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 26, verses 36 to 46.

Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and said to his disciples, “Sit here, while I go there and pray.” He took with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, and began to be sorrowful and severely troubled. Then Jesus said to them, “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch with me.” He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” He came to the disciples and found them sleeping, and said to Peter, “What, couldn’t you watch with me for one hour? Watch and pray, that you don’t enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Again, a second time he went away and prayed, saying, “My Father, if this cup can’t pass away from me unless I drink it, your desire be done.” He came again and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. He left them again, went away, and prayed a third time, saying the same words. Then he came to his disciples and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Behold, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Arise, let’s be going. Behold, he who betrays me is at hand.”

The Story.

After the last meal, Jesus goes with his disciples to a garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives: Gethsemane. The name means "oil press." This is where olives were crushed under heavy stones to extract their oil. And that night, it is Jesus' heart that will be crushed.

He takes Peter, James, and John a little further, and for the first time, he shows them his distress: "Then he said to them, 'My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch with Me.' He went a little farther and fell on His face, and prayed, saying, 'O My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will.'" (Matthew, chapter 26, verses 38 to 39)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Jesus is not an unfeeling hero walking toward death without emotion. He is "exceedingly sorrowful, even to death." Luke even notes that his sweat became like great drops of blood falling to the ground (Luke, chapter 22, verse 44). He knows what awaits him: physical suffering, yes, but above all the cup—that is, to bear the sin of the world and God's wrath against that sin.

And he prays the same prayer three times, with disarming honesty: "If it is possible, let this cup pass from Me!" Then he adds: "Nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will." He does not hide his struggle. But he submits his desire to the Father's.

Gethsemane teaches us that true prayer is not always the kind where we get what we want. Sometimes it is the kind where we end up wanting what God wants.

Meanwhile, the disciples are sleeping. Three times, Jesus comes back and finds them asleep. And he says to them: "Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak." (Matthew, chapter 26, verse 41)

For Your Life.

Olives never yielded their oil without being pressed. And it is often in our Gethsemanes that God causes something precious to flow through us.

Maybe you are going through a press right now: a trial that is crushing you, a decision that costs you, an obedience that hurts. Jesus understands you. He has been there before you. You have the right to tell him honestly: "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me." This is not a lack of faith. But also ask him for the grace to add: "Not what I want, but what You want."

It is through the "yes" of Gethsemane that we have the cross, and through the cross that we have the resurrection. Your "yes" in the press can also open the way to something you cannot yet see.

And do not sleep during the struggles of others. Someone around you may be in their own Gethsemane. Watch and pray with them.

Put it into practice.

One. Your Press. Write down what is crushing you right now. Tell it honestly to God, as Jesus did: "If it is possible, let this cup pass from me."

Two. The Difficult "Yes". Then add, even if it's hard: "Not what I want, but what You want." If you cannot say it yet, ask for the grace to be able to say it.

Three. Watch With Someone. Think of someone in their Gethsemane (illness, grief, trial). Do not sleep during their struggle: call them, pray with them this week.

To reflect on. What is the "press" I am going through right now? Am I able to say to God: "Not what I want, but what You want"?

Prayer. Father, you see what is crushing me right now. I tell you honestly: if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. But I choose to trust you: not what I want, but what You want. Let my life, even pressed, pour out the oil of your presence. Amen.

Key takeaway. True prayer is not always the kind where we get what we want, but the kind where we end up wanting what God wants.

The Lord turned and looked at Peter. Then Peter remembered the Lord’s word, how he said to him, “Before the rooster crows you will deny me three times.” He went out, and wept bitterly.

Key verses.

Luke, chapter 22, verses 31 to 32. The Lord said, “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat, but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.”

The Story.

A crowd arrives in the garden with swords and clubs. Leading them, Judas. He approaches Jesus to kiss him: it is the agreed signal. Jesus simply says to him: "Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?"

Peter draws his sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant. But Jesus stops him, touches the man's ear, and heals him. Even during his arrest, Jesus heals one of those coming to arrest him.

They take Jesus to the high priest's house. Peter follows at a distance. He enters the courtyard and sits by the fire with the servants. And three times, someone recognizes him. Three times, he denies it: "I do not know him." The third time, as he is still speaking, the rooster crows.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

"And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how He had said to him, 'Before the rooster crows today, you will deny Me three times.' So Peter went out and wept bitterly." (Luke, chapter 22, verses 61 to 62)

Jesus is being tried, beaten, humiliated. And in the midst of all this, he turns and looks at Peter. What kind of look? Not a look of anger, not "I told you so." I believe it was a look of wounded love, of compassion. A look that said: "I know. And I still love you."

Because Jesus had warned Peter a few hours earlier: "And the Lord said, 'Simon, Simon! Indeed, Satan has asked for you, that he may sift you as wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith should not fail; and when you have returned to Me, strengthen your brethren.'" (Luke, chapter 22, verses 31 to 32)

Jesus knew Peter would fall. And he had already prayed for him. He had even already planned what comes after: "when you have returned to Me." Not "if," but "when."

For Your Life.

That night, two disciples betrayed Jesus. Judas delivered him, Peter denied him. Both felt remorse. But their stories end in opposite ways. Judas, crushed by his guilt, took his own life. Peter, on the other hand, wept bitterly, then came back. The difference was not the seriousness of their fall, but what they did afterward.

Remorse looks at the fault; repentance looks at Jesus.

Maybe you have denied Jesus in some way: out of fear, out of cowardice, out of a fall you never thought possible. You tell yourself: "I never would have thought I could do that." Peter had also said: "Lord, I am ready to go with You, both to prison and to death."

Listen carefully: your fall did not surprise Jesus. He had already prayed for you. And he looks at you today, not to crush you, but to bring you back. Do not do as Judas did, staying alone with his guilt. Do as Peter did: weep if you must, but come back. And when you are lifted up, you will be able to strengthen your brethren.

Put it into practice.

One. Look at Jesus, Not Your Fall. If you remain in the remorse of a fault, tell it to Jesus, receive his forgiveness, and read Luke 22:32. He had already prayed for you.

Two. Do Not Stay Alone. Judas stayed alone with his guilt. If guilt is crushing you, talk about it this week with someone you trust or with a pastor.

Three. Strengthen Your Brethren. Your lifted-up fall can become strength for others. Think of someone who has fallen and encourage them: "Jesus lifted me up too."

To reflect on. Is there a fall for which I remain in remorse instead of returning to Jesus? What does his gaze tell me today?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you know my falls, even those I never thought possible. Thank you for praying for me before I even fell. I do not want to stay alone with my fault. I return to you. Lift me up, and make me someone who strengthens others. Amen.

Key takeaway. Remorse looks at the fault; repentance looks at Jesus.

Day 36. Father, Forgive Them.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 23, verses 26 to 49.

A great multitude of the people followed him, including women who also mourned and lamented him. When they came to the place that is called “The Skull”, they crucified him there with the criminals, one on the right and the other on the left. Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” Dividing his garments among them, they cast lots. The people stood watching. The rulers with them also scoffed at him, saying, “He saved others. Let him save himself, if this is the Christ of God, his chosen one!” The soldiers also mocked him, coming to him and offering him vinegar, and saying, “If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!” An inscription was also written over him in letters of Greek, Latin, and Hebrew: “THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.” One of the criminals who was hanged insulted him, saying, “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us!” But the other answered, and rebuking him said, “Don’t you even fear God, seeing you are under the same condemnation? The sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was torn in two. Jesus, crying with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” Having said this, he breathed his last. When the centurion saw what was done, he glorified God, saying, “Certainly this was a righteous man.” All the multitudes that came together to see this, when they saw the things that were done, returned home beating their chests. All his acquaintances and the women who followed with him from Galilee stood at a distance, watching these things.

The Story.

Jesus has been beaten, whipped, crowned with thorns, condemned. Too weakened to carry his cross all the way, they force a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, to carry it behind him. Then they arrive at the place called The Skull, Golgotha in Hebrew. "When they had come to the place called Calvary, there they crucified Him, and the criminals, one on the right hand and the other on the left. Then Jesus said, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do.' And they divided His garments and cast lots." (Luke, chapter 23, verses 33 to 34)

Jesus' first words on the cross are not a curse. Not a cry for revenge. As they drive nails through his hands, he prays for his executioners: "Father, forgive them."

What This Reveals About Jesus.

All around, people mock him. The leaders: "He saved others; let Him save Himself if He is the Christ." The soldiers: "If You are the King of the Jews, save Yourself!" And it is true: Jesus could have come down from the cross. But he could not save himself and save us at the same time. It was not the nails holding Jesus to the cross; it was love.

Two criminals are crucified with him. One insults him. The other rebukes him: "And we indeed justly, for we receive the due reward of our deeds; but this Man has done nothing wrong." Then he turns to Jesus: "Then he said to Jesus, 'Lord, remember me when You come into Your kingdom.' And Jesus said to him, 'Assuredly, I say to you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.'" (Luke, chapter 23, verses 42 to 43)

This man was never baptized. He never followed Jesus on the roads, never did good works to repair his faults. He has only a few hours left to live, nailed to a cross. He has nothing to offer except a prayer of faith. And Jesus promises him paradise, today.

There were three crosses on that hill: on one, a man died in his sin; on another, a man died to his sin; and on the one in the middle, a man died for sin.

For Your Life.

At Jesus' death, the veil of the temple tears in two from top to bottom (Luke, chapter 23, verse 45). This veil separated the Holy of Holies, God's presence, from the rest of the people. Only the high priest could enter there, once a year. Now, the path to God is open to all.

Look at the cross today, and let it tell you three things.

You are forgiven. If Jesus could pray for those nailing him, there is no sin his blood cannot cover.

It is never too late. The criminal was saved in his final hour. While there is a breath, there is hope.

You can forgive. The one who said "Father, forgive them" lives in you. Think of someone you cannot forgive. You may not have the strength, but he does. Ask him to forgive through you.

Put it into practice.

One. Receive Forgiveness. Read slowly Luke 23:34 and Isaiah 53:5. Say to Jesus: "Thank you, what you bore, you bore for me."

Two. Forgive in Light of the Cross. Think of someone you cannot forgive. Pray: "Father, forgive them; and give me the strength to forgive." Repeat it every day of the week.

Three. It Is Never Too Late. Think of someone who seems too far from God. Pray for them, and if possible, tell them gently that it is never too late to turn to Jesus.

To reflect on. What does the cross tell me personally today? Is there someone I need to forgive in light of the cross?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you were nailed to the cross for me, and it was not the nails holding you there, but your love. Thank you for your forgiveness. Remember me, as you remembered the criminal. And give me the strength to forgive as you have forgiven. Amen.

Key takeaway. It was not the nails holding Jesus to the cross: it was love.

Part 6: He Is Alive.

The cross is not the end of the story. Over the next four days, we will discover how the Risen One encounters His own, one by one, and transforms their sorrow into joy.

The Story.

On the first day of the week, very early in the morning, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb. She came to weep, and no doubt to finish anointing the body. She loved Jesus deeply: He had delivered her from seven demons (Luke, chapter 8, verse 2). When all the men fled, she remained at the foot of the cross.

But the stone had been rolled away, and the tomb was empty. She ran to tell Peter and John, who came, saw, and left. Mary stayed. She wept before the tomb. She saw two angels, and even that didn't stop her: "They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid Him."

She turned around and saw Jesus, but did not recognize Him. "Jesus said to her, 'Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you seeking?' She, thinking He was the gardener, said to Him, 'Sir, if you have carried Him away, tell me where you have laid Him, and I will take Him away.' Jesus said to her, 'Mary!' She turned and said to Him in Hebrew, 'Rabboni!' (which means, Teacher!" (John, chapter 20, verses 15 to 16)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

She was looking for a body; she found a living Lord who called her by name.

It took just one word. Not a sermon, not theological proof: her name. "Mary." And she recognized Him. Jesus had said: "My sheep hear My voice; I know them, and they follow Me" (John, chapter 10, verse 27).

The Risen One, the victor over death, in the first moments of His victory, does not appear first to Pilate, the high priest, or the crowd. He appears to a weeping woman with a tormented past. And to her He entrusts the first message of the resurrection: "Jesus said to her, 'Do not cling to Me, for I have not yet ascended to My Father. But go to My brethren and say to them, "I am ascending to My Father and your Father, and to My God and your God."' Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that He had said these things to her." (John, chapter 20, verses 17 to 18)

Notice Jesus's words: "My Father and your Father, My God and your God." For the first time, He calls His disciples "My brethren." The cross has made us the family of God.

For Your Life.

Perhaps you are like Mary: you are weeping before a tomb. Something has died, and you are searching in the wrong place. You are looking for a memory, a tradition, a past. Your tears prevent you from recognizing the One who is standing right beside you.

Listen: Jesus is alive, and He knows your name. He does not speak to you as to an anonymous crowd. He calls you personally, with the same tenderness He showed to Mary.

And note that Mary was the only one who remained at the tomb when the others left. Those who persevere in their search for Jesus, even through tears, end up meeting Him.

Today, take a moment of silence and listen to Jesus speak your name. Then do as Mary did: go tell someone "I have seen the Lord."

Put it into practice.

One. Hear Your Name. Take a moment of silence and listen to Jesus speak your name with tenderness. Write down what you hear in your heart.

Two. Stop Looking Among the Dead. Is there a past, a tradition, or a memory where you are seeking Jesus instead of meeting Him alive today? Give it to Him.

Three. Proclaim It. Like Mary, tell someone this week: "Jesus is alive, and He has changed something in my life." Tell them one specific thing.

To reflect on. Am I seeking Jesus among the dead, in the past or in memories? What changes when I know He is alive and knows my name?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, You are alive! You have conquered death, and You know my name. Wipe away my tears and open my eyes to recognize You at my side. Thank You for calling me Your brother, Your sister. Give me the courage to go tell others: I have seen the Lord. Amen.

Key takeaway. She was looking for a body; she found a living Lord who called her by name.

Day 38. The Road to Emmaus.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 24, verses 13 to 35.

Behold, two of them were going that very day to a village named Emmaus, which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem. They talked with each other about all of these things which had happened. While they talked and questioned together, Jesus himself came near, and went with them. But their eyes were kept from recognizing him. He said to them, “What are you talking about as you walk, and are sad?” One of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem who doesn’t know the things which have happened there in these days?” He said to them, “What things?” They said to him, “The things concerning Jesus the Nazarene, who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people; and how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him. But we were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened. Also, certain women of our company amazed us, having arrived early at the tomb; and when they didn’t find his body, they came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. Some of us went to the tomb and found it just like the women had said, but they didn’t see him.” He said to them, “Foolish people, and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken! Didn’t the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?” Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. They came near to the village where they were going, and he acted like he would go further. They urged him, saying, “Stay with us, for it is almost evening, and the day is almost over.” He went in to stay with them. When he had sat down at the table with them, he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them. Their eyes were opened and they recognized him; then he vanished out of their sight. They said to one another, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?” They rose up that very hour, returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them, saying, “The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!” They related the things that happened along the way, and how he was recognized by them in the breaking of the bread.

The Story.

On the same day, two disciples left Jerusalem to return to Emmaus, about seven miles away. They walked with sad faces, talking about everything that had just happened. Jesus Himself approached and walked with them, but their eyes were kept from recognizing Him.

He asked them what they were talking about. And one of them, Cleopas, told Him everything. Then he spoke this sentence, one of the saddest in the Bible: "We were hoping that it was He who was going to redeem Israel; and besides all this, it is the third day since these things happened." (Luke, chapter 24, verse 21)

"We were hoping." In the past tense. They had hoped. Now it was over.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Jesus did not perform a spectacular miracle to make Himself known. He opened the Scriptures. Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, He explained to them everything concerning Himself in the Old Testament. Imagine that Bible study: seven miles of walking with Jesus Himself explaining the Scriptures to you!

When they reached the village, Jesus acted as though He were going farther. He did not impose Himself. But they urged Him: "Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is far spent." And at the table, He took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them. "Then their eyes were opened and they recognized Him; and He vanished from their sight. And they said to one another, 'Did not our heart burn within us while He talked with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?'" (Luke, chapter 24, verses 31 to 32)

"Did not our heart burn within us?" The Word had lit a fire in them before they even understood who was speaking to them.

For Your Life.

Jesus sometimes walks beside you in your disappointment, even when you do not recognize Him.

Perhaps you are on the road to Emmaus. You are leaving Jerusalem, the place of your faith, the church, your dreams. You say: "We were hoping..." I was hoping my marriage would hold together, that this healing would come, that this project would succeed, that God would intervene. And you walk on with a sad face.

These two disciples were disappointed because Jesus had not done what they expected. They hoped for a political deliverer; He had come for a far greater liberation. Their disappointment came from their expectations, not from Jesus's failure. Often, our greatest disappointments are the place where God prepares a revelation greater than our expectations.

Notice what changed everything: the Word that makes the heart burn, and the broken bread. The Bible and communion. These are still today the places where we recognize Jesus.

And the end of the story is wonderful: "And they rose up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem." At night, seven miles in the opposite direction. Disappointment had driven them away; meeting Him brought them back.

Today, tell Jesus what you "were hoping" for. Then open your Bible and ask Him to set your heart on fire again. Invite Him: "Stay with us, for it is toward evening."

Put it into practice.

One. Tell What You Were Hoping For. Write down the disappointment you carry: "I was hoping that..." Then present it to Jesus who walks with you.

Two. Let the Word Burn. Choose a passage of Scripture about hope (Romans 8, Psalm 42, Isaiah 40) and read it slowly each day this week.

Three. Return to Jerusalem. If disappointment has driven you away from church or your brothers and sisters, take a step to return this week: a worship service, a phone call, a small group.

To reflect on. What were "we hoping" for that didn't happen as planned? How might Jesus be walking with me in this disappointment?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, You walk with me even when I do not recognize You. You know my disappointments, all that I was hoping for. Open the Scriptures to me, set my heart on fire, open my eyes. Stay with me, for it is toward evening. And bring me back to where You are calling me. Amen.

Key takeaway. Disappointment drove them away; meeting Him brought them back.

Day 39. Do You Love Me?.

Today's reading : John, chapter 21, verses 1 to 19.

Simon Peter said to them, “I’m going fishing.” They told him, “We are also coming with you.” They immediately went out and entered into the boat. That night, they caught nothing. That disciple therefore whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It’s the Lord!” So when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he wrapped his coat around himself (for he was naked), and threw himself into the sea. But the other disciples came in the little boat (for they were not far from the land, but about two hundred cubits away), dragging the net full of fish. So when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there, with fish and bread laid on it. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep. Most certainly I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted to. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you don’t want to go.” Now he said this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God. When he had said this, he said to him, “Follow me.”

The Story.

After the resurrection, Peter went back to fishing. With six other disciples, he spent the whole night on the lake. And they caught nothing. Doesn't that remind you of something? It's exactly like the day he was called, three years earlier (Luke 5).

In the early morning, a man on the shore told them: "Cast the net on the right side of the boat." They obeyed, and the net was so full they couldn't pull it in: one hundred fifty-three large fish. John understood: "It is the Lord!" And Peter threw himself into the water to reach Jesus as quickly as possible.

On the shore, Jesus had kindled a fire of coals, with fish and bread. He prepared breakfast for them.

What This Reveals About Jesus.

Notice this detail: a fire of coals. The last time Peter had stood near a fire, in the courtyard of the high priest, he had denied Jesus three times (John, chapter 18, verse 18). Jesus brings him back before a fire to rewrite the story.

After the meal, Jesus asks Peter a question: "So when they had eaten, Jesus said to Simon Peter, 'Simon, son of Jonah, do you love Me more than these?' He said to Him, 'Yes, Lord; You know that I love You.' He said to him, 'Feed My lambs.'" (John, chapter 21, verse 15)

Three times, Jesus asks him the question. Three times, like the three denials. The third time, Peter is grieved: "He said to him the third time, 'Simon, son of Jonah, do you love Me?' Peter was grieved because He said to him the third time, 'Do you love Me?' And he said to Him, 'Lord, You know all things; You know that I love You.' Jesus said to him, 'Feed My sheep.'" (John, chapter 21, verse 17)

Jesus does not reproach him. He does not ask: "Why did you deny Me?" or "Promise Me you'll never do it again." He asks one question: "Do you love Me?" What concerns Jesus first is not your past performance, but your present love.

And with each answer, Jesus entrusts him with a mission: "Feed My sheep." The one who failed is not benched; he is restored to service. Peter became a pillar of the Jerusalem church and preached at Pentecost to thousands of people.

For Your Life.

With Jesus, your failure is never the final chapter.

Perhaps you are like Peter: you have failed, you have disappointed, and you've gone back to your old nets. You tell yourself that God can no longer use you. That you've lost your place. But Jesus comes to find you on the shore of your life, kindles a fire, and prepares a meal. He does not want to condemn you; He wants to restore you.

Shortly before, Jesus had also restored Thomas, who doubted: instead of rejecting him, He had held out His hands (John, chapter 20, verses 24 to 29). The Risen One rejects neither those who doubt nor those who have fallen.

Today, Jesus asks you the same question: "Do you love Me?" Take time to answer Him, honestly. Then listen to the mission He wants to entrust to you. You are not disqualified. You are called.

Put it into practice.

One. Answer "Do You Love Me?". Write your honest answer to Jesus. Not a heroic promise: the truth of your heart today.

Two. Accept Being Restored to Service. If a failure has benched you, ask Jesus what mission He is entrusting to you now and take a first step this week.

Three. Feed His Sheep. Your love for Jesus is seen in how you care for others. Choose one person you will care for this week: a phone call, a visit, a helping hand.

To reflect on. Is there a failure that makes me believe God can no longer use me? How will I answer today the question "Do you love Me?"

Prayer. Lord Jesus, You know all things; You know that I love You. Thank You for not disqualifying me because of my failures. Restore me as You restored Peter. I receive the mission You want to entrust to me. May my love for You be seen in the care I take of others. Amen.

Key takeaway. With Jesus, your failure is never the final chapter.

Day 40. Go, I Am With You.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 28, verses 16 to 20.

But the eleven disciples went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had sent them. When they saw him, they bowed down to him; but some doubted. Jesus came to them and spoke to them, saying, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” Amen.

Key verses.

Acts, chapter 1, verse 8. But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.”

The Story.

The eleven disciples go to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had designated for them. They see him, and bow down before him. And Matthew adds a surprising note of honesty: "But some doubted." Even on that day, before the Risen One, some still doubted. And Jesus entrusts his mission to them anyway. He doesn't wait for everyone to be perfect before sending them out.

Then Jesus comes near and speaks his final words in the Gospel of Matthew: "Jesus came and told them, 'All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.'" (Matthew, chapter 28, verses 18 to 20)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

It all begins with authority: "All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth." And it all ends with presence: "I am with you always." Between the two, the mission: "Go, make disciples." You are not sent with your own authority, nor alone. You are sent with his, and he walks with you.

Notice also that the mission is not just to make converts, but disciples: people who learn to "observe all that I have commanded you." For 40 days, you have followed Jesus. Now, it's your turn to help others follow him.

Before ascending to heaven, Jesus also promises the power to accomplish this mission: "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth." (Acts, chapter 1, verse 8) The power of the Holy Spirit, to be his witnesses, from your city to the ends of the earth.

For Your Life.

There's an old story, a kind of parable. When Jesus went back to heaven, an angel asked him: "Lord, how will the world hear about what you've done?" Jesus answered: "I've entrusted the message to Peter, to John, to Mary, and to a few others." The angel worried: "What if they fail? What's your plan B?" And Jesus said: "I don't have a plan B."

God's plan to reach your coworker, your neighbor, your cousin, is you. You don't need to be perfect: the disciples doubted too. You don't need to be strong: the Spirit gives you power. You don't need to fear being alone: he is with you every day, to the end of the age.

For 40 days, you walked with Jesus. You saw him born, call, heal, forgive, weep, serve, die, and rise. This is not the end of the journey—it's the beginning of your mission.

To finish, do three things. Reread the key phrases from these 40 days and choose the three that touched you most. Write down the name of one person you want to tell about Jesus. And pray to be filled with the Holy Spirit, to be his witness where you are.

Put it into practice.

One. Your Three Phrases. Reread the "Key Phrases" from these 40 days and choose the three that touched you most. Write them down and display them.

Two. One Name. Write down the name of one person you want to tell about Jesus. Pray for them each day, and ask God for the opportunity to speak with them.

Three. Keep Going. Decide what you'll do tomorrow: start another plan, read an entire Gospel, join a group. The journey continues with him.

To reflect on. Who will I tell about Jesus in the coming days? What do I take away from these 40 days with him?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for these 40 days with you. You have all authority in heaven and on earth, and you are with me every day. I receive your mission: fill me with your Holy Spirit, and make me your witness where you have placed me. Here I am, send me. Amen.

Key takeaway. This isn't the end of the journey: it's the beginning of your mission.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 1
texte:
Day 1. Created in the Image of God.

Today's reading : Genesis, chapter 1, verses 26 to 31.

God said, “Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them. God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.” God said, “Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed, which is on the surface of all the earth, and every tree, which bears fruit yielding seed. It will be your food. To every animal of the earth, and to every bird of the sky, and to everything that creeps on the earth, in which there is life, I have given every green herb for food;” and it was so. God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.

Key verses.

Psalms, chapter 139, verse 14. I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.

Week 1: Who I Am.

For three weeks, we're going to answer just one question—probably the most important one in your life: who am I? And to answer it, we need to start at the very beginning, before the fall, before your wounds, before your mistakes: in God's heart.

What the Word Says.

On the sixth day of creation, God does something different. For everything else, he said "let there be light," "let the earth bring forth." For the human being, he consults with himself: "Then God said, 'Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness, so that they may rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky, over the livestock and all the wild animals, and over all the creatures that move along the ground.' So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them." (Genesis, chapter 1, verses 26 to 27)

You're not an accident of evolution, not a mistake of your parents, not a number in a statistic. You bear God's imprint. Like a coin bears the face of the king, your life bears the image of your Creator: your capacity to love, to create, to think, to choose, to govern, to connect with God.

And when God looked at the humanity he had just created, he didn't say "good." He said: "God saw all that he had made, and it was very good. And there was evening, and there was morning—the sixth day." (Genesis, chapter 1, verse 31)

Michelangelo is credited with saying something like this about his famous statue of David: "I simply removed the marble that wasn't David." God does something similar with you. He doesn't want to make you into someone else. He wants to remove everything that isn't you—everything that sin, lies, and wounds have added—to reveal the person he thought of before you were even born.

David, the king, understood this as he reflected on his own life: "I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made; your works are wonderful, I know that full well." (Psalm, chapter 139, verse 14)

It's not pride to say that. Pride is boasting about what you've done. Here, we're praising God for what he has done. To despise the work is to despise the artist.

You may not be a finished masterpiece, but you are God's masterpiece in progress.

Put it into practice.

One. The Mirror Test. Stand in front of a mirror and read aloud Psalm 139:14. Then thank God for three specific things about your body or character, even those you don't fully love yet.

Two. Change One Sentence. Find the negative sentence you say most often about yourself ("I'm useless," "I never succeed"). Write down what God says instead, and every time it comes back today, replace it.

Three. If You Have Children or Young People Around You. Tell one of them today a sentence that builds their identity: "You have value, God wanted you." What a child hears from their parents often becomes their inner voice.

To reflect on. What negative sentence about myself do I repeat most often, and what does God say instead?

Prayer. Father, thank you for creating me in your image. Forgive me for the times I've despised your work. I praise you that I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Remove everything that isn't me, and reveal the person you thought of. Amen.

Key takeaway. I am not an accident: I bear God's imprint.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 2
texte:
Day 2. What Sin Has Broken, What the Cross Has Redeemed.

Today's reading : Genesis, chapter 3, verses 1 to 15.

Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it. You shall not touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t really die, for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too. Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves. They heard the LORD God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden. The LORD God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?” The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.” God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?” The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” The LORD God said to the woman, “What have you done?” The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” The LORD God said to the serpent, “Because you have done this, you are cursed above all livestock, and above every animal of the field. You shall go on your belly and you shall eat dust all the days of your life. I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”

Key verses.

Romans, chapter 3, verses 23 to 24. for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,

1 Peter, chapter 1, verses 18 to 19. knowing that you were redeemed, not with corruptible things like silver or gold, from the useless way of life handed down from your fathers, but with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish or spot, the blood of Christ,

The Context.

Yesterday we saw the original design: the human being created in God's image, "very good." But something broke. The serpent planted a doubt in Eve's heart: "Did God really say...?" And the first sin didn't start with fruit, but with a question about God's goodness.

After disobedience, Adam and Eve's first reaction is to hide. "Then the man and his wife heard the sound of the Lord God as he was walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and they hid from the Lord God among the trees of the garden. But the Lord God called to the man, 'Where are you?'" (Genesis, chapter 3, verses 8 to 9)

What the Word Says.

Sin broke three relationships. With God: they hide from him. With themselves: they discover they're naked and feel ashamed. With others: Adam blames Eve, Eve blames the serpent. Shame, fear, and accusation entered the world, and they're still there in our lives.

And Paul leaves no one out: "for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus." (Romans, chapter 3, verses 23 to 24)

But look at the second part of the verse: "justified freely by his grace." From Genesis 3 on, God takes the initiative. He's the one who seeks the man: "Where are you?" It's not the question of a God who doesn't know, it's the call of a Father who wants his child to come out of hiding. And in that very chapter, God promises that a descendant of the woman will crush the serpent's head: it's the first promise of Jesus in the Bible.

Imagine a fifty-dollar bill. If I crumple it, step on it, soil it, how much is it worth? Still fifty dollars. Its value doesn't come from its condition, but from what's written on it. Sin has crumpled you, soiled you, damaged you. But your value has never disappeared, because God paid a price for you: "For you know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life handed down to you from your ancestors, but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or defect." (1 Peter, chapter 1, verses 18 to 19)

Your value is measured by the price God paid for you. And he paid it with the blood of his Son.
