Put it into practice.

One. Come Out of Hiding. Take ten minutes alone with God and honestly answer his question: "Where are you?" Tell him what you're hiding, what you're ashamed of, without justifying yourself or blaming anyone else.

Two. Stop the Cycle of Blame. Adam blamed Eve, Eve blamed the serpent. Is there a situation where you're putting all the blame on others? Take your share of responsibility before God, and if possible before the person involved.

Three. Remember the Price. Write on a piece of paper: "I have been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ" (1 Peter, chapter 1, verses 18 to 19) and slip it into your wallet. When you feel worthless, look at the price paid for you.

To reflect on. Is there an area of my life where I still "hide" from God out of shame or fear?

Prayer. Lord, you call me as you called Adam: "Where are you?" I come out of hiding. I confess what shames me. Thank you for redeeming me, not with gold or silver, but with the precious blood of Jesus. Amen.

Key takeaway. My value is measured by the price God paid for me.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 3
texte:
Day 3. Born Again.

Today's reading : John, chapter 3, verses 1 to 16.

Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher who has come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do, unless God is with him.” Jesus answered him, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom.” Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?” Jesus answered, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born of water and Spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom. That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit. Don’t marvel that I said to you, ‘You must all be born anew.’ The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.” Nicodemus answered him, “How can these things be?” Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel, and don’t understand these things? Most certainly I tell you, we speak that which we know and testify of that which we have seen, and you don’t receive our witness. If I told you earthly things and you don’t believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? No one has ascended into heaven but he who descended out of heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.

Key verses.

1 Peter, chapter 1, verse 23. having been born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, through the word of God, which lives and remains forever.

The Context.

Nicodemus is an impressive man: a Pharisee, a teacher of the law, a member of the Sanhedrin, the great council of Israel. If anyone thinks they're in good standing with God, it's him. He comes to see Jesus at night, maybe so he won't be seen, and starts with a polite compliment. Jesus gets straight to the point: "Jesus replied, 'Very truly I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless they are born again.'" (John, chapter 3, verse 3)

What the Word Says.

Nicodemus doesn't understand: "How can someone be born when they are old?" Jesus explains that it's not a physical birth but a spiritual one: "Jesus answered, 'Very truly I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God unless they are born of water and the Spirit. Flesh gives birth to flesh, but the Spirit gives birth to spirit.'" (John, chapter 3, verses 5 to 6)

What Jesus is announcing is not an improvement, it's a birth. Religion tries to make a man better; Jesus makes him new. You don't become a Christian by adding a few good habits to your life, but by receiving a new life that comes from God.

Think of a caterpillar. No matter how hard it tries, it will never fly by flapping its legs faster. To fly, it needs a transformation it cannot produce itself: in the chrysalis, its entire being is reorganized, and a butterfly emerges. Being born again is the work of the Spirit, not your effort.

Peter clarifies how this life comes to us: "For you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God." (1 Peter, chapter 1, verse 23) God's Word is like a seed. When it's received in faith, it produces a life that cannot die.

And at the heart of this night-time conversation, Jesus speaks the most famous verse in the Bible, John 3:16: God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son. Being born again is not a reward for the good, it's a gift for those who believe.

You don't need a new resolution, you need a new birth.

Put it into practice.

One. Be Sure You're Born. If you have any doubt, settle it today: tell Jesus in your own words that you believe he died and rose again for you, that you turn from your sin, and that you receive him as your Savior and Lord. Then tell a trusted Christian.

Two. Tell Your Birth Story. Write in a few lines how you met Jesus: before, the encounter, after. This little testimony will often help you share your faith simply.

Three. Feed the Newborn. A baby needs milk every day. Choose a realistic rhythm for the week: one chapter from the Gospel of John daily, for example, and a church where you can grow with others.

To reflect on. Am I certain that I've been born again? What is my certainty based on: my efforts, or God's work?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for being born again. I don't just want an improved life, I want your life in me. I receive you as my Savior and my Lord. May your Word, incorruptible seed, bear fruit in my heart. Amen.

Key takeaway. Religion tries to make man better; Jesus makes him new.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 4
texte:
Day 4. Adopted as God's Child.

Today's reading : Romans, chapter 8, verses 12 to 17.

So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live after the flesh. For if you live after the flesh, you must die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God. For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!” The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God; and if children, then heirs—heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him.

Key verses.

John, chapter 1, verse 12. But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name:

The Context.

When Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, he uses an image that everyone understands in the Roman Empire: adoption. For the Romans, adoption was a very strong legal act. The adopted child received the name of his new family, all the rights of a legitimate son, a share of the inheritance, and his former debts were erased. He literally began a new life.

What Scripture Says.

John announces it at the very beginning of his Gospel: "But as many as received Him, to those who believe in His name, He gave the right to become children of God, who were born" (John, chapter 1, verse 12). This is not an honorary title. It is a change of status, of family, of name.

And Paul adds that this is not only a legal truth, it is a lived experience: "The Spirit Himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God. Now if we are children, then we are heirs—heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with Him, that we may also be glorified together with Him" (Romans, chapter 8, verses 16 to 17). The Holy Spirit whispers deep inside you: "You are mine." He is the one who makes you cry out "Abba, Father!" Not a slave trembling in fear, but a child running into the arms of his Father.

Notice also the word "heirs." Everything that belongs to the Father belongs to you in Christ. You are not a tolerated guest in God's house, nor a servant: you are family, with the same table, the same name, the same inheritance.

There is an enormous difference between an orphan and a child. An orphan lives with the fear of lacking, fights for his place, constantly seeks approval, and protects himself. A loved child rests, dares, asks, and knows that his father's door is always open. Many Christians are adopted on paper but still live with an orphan's heart.

God did not save you to make you a weary servant, but a beloved son and daughter.

For Your Life.

Test yourself honestly: in your relationships, your prayers, your service at church, are you acting like an orphan who must earn his place, or like a child who already knows he is loved?

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to bear this witness in your heart. Take some time in silence, and simply say: "Abba, Father." Let Him answer you: "You are My child."

And if you grew up without a father, without affection, or rejected by your family, hear this truth: God chose you. Paul says He predestined us "in love to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ" (Ephesians, chapter 1, verse 5). You were not adopted by default; you were wanted.

Put it into practice.

One. Pray "Abba". Take five minutes of silence and simply say: "Abba, Father." Let the Holy Spirit remind you that you are His child. Write down what you feel or what comes to you.

Two. Spot Your Orphan Reflexes. Do you feel obliged to earn your place at church, at work, in your family? Choose a situation from this week and live it as a loved child: without trying to prove yourself, without fear of rejection.

Three. If You've Lacked a Father. If this word is painful, tell God without hesitation and read Psalm 27:10. If the wound is deep, talk to a pastor or someone you trust: healing also comes through relationships.

To reflect on. In my relationship with God, do I live more like an orphan who must earn his place, or like a loved child?

Prayer. Abba, Father, thank you for adopting me. Thank you for Your name, Your house, and Your inheritance. Holy Spirit, bear witness with my spirit that I am a child of God. Heal my orphan heart and teach me to live as a loved child. Amen.

Key takeaway. I am not an orphan who must earn his place, but a loved child who already has one.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 5
texte:
Day 5. Forgiven, Without Condemnation.

Today's reading : Romans, chapter 8, verses 1 to 11.

There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death. For what the law couldn’t do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, that the ordinance of the law might be fulfilled in us who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit. For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace; because the mind of the flesh is hostile toward God, for it is not subject to God’s law, neither indeed can it be. Those who are in the flesh can’t please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if it is so that the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if any man doesn’t have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. If Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is alive because of righteousness. But if the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised up Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.

Key verses.

Colossians, chapter 2, verses 13 to 14. You were dead through your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh. He made you alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, wiping out the handwriting in ordinances which was against us. He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.

The Context.

Romans 7 ends with a cry of despair: Paul describes the internal struggle between what he wants to do and what he actually does, and cries out: "O wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?" (Romans, chapter 7, verse 24). And just after, like a sunrise, he writes: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans, chapter 8, verse 1).

What Scripture Says.

"No condemnation." Not "less condemnation," not "condemnation on probation": no condemnation. For the one who is in Christ Jesus, the case is closed.

Paul explains how this is possible: "And you, being dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, He has made alive together with Him, having forgiven you all trespasses, having wiped out the handwriting of requirements that was against us, which was contrary to us. And He has taken it out of the way, having nailed it to the cross" (Colossians, chapter 2, verses 13 to 14). In ancient times, when a condemned man was crucified, sometimes the charge against him was nailed above him. Above Jesus's cross was written "King of the Jews." But spiritually, it was your list of faults that was nailed there. Your debt was paid, in full.

David had already glimpsed this reality: "As far as the east is from the west, So far has He removed our transgressions from us" (Psalm, chapter 103, verse 12). He did not say "from north to south" because north and south meet at the poles. East and west never meet.

Corrie ten Boom, who had known concentration camps and God's immense forgiveness, loved to say that God casts our sins into the deepest sea, then posts a sign: "No Fishing." Many Christians return to fish out what God has already thrown away.

You must distinguish between conviction and condemnation. Conviction comes from the Holy Spirit: it is specific, shows you a sin, drives you toward God, and stops when you repent. Condemnation comes from the accuser: it is vague, crushes you, makes you flee from God, and never stops. One lifts you up; the other pulls you down.

God does not forgive you halfway: when He erases, He erases everything.

For Your Life.

Is there a fault for which you continue to punish yourself, though you have already confessed it to God? You pull it out at night, you recall it when you want to serve God, and a voice says: "You cannot do this."

Today, refuse that voice. Not by denying your fault, but by proclaiming what Jesus did. Say out loud: "There is now no condemnation for me, because I am in Christ Jesus." And if an accusation returns, answer it with this verse. You do not have to go back and fish out what God has drowned.

Put it into practice.

One. Answer the Accuser. When a fault you've already confessed haunts you again, say Romans 8:1 out loud. Memorize this verse today so you have it ready in the middle of the night or when you want to serve.

Two. Tell the Difference. The conviction of the Holy Spirit is specific and brings you back to God; accusation is vague and drives you away from Him. This week, every time you feel guilty, ask yourself: Is this pushing me toward Jesus or away from Him?

Three. If You Need to Make Repair. God's forgiveness is complete, but sometimes a relationship needs healing. If you have hurt someone, take a step this week: a message, an apology, a restitution.

To reflect on. Which fault I've already confessed do I keep "fishing back up" in my mind, and how am I going to answer the accusation?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for nailing to the cross the charge that condemned me. I receive Your complete forgiveness. I refuse the voice of the accuser and listen to the voice of Your Spirit. There is now no condemnation for me. Amen.

Key takeaway. God does not forgive me halfway: when He erases, He erases everything.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 6
texte:
Day 6. Declared Righteous.

Today's reading : Romans, chapter 5, verses 1 to 11.

Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ; through whom we also have our access by faith into this grace in which we stand. We rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Not only this, but we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope; and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us. For while we were yet weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will hardly die for a righteous man. Yet perhaps for a good person someone would even dare to die. But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Much more then, being now justified by his blood, we will be saved from God’s wrath through him. For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we will be saved by his life. Not only so, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation.

Key verses.

2 Corinthians, chapter 5, verse 21. For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

The Context.

Yesterday, we saw that forgiveness erases the debt. Today, we go further. Being forgiven is like leaving the courtroom with a clean record. Being justified is leaving the courtroom declared righteous, as if you had never committed the fault, and even as if you had always done what was right.

What Scripture Says.

Paul sums up the Gospel in one breathtaking sentence: "For He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him" (2 Corinthians, chapter 5, verse 21).

This is what theologians call the "great exchange." At the cross, Jesus took what was mine—my sin—and gave me what was His—His righteousness. He was treated as I deserved, so that I would be treated as He deserved.

And the consequence is immediate: "Therefore, being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans, chapter 5, verse 1). Peace with God. Not a fragile truce that depends on your week, but peace founded on what Jesus did once and for all.

Think of the parable of the prodigal son. The son returns in rags, reeking of pigs, with a little prepared speech: "Treat me as one of your hired servants." But the father does not even let him finish. He cries to his servants: "Bring out the best robe and put it on him." The robe was the sign of restored dignity. The son did not have time to wash, to redeem himself, to prove he had changed. He was clothed.

Isaiah sang of this reality: "I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, My soul shall be joyful in my God; For He has clothed me with the garments of salvation, He has covered me with the robe of righteousness, As a bridegroom decks himself with ornaments, And as a bride adorns herself with her jewels" (Isaiah, chapter 61, verse 10).

God's righteousness is not a wage you earn; it is a garment you receive.

For Your Life.

Many Christians live like employees on probation: they feel they must prove every day that they still deserve their place. When they have prayed well, they feel close to God. When they have fallen, they feel rejected.

But your standing before God does not depend on your performance today. It depends on the righteousness of Jesus, which never fluctuates. That does not mean sin does not matter: you do not live in sin when you wear the King's robe. But your holiness becomes a response of love, not an attempt to be accepted.

Today, when you pray, do not enter God's presence hanging your head like a beggar. Enter clothed in the robe your Father has given you. You are righteous before Him, in Christ.

Put it into practice.

One. Change Your Thermometer. Tonight, instead of rating your day on a scale of 10 to see if God is pleased with you, say: "I am accepted because of Jesus's righteousness." Then thank Him for something specific from your day.

Two. Serve Out of Love, Not Fear. Choose a service at church or home that you often do out of obligation. This week, do it while saying inwardly: "I do this because I am loved, not to be loved."

Three. Let Peace Rule. Romans 5:1 speaks of peace with God. When spiritual anxiety rises ("Is God angry with me?"), reread this verse and breathe slowly while meditating on it.

To reflect on. Do I live my relationship with God like an employee on probation, or like a child clothed in the righteousness of Christ?

Prayer. Father, thank you for the great exchange. Jesus took my sin and gave me His righteousness. I receive the robe You hold out to me. I want to live in peace with You, not because of my efforts, but because of the cross. Amen.

Key takeaway. God's righteousness is not a wage I earn; it is a garment I receive.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 7
texte:
Day 7. A New Creation.

Today's reading : 2 Corinthians, chapter 5, verses 14 to 21.

For the love of Christ compels us; because we judge thus: that one died for all, therefore all died. He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again. Therefore we know no one according to the flesh from now on. Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no more. Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new. But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation; namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning to them their trespasses, and having committed to us the word of reconciliation. We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us: we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God. For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

Key verses.

Ezekiel, chapter 36, verse 26. I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.

The Context.

This first week ends with one of the most liberating verses in the Bible: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. Old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new." (2 Corinthians, chapter 5, verse 17)

Paul writes these words to a church in Corinth full of people with heavy pasts. In another letter, he reminds them that before knowing Christ, some were thieves, drunkards, sexually immoral… then he adds: "And such were some of you. But you were washed."

What Scripture Says.

Notice the word "creation." Paul doesn't say "a repaired creature" or "an improved version." He uses the same word as for the creation of the world. What God did on the first day with light, he does in you through the Spirit: he creates something that never existed.

Centuries earlier, God had promised it through Ezekiel: "I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you; I will remove from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh." (Ezekiel, chapter 36, verse 26)

In 1967, in South Africa, surgeon Christiaan Barnard performed the first human heart transplant. For the first time, a man lived with another person's heart. What medicine learned to do in the twentieth century, God had been promising spiritually for millennia: he removes the stone heart, hard and insensible, and puts in a new one, capable of love, repentance, and obedience.

That doesn't mean you'll never struggle with old habits again. But those struggles no longer define who you are. Your past may explain some of your wounds, but it no longer dictates your future.

Your past is no longer your prison—it's your testimony.

For Your Life.

Maybe you've worn labels for a long time: "the troubled kid," "the divorcee," "the former addict," "the one who had an abortion," "the worthless one." People have stuck them on you, or you've stuck them on yourself. But if you're in Christ, these labels belong to "old things."

Today, write down on a sheet the labels that stick to your skin. Then, one by one, cross them out and write next to each what God says about you: child of God, forgiven, righteous, loved, new creation. Keep this sheet. It sums up this first week.

Here's what you are now: created in God's image, redeemed, born again, adopted, forgiven, declared righteous, new creation. Next week, we'll discover everything you received with this new identity.

Put it into practice.

One. Cross Out Your Labels. Write down the labels that stick to your skin, cross them out one by one, and write next to each what God says about you. Keep this sheet: you'll use it again on the last day of the plan.

Two. Don't Relabel Others. Is there someone you reduce to their past (a brother, an ex, a colleague)? This week, say or write something that sees them the way God sees them.

Three. Celebrate What's New. Write down one thing that has already changed in your life since you've known Jesus, even if it's small. Thank God and share it with someone: gratitude strengthens the new creation.

To reflect on. What label from my past am I still letting define who I am, and what does God say instead?

Prayer. Lord, thank you for making me a new creation. Old things have passed away. I renounce the labels my past has stuck on me, and I receive the new heart you have given me. Let my past become a testimony of your grace. Amen.

Key takeaway. My past is no longer my prison—it's my testimony.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 8
texte:
Day 8. The Temple of the Holy Spirit.

Today's reading : 1 Corinthians, chapter 6, verses 12 to 20.

“All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are expedient. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be brought under the power of anything. “Foods for the belly, and the belly for foods,” but God will bring to nothing both it and them. But the body is not for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. Now God raised up the Lord, and will also raise us up by his power. Don’t you know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? May it never be! Or don’t you know that he who is joined to a prostitute is one body? For, “The two”, he says, “will become one flesh.” But he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit. Flee sexual immorality! “Every sin that a man does is outside the body,” but he who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body. Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.

Key verses.

1 Corinthians, chapter 3, verse 16. Don’t you know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit lives in you?

Week 2: What I Have in Christ.

Last week, we discovered who you are. This week, we're opening the treasure chest: everything God has given you in Christ. And we start with the greatest gift: God himself, coming to live in you.

What Scripture Says.

In the Old Testament, God's presence lived in the Temple in Jerusalem, specifically in the Holy of Holies, a room only the high priest could enter, just once a year, with the blood of a sacrifice. Imagine the shock of the early Christians when Paul writes to them: "Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?" (1 Corinthians, chapter 3, verse 16)

The Temple is no longer a stone building in Jerusalem. The Temple is you. The presence that Moses saw in the cloud, that priests could only approach with trembling, now lives in every believer.

Paul draws a very concrete consequence: "Do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God's." (1 Corinthians, chapter 6, verses 19 to 20) Your body is not an unimportant detail. What you watch, what you do with your sexuality, how you eat, rest, and take care of yourself—it all matters to God's house.

And he adds elsewhere that the Holy Spirit is like a seal on your life: "In him you also trusted, after you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation; in whom also, having believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession, to the praise of his glory." (Ephesians, chapter 1, verses 13 to 14) In ancient times, a seal marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity. The Spirit in you is God's signature on your life: "This one is mine."

You are never alone: you are God's portable house.

For Your Life.

This truth has two sides. First, immense comfort: in the hospital room, at work, in your solitude, in the night when you can't sleep, God is not far away. He is in you. You can talk to him anytime, in a whisper, and he hears.

Second, a call to holiness. Not the holiness of cold rules, but that of someone who knows they're hosting an honored guest. If Jesus were coming to sleep at your house tonight, you'd tidy up certain things, wouldn't you? He already lives with you.

Today, walk through your "house" with the Holy Spirit. Ask him: "Is there a room I've closed to you?" And invite him to fill every space.

Put it into practice.

One. Walk Through Your House. Ask the Holy Spirit: "What in my life doesn't honor you?" Listen, then act on one thing today (content, a habit, words, a relationship).

Two. Care for the Temple. Your body is the temple of the Spirit: sleep, food, rest, and movement matter too. Choose one small, realistic change for this week.

Three. In Loneliness. If you feel alone (in the hospital, at night, far from your family), speak softly to the Holy Spirit who lives in you. Tell him: "You are here." Then reread John 14:16-17.

To reflect on. If I truly took seriously the fact that I am God's house, what would I change in how I live or treat my body?

Prayer. Holy Spirit, thank you for living in me. I am your temple. I open to you every room of my life, even those I had closed. Fill me with your presence, and teach me to live and care for my body as your house. Amen.

Key takeaway. I am never alone: I am God's portable house.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 9
texte:
Day 9. Free Access to the Father.

Today's reading : Hebrews, chapter 4, verses 14 to 16.

Having then a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let’s hold tightly to our confession. For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin. Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and may find grace for help in time of need.

Key verses.

Ephesians, chapter 2, verse 18. For through him we both have our access in one Spirit to the Father.

The Context.

At the moment Jesus dies on the cross, Matthew reports an extraordinary detail: the veil of the Temple is torn in two from top to bottom. This veil separated the holy place from the Holy of Holies, where God's presence was manifested. According to Jewish tradition, it was a thick and enormous curtain. It said to everyone: "No entry."

And it was torn from top to bottom. Not from bottom to top, as if men had ripped it: from top, as if God himself had opened it.

What Scripture Says.

The author of Hebrews explains what this means: "Therefore, brethren, having boldness to enter the Holiest by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way which he consecrated for us, through the veil, that is, his flesh;" (Hebrews, chapter 10, verses 19 to 20) The way to God's presence is open, permanently, through Jesus's sacrifice.

And he draws an invitation: "Let us therefore come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need." (Hebrews, chapter 4, verse 16) Notice the word "boldly." Not with fear, not crawling, not wondering if you have the right. Boldly. And notice the name of the throne: not the throne of judgment, but "the throne of grace."

Paul adds that this access is given to us by the Spirit: "for through him we both have access by one Spirit to the Father." (Ephesians, chapter 2, verse 18)

Imagine the President gives you a permanent access badge to his office with this message: "Come whenever you want." Maybe you wouldn't dare use it. That's exactly what many Christians do with prayer: they have the badge, but they stay in the hallway.

The veil is torn: you don't need to wait in the hallway anymore.

For Your Life.

What's holding you back from coming to God boldly? The feeling of not being holy enough? Fear of bothering him? The impression he has better things to do? Remember: your access doesn't rest on your holiness, but on Jesus's blood. And the throne you're approaching is one of grace, specifically "to help in time of need."

Today, go in. Don't pray at the edge of your lips, like someone who stays on the threshold. Tell him: "Father, I enter boldly through Jesus's blood." Then present to him what weighs on you, without detour.

Put it into practice.

One. Enter Boldly. Start your prayer with: "Father, I enter through Jesus's blood." Then present to him without hesitation what weighs on you most today, like a child knocking on his father's door.

Two. Pray for a Specific Need. Hebrews 4:16 speaks of help "in time of need." Write down one specific need (a job, a child, health, a decision) and present it each day this week, noting the date.

Three. Open the Door for Someone. You have access to the Father: use it for others. Pray today for someone who no longer dares come to God, and tell them you prayed for them.

To reflect on. Do I pray like someone staying in the hallway, or like someone entering boldly?

Prayer. Father, thank you for tearing the veil. Through Jesus's blood, I enter your presence boldly. I approach the throne of grace to receive mercy and help. Thank you for always welcoming me. Amen.

Key takeaway. The veil is torn: I don't need to wait in the hallway anymore.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 10
texte:
Day 10. Free from Sin.

Today's reading : Romans, chapter 6, verses 1 to 14.

What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? May it never be! We who died to sin, how could we live in it any longer? Or don’t you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life. For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will also be part of his resurrection; knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin. For he who has died has been freed from sin. But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him, knowing that Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more. Death no longer has dominion over him! For the death that he died, he died to sin one time; but the life that he lives, he lives to God. Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Therefore don’t let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts. Also, do not present your members to sin as instruments of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God. For sin will not have dominion over you, for you are not under law, but under grace.

Key verses.

John, chapter 8, verse 36. If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.

The Context.

After proclaiming grace, Paul anticipates an objection: "If God forgives everything, why not keep on sinning?" His answer is emphatic: "Absolutely not!" And he explains that grace doesn't just make us forgiven—it makes us free.

What the Word Says.

"knowing that our old man was crucified with Him, that the body of sin might be done away with, that we should no longer be slaves of sin" (Romans, chapter 6, verse 6)

Paul doesn't say that sin has disappeared from the world, or that you'll never be tempted again. He says that sin is no longer your master. Before Christ, you were enslaved: you sinned because you couldn't do otherwise. In Christ, you are free: you can still sin, but you're no longer forced to.

There's a story from India about young elephants that used to be tied with a simple rope to a stake. When small, they'd pull with all their strength without managing to break free, and eventually they'd give up. As adults, strong enough to uproot a tree, they'd remain tied with the same fragile rope because they were convinced they couldn't leave. Many Christians live this way: freed, but still convinced they're tied down.

That's why Paul asks us to change how we see ourselves: "Likewise you also, reckon yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body, that you should obey it in its lusts." (Romans, chapter 6, verses 11 to 12) "Reckon yourselves dead to sin." It's not pretending—it's believing what God has done. Your freedom begins with how you see yourself.

And Jesus made a promise without reservation: "Therefore if the Son makes you free, you shall be free indeed." (John, chapter 8, verse 36) Free indeed. Not halfway, not in theory.

The rope is no longer tied: stop believing you can't leave.

For Your Life.

Is there a sin that keeps coming back into your life, to the point that you've finally told yourself: "I'm just like this, I'll never get free"? Pornography, anger, lying, alcohol, gossip, an addiction?

Today, change your declaration. Stop saying "I'm just like this" and start saying "I was enslaved, and Jesus set me free." Then take action: Paul says to stop "presenting your members as instruments of unrighteousness to sin." Concretely: cut off access, change the habit, talk to a trusted brother or sister, ask for help and prayer. Freedom is already won; now you need to live in it.

And if you fall, get back up immediately. A child learning to walk falls often; his father doesn't disown him. He lifts him up.

Put it into practice.

One. Change Your Declaration. Stop saying "I'm just like this." Say instead: "I was enslaved, Jesus set me free." Write this sentence down and say it out loud each time temptation returns this week.

Two. Cut Off Access. Make one concrete, visible decision: add a filter to your phone, delete a contact, stop keeping alcohol at home, change your route. Freedom is protected by choices.

Three. Don't Fight Alone. Choose someone you trust who you can give an account to once a week. If it's a serious addiction, also ask for help from a professional: that's not a lack of faith.

To reflect on. What sin have I ended up considering as "part of me," and what concrete decision will I make to walk in my freedom?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for crucifying my old self. I am no longer enslaved to sin. I reckon myself dead to sin and alive to God. Give me the strength to walk in the freedom you won for me. Amen.

Key takeaway. The rope is no longer tied: I stop believing I can't leave.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 11
texte:
Day 11. More Than a Conqueror.

Today's reading : Romans, chapter 8, verses 28 to 39.

We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose. For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Whom he predestined, those he also called. Whom he called, those he also justified. Whom he justified, those he also glorified. What then shall we say about these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things? Who could bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, yes rather, who was raised from the dead, who is at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? Even as it is written, “For your sake we are killed all day long. We were accounted as sheep for the slaughter.” No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

The Context.

Paul is not writing these words from a comfortable living room. Just before, he lists everything Christians of his time went through: "tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword." He knows these trials firsthand: he's been beaten, stoned, imprisoned, shipwrecked. And yet, he concludes: "Yet in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us." (Romans, chapter 8, verse 37)

What the Word Says.

Notice the phrase: "in all these things." Not "by avoiding all these things," nor "once all these things are over." Right in the middle of the trial, you can be more than a conqueror.

And what does "more than a conqueror" mean? There's a story about a boxer who wins a championship. He comes home exhausted, his face swollen, and gives his victory check to his wife. He is a conqueror; she is "more than a conqueror": she enjoys the victory without taking the blows. Jesus took the blows at the cross. He conquered sin, death, and the devil. And you receive His victory.

Paul begins this passage with a question that changes everything: "What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?" (Romans, chapter 8, verse 31) He doesn't say no one will be against you. He says: what opponent could win if God is on your side?

And he ends with a staggering list: "For I am persuaded that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor height nor depth, nor any other created thing, shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." (Romans, chapter 8, verses 38 to 39) Nothing. Not your sickness, not your failures, not the devil, not the future that worries you. Nothing can separate you from God's love.

I don't fight to win the victory; I fight from the victory.

For Your Life.

What battle are you walking through right now? A diagnosis, a crisis in your marriage, debt, depression, a lawsuit, a spiritual attack? The enemy wants you to believe that this trial proves God has abandoned you. Paul says the exact opposite: nothing can separate you from His love.

Today, name your battle before God. Then speak Romans 8:31 and 8:37 out loud, putting your own name in: "If God is for me, who can be against me? In all these things, I am more than a conqueror through Him who loved me."

This isn't positive thinking. It's God's truth, spoken in the middle of the storm.

Put it into practice.

One. Name Your Battle. Write in one sentence the battle you're walking through. Then speak Romans 8:31 and 8:37, putting your own name in them. Do this morning and evening for a week.

Two. Make a List of Victories. Write down three times when God brought you through a trial. Read them again when you doubt: the One who did it yesterday will do it again.

Three. Carry Someone in Their Battle. Think of someone who is fighting (illness, divorce, grief, job loss). Send them Romans 8:38-39 today with a personal word, or offer to pray with them.

To reflect on. What battle am I waging as if I had to win it alone, instead of leaning on Jesus's victory?

Prayer. Father, if You are for me, who can be against me? In all these things, I am more than a conqueror through Him who loved me. I trust You with this battle. Thank You that nothing can separate me from Your love in Jesus Christ. Amen.

Key takeaway. I don't fight to win the victory; I fight from the victory.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 12
texte:
Day 12. Seated with Christ: The Authority of the Believer.

Today's reading : Ephesians, chapter 1, verses 15 to 23.

For this cause I also, having heard of the faith in the Lord Jesus which is among you and the love which you have toward all the saints, don’t cease to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, and what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to that working of the strength of his might which he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule, authority, power, dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in that which is to come. He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.

Key verses.

Ephesians, chapter 2, verse 6. and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,

Luke, chapter 10, verse 19. Behold, I give you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Nothing will in any way hurt you.

The Context.

In his letter to the Ephesians, Paul doesn't pray for Christians to receive more power. He prays that they would understand the power they already have: "and what is the exceeding greatness of His power toward us who believe, according to the working of His mighty power which He worked in Christ when He raised Him from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly places, far above all principality and power and might and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in that which is to come." (Ephesians, chapter 1, verses 19 to 21)

After the resurrection, Jesus was raised to the highest position there is: at the right hand of the Father, above all spiritual authority, above every name.

What the Word Says.

And just a few lines later, Paul makes a stunning claim: "and raised us up together, and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus" (Ephesians, chapter 2, verse 6) Not only is Jesus seated above all power, but you are also seated there, in Him. Your spiritual position is not down below, struggling to survive; it's up above, with Christ.

Jesus had already given this authority to His disciples: "Behold, I give you the authority to trample on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall by any means hurt you." (Luke, chapter 10, verse 19) And after His resurrection, He declared: "All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore..." He received all authority, then He sent us in His name.

We must distinguish between power and authority. A police officer directing traffic cannot stop a 40-ton truck with his muscles. But when he raises his hand, the truck stops. Why? Because behind him stands the State. It's not his strength; it's his authority. When you speak in Jesus's name, it's not your strength that acts—it's the authority of the Son of God who sent you.

This authority is not exercised over people to dominate or manipulate them. It's exercised over the enemy and his works: disease, oppression, fear, the forces of darkness.

The enemy doesn't fear your strength; he fears the name you bear.

For Your Life.

Many Christians pray like victims: "Lord, the devil is attacking me, do something." God invites us to also pray as sons and daughters who have received authority: "In the name of Jesus, I resist fear. In the name of Jesus, I refuse this lie. In the name of Jesus, I declare that this house belongs to God."

This authority doesn't come from pride but from submission: you have authority only if you yourself are under Jesus's authority. Today, start by submitting to Him. Then identify one area of your life where the enemy has set up: fear, division, oppression. And speak with authority, in Jesus's name.

Put it into practice.

One. Submit First. Before you resist, submit (James, chapter 4, verse 7). Start your prayer with: "Jesus, You are my Lord, I place myself under Your authority." Spiritual authority comes from submission.

Two. Take Authority Over One Specific Area. Identify one domain where the enemy has established himself (fear, conflicts, nightmares, discouragement). Pray with calm: "In the name of Jesus, I resist... and I declare that this domain belongs to God."

Three. Bless Your Home. If you live with family, take a moment to pray in each room of your home and declare God's peace. Do this with your children if possible: they'll learn that prayer has authority.

To reflect on. In what area am I still praying like a victim, when Jesus has given me authority?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank You for seating me with You in the heavenly places. I submit myself to You, and I take the authority You have given me. In the name of Jesus, I resist the enemy in my life, my family, and my home. All power belongs to You. Amen.

Key takeaway. The enemy doesn't fear my strength; he fears the name I bear.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 13
texte:
Day 13. Baptized with the Holy Spirit.

Today's reading : Acts, chapter 2, verses 1 to 21.

Now when the day of Pentecost had come, they were all with one accord in one place. Suddenly there came from the sky a sound like the rushing of a mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak. Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men, from every nation under the sky. When this sound was heard, the multitude came together and were bewildered, because everyone heard them speaking in his own language. They were all amazed and marveled, saying to one another, “Behold, aren’t all these who speak Galileans? How do we hear, everyone in our own native language? Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and people from Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, the parts of Libya around Cyrene, visitors from Rome, both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians—we hear them speaking in our languages the mighty works of God!” They were all amazed and were perplexed, saying to one another, “What does this mean?” Others, mocking, said, “They are filled with new wine.” But Peter, standing up with the eleven, lifted up his voice and spoke out to them, “You men of Judea and all you who dwell at Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and listen to my words. For these aren’t drunken, as you suppose, seeing it is only the third hour of the day. But this is what has been spoken through the prophet Joel: ‘It will be in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your young men will see visions. Your old men will dream dreams. Yes, and on my servants and on my handmaidens in those days, I will pour out my Spirit, and they will prophesy. I will show wonders in the sky above, and signs on the earth beneath: blood, and fire, and billows of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and glorious day of the Lord comes. It will be that whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.’

Key verses.

Acts, chapter 1, verse 8. But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.”

Acts, chapter 2, verses 38 to 39. Peter said to them, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is to you and to your children, and to all who are far off, even as many as the Lord our God will call to himself.”

The Context.

Before ascending to heaven, Jesus gives His disciples one final command: don't start the mission right away. Wait. "But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you shall be My witnesses both in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and even to the remotest part of the earth." (Acts, chapter 1, verse 8)

Yet these men had spent three years with Jesus. They had seen the miracles, heard the teachings, seen the empty tomb. They believed. And Jesus told them: you're still missing something—power from on high.

What Scripture Says.

Ten days later, on the day of Pentecost, as they gathered and prayed: "And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit was giving them utterance." (Acts, chapter 2, verse 4)

The result was spectacular. Peter, who had denied Jesus before a servant girl just weeks earlier, stands before thousands and preaches with incredible boldness. That day, about three thousand people converted. The difference between the Peter of the denial and the Peter of Pentecost is the baptism of the Holy Spirit.

And this experience wasn't just for the apostles. Peter makes it clear to the crowd: "Peter said to them, 'Repent, and each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins; and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and your children and for all who are far off, as many as the Lord our God will call to Himself.'" (Acts, chapter 2, verses 38 to 39) "For you, your children, and all who are far off." That means you, today.

In the book of Acts, this experience repeats: in Samaria, at Cornelius's house, in Ephesus. Paul meets disciples there and asks them a question: "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?" They said to him, "We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit." (Acts, chapter 19, verse 2) Then he laid his hands on them, and the Holy Spirit came upon them: they spoke in tongues and prophesied.

In 1906, in Los Angeles, in a modest building on Azusa Street, a group of believers around an African-American preacher, William Seymour, began to pray to receive the Holy Spirit as on the day of Pentecost. What happened there marked the beginning of the Pentecostal movement, which today counts hundreds of millions of Christians around the world. The same Spirit, the same promise.

The Holy Spirit is not an option for special Christians: it's the power promised to every believer.

For Your Life.

Have you been baptized in the Holy Spirit? This isn't a question to judge you—it's an invitation. Jesus made a simple promise: "If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him."

Today, ask Him. Simply, with faith, like a child asking his father. Open your mouth to praise God, and let the Spirit give you new words. Don't be afraid: your Father won't give you a serpent when you ask Him for a fish.

And if you've already received it, remember that Paul urges: "be filled with the Spirit." You can be filled again and again. The disciples, filled at Pentecost, are filled again a few chapters later.

Put it into practice.

One. Ask. If you haven't yet received the baptism of the Holy Spirit, take time alone or with a leader from your church. Read Luke 11:13, ask simply, then open your mouth to praise God without fear.

Two. If You've Already Received It. Paul says "be filled"—it's continuous. This week, take five minutes each day to pray in the Spirit and praise God, even in your car or while walking.

Three. To Testify. The baptism of the Holy Spirit gives power to be a witness (Acts, chapter 1, verse 8). Ask God for an opportunity this week to speak about Jesus, then seize it, even if awkwardly.

To reflect on. Have I already asked for and received the baptism of the Holy Spirit? What's keeping me from asking today, or from being filled again?

Prayer. Heavenly Father, You have promised to give the Holy Spirit to those who ask You. I ask You today, with faith. Baptize me, fill me with Your Spirit and Your power, so that I may be Your witness. I receive Your promise. Amen.

Key takeaway. The Holy Spirit is not an option for special Christians: it's the power promised to every believer.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 14
texte:
Day 14. Equipped with Spiritual Gifts.

Today's reading : 1 Corinthians, chapter 12, verses 1 to 11.

Now concerning spiritual things, brothers, I don’t want you to be ignorant. You know that when you were heathen, you were led away to those mute idols, however you might be led. Therefore I make known to you that no man speaking by God’s Spirit says, “Jesus is accursed.” No one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” but by the Holy Spirit. Now there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit. There are various kinds of service, and the same Lord. There are various kinds of workings, but the same God who works all things in all. But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of all. For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, and to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, and to another gifts of healings by the same Spirit, and to another workings of miracles, and to another prophecy, and to another discerning of spirits, to another different kinds of languages, and to another the interpretation of languages. But the one and the same Spirit produces all of these, distributing to each one separately as he desires.

Key verses.

1 Corinthians, chapter 14, verse 1. Follow after love and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy.

The Context.

The church at Corinth was a living church, where spiritual gifts were manifesting frequently, sometimes in disorder. Paul doesn't tell them to stop. He teaches them how to exercise them properly, with love. And he begins with a fundamental principle: "But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good." (1 Corinthians, chapter 12, verse 7)

What Scripture Says.

"To each one." Not just the pastor, the elders, or "spiritual" Christians. Every believer receives a manifestation of the Spirit. And why? "For the common good." Gifts aren't medals to show off—they're tools to serve.

Paul gives a list: "To one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the distinguishing of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues." (1 Corinthians, chapter 12, verses 8 to 10)

And he clarifies who decides: "But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one individually just as He wills." You don't need to envy someone else's gift, nor despise your own.

Elsewhere, Paul mentions other gifts: serving, teaching, exhorting, giving, leading, showing mercy. Peter sums it up: "As each one has received a special gift, employ it in serving one another as good stewards of the manifold grace of God." (1 Peter, chapter 4, verse 10)

Are these gifts still for today? The Bible never says they ceased with the apostles. On the contrary, Paul writes that we await Jesus's return without lacking any gift, and he urges: "Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy." (1 Corinthians, chapter 14, verse 1) To desire earnestly means to long for them intensely. God doesn't distribute His gifts to those who mock them, but to those who desire them to bless others.

And at the heart of this passage, Paul places the famous chapter 13: love. Without love, even the most spectacular gifts are just noise. Gifts are the means; love is the goal.

Imagine at Christmas someone leaves their gifts wrapped under the tree for years, afraid to open them or use them wrongly. Many Christians have God's gifts still wrapped up.

An unopened gift blesses no one.

For Your Life.

What is your gift? If you don't know yet, ask yourself these questions: What makes me come alive when I serve God? When have I seen God work through me? What do others recognize in me? And most importantly, ask God, as Paul recommends.

Then take action in a healthy setting: your local church, a prayer group, a service team. If you feel God giving you a word of encouragement for someone, dare to share it humbly. If you feel compassion for a sick person, offer to pray for them. Gifts grow when you use them with love.

Put it into practice.

One. Identify Your Gift. Answer three questions in writing: What makes me come alive when I serve God? When have I seen God work through me? What do others recognize in me? Then pray over your answers.

Two. Dare Within a Healthy Framework. Offer your help in a service at your church or a prayer group. Gifts develop through serving, and they're protected when you stay in fellowship and under the guidance of leaders.

Three. A Word for Someone. Ask God for a word of encouragement for a person. If something comes to you, share it humbly: "I believe God is putting on my heart to tell you…" and let them judge.

To reflect on. What gift has God placed in me, and how can I start using it this week to bless someone?

Prayer. Holy Spirit, thank You for the gifts You distribute as You will. I earnestly desire spiritual gifts to bless others. Reveal to me what You have placed within me, and give me courage to use it with love, for the common good. Amen.

Key takeaway. An unopened gift blesses no one.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 15
texte:
Day 15. Laying Hands on the Sick.

Today's reading : Acts, chapter 3, verses 1 to 16.

Peter and John were going up into the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. A certain man who was lame from his mother’s womb was being carried, whom they laid daily at the door of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask gifts for the needy of those who entered into the temple. Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive gifts for the needy. Peter, fastening his eyes on him, with John, said, “Look at us.” He listened to them, expecting to receive something from them. But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!” He took him by the right hand and raised him up. Immediately his feet and his ankle bones received strength. Leaping up, he stood and began to walk. He entered with them into the temple, walking, leaping, and praising God. All the people saw him walking and praising God. They recognized him, that it was he who used to sit begging for gifts for the needy at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. They were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. As the lame man who was healed held on to Peter and John, all the people ran together to them in the porch that is called Solomon’s, greatly wondering. When Peter saw it, he responded to the people, “You men of Israel, why do you marvel at this man? Why do you fasten your eyes on us, as though by our own power or godliness we had made him walk? The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Servant Jesus, whom you delivered up and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had determined to release him. But you denied the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and killed the Prince of life, whom God raised from the dead, to which we are witnesses. By faith in his name, his name has made this man strong, whom you see and know. Yes, the faith which is through him has given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all.

Key verses.

Mark, chapter 16, verses 17 to 18. These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak with new languages; they will take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it will in no way hurt them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover.”

James, chapter 5, verses 14 to 15. Is any among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the assembly, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will heal him who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. If he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.

Week 3: Living Out My Identity.

The first two weeks, we discovered who you are and what you've received. This final week, we put it into practice: how to live out this identity concretely. And we start with a mission Jesus entrusted to all who believe.

What Scripture Says.

After His resurrection, Jesus announces the signs that will accompany His disciples: "These signs will accompany those who have believed: in My name they will cast out demons, they will speak with new tongues; they will pick up serpents, and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover." (Mark, chapter 16, verses 17 to 18) Notice well: "those who have believed." Not just the apostles, not just pastors. Believers.

The first disciples took this seriously. Peter and John go up to the temple to pray. At the gate, a man crippled from birth begs. Peter has no money, but he has something else: "Then Peter said, 'I do not possess silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you: In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene—walk!'" (Acts, chapter 3, verse 6) And the man gets up, walks, leaps, and praises God.

Where does this boldness come from? The cross. Isaiah had announced: "But He was pierced through for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; The chastening for our well-being fell upon Him, and by His scourging we are healed." (Isaiah, chapter 53, verse 5) And Matthew shows that Jesus fulfilled this prophecy when He healed the sick: "He Himself took our infirmities and carried away our diseases." Jesus hasn't changed—He's the same yesterday, today, and forever.

James also gives a framework for the church: "Is anyone among you sick? Then he must call for the elders of the church and they are to pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up, and if he has committed sins, they will be forgiven him." (James, chapter 5, verses 14 to 15)

In the early twentieth century, in England, a former plumber who was almost illiterate, Smith Wigglesworth, became a preacher known worldwide for his healing ministry. What struck people wasn't his eloquence, but his simple faith: he believed Jesus did what He promised.

Let's be honest: not everyone is healed immediately when we pray, and we don't always understand why. Praying for the sick doesn't mean refusing doctors; God uses medicine too. But these mysteries should never make us stop obeying. We don't heal anyone; Jesus heals. Our part is to believe and obey.

You may have neither silver nor gold, but you have the name of Jesus.

For Your Life.

This week, dare to pray for a sick person. It could be a family member, a coworker, a neighbor. Ask them first: "Can I pray for you?" Most people say yes.

Then pray simply, without theatrics: place your hand on their shoulder if they're comfortable with it, and say for example: "In the name of Jesus, I command this pain to leave. Be healed." Ask them afterward how they feel. If nothing changes, don't be ashamed: thank them, and keep praying. And if something happens, give glory to God.

Put it into practice.

One. Pray for a Sick Person This Week. Choose someone sick (family, coworker, neighbor) and ask them: "Can I pray for you?" Pray briefly, in Jesus's name, then ask them how they feel.

Two. Keep Wisdom. Praying for healing doesn't replace medical care. Always encourage the person to continue their treatment and see their doctor: God heals also through medicine.

Three. Persevere Without Shame. If nothing changes, thank the person, never make them feel guilty about their faith, and keep praying in the following days. If something changes, give glory to God together and tell others.

To reflect on. Who around me is sick and needs me to pray for them this week? What's keeping me from offering?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, You bore our diseases and You are the same today. Give me the boldness of Peter and John. I have neither silver nor gold, but I have Your name. Use me to lay hands on the sick, and confirm Your Word with healings, for Your glory. Amen.

Key takeaway. I may have neither silver nor gold, but I have the name of Jesus.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 16
texte:
Day 16. Casting Out Demons in Jesus's Name.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 10, verses 1 to 20.

Now after these things, the Lord also appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he was about to come. Then he said to them, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest, that he may send out laborers into his harvest. Go your ways. Behold, I send you out as lambs among wolves. Carry no purse, nor wallet, nor sandals. Greet no one on the way. Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house.’ If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; but if not, it will return to you. Remain in that same house, eating and drinking the things they give, for the laborer is worthy of his wages. Don’t go from house to house. Into whatever city you enter and they receive you, eat the things that are set before you. Heal the sick who are there and tell them, ‘God’s Kingdom has come near to you.’ But into whatever city you enter and they don’t receive you, go out into its streets and say, ‘Even the dust from your city that clings to us, we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that God’s Kingdom has come near to you.’ I tell you, it will be more tolerable in that day for Sodom than for that city. “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon which were done in you, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the judgment than for you. You, Capernaum, who are exalted to heaven, will be brought down to Hades. Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me. Whoever rejects me rejects him who sent me.” The seventy returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” He said to them, “I saw Satan having fallen like lightning from heaven. Behold, I give you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Nothing will in any way hurt you. Nevertheless, don’t rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”

The Context.

Jesus sends seventy disciples two by two into the cities where he will go. These are not apostles, not "super-Christians": ordinary disciples. He tells them to heal the sick and announce that the kingdom of God is near. They return overjoyed: "The seventy returned with joy, saying, 'Lord, even the demons are subject to us in Your name.'" (Luke, chapter 10, verse 17)

What Scripture Says.

Jesus confirms their experience: "I saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning." Then he adds: "Behold, I give you the authority to trample on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall by any means hurt you. Nevertheless do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rather rejoice because your names are written in heaven." (Luke, chapter 10, verses 18 to 20)

Spiritual warfare is a reality in Scripture. John sums up Jesus' mission in one sentence: "He who sins is of the devil, for the devil has sinned from the beginning. For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that He might destroy the works of the devil." (1 John, chapter 3, verse 8) About a third of Jesus' ministry in the Gospels concerns delivering people who are tormented. And he entrusted this mission to his disciples: "In My name they will cast out demons."

In the book of Acts, at Philippi, a slave girl possessed by a spirit of divination follows Paul for several days. Finally: "This she kept doing for many days. But Paul, greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.' And he came out that very hour." (Acts, chapter 16, verse 18) Notice how Paul acts: he doesn't cry out for hours, he doesn't dialogue with the spirit, he doesn't make a show. He gives a clear command, in the name of Jesus Christ, and the spirit leaves.

Three principles of wisdom. First, don't see demons everywhere: many difficulties come from our choices, our wounds, or our health, and they demand other answers, like repentance, support, or care. Next, don't be afraid: the one in you is greater than the one in the world. Finally, don't exalt yourself: Jesus says to rejoice first that our names are written in heaven. Authority is a tool, not an identity; your identity is being a child of God.

And be wise: deliverance is best experienced with the support of mature leaders in faith, within the context of the church.

Darkness does not flee before the volume of your voice, but before the authority of the name of Jesus.

Put it into practice.

One. Close the Doors. If you or your family have touched occultism (fortune telling, horoscopes, witch doctors, spiritism, "lucky" objects), renounce it clearly in the name of Jesus and get rid of the objects connected to it.

Two. Take Authority with Calm. Pray aloud, without shouting or being afraid: "In the name of Jesus, I cast out every spirit of fear, torment, and oppression from my life and my house." Then fill your home with praise.

Three. Get Support. If the oppression is strong or long-standing, don't face it alone: ask leaders from your church to pray with you. Deliverance happens in the body of Christ, with wisdom and love.

To reflect on. Is there a door open to the enemy in my life (occultism, fear, unforgiveness, hidden sin) that I need to close in the name of Jesus?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you came to destroy the works of the devil. I close every door I have opened to the enemy, and I renounce it. In the name of Jesus, I cast out all oppression from my life and my house. Thank you especially that my name is written in heaven. Amen.

Key takeaway. Darkness does not flee before the volume of my voice, but before the name of Jesus.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 17
texte:
Day 17. Unmask the Lies.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 4, verses 1 to 11.

Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. When he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was hungry afterward. The tempter came and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.” But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.’” Then the devil took him into the holy city. He set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you,’ and, ‘On their hands they will bear you up, so that you don’t dash your foot against a stone.’” Jesus said to him, “Again, it is written, ‘You shall not test the Lord, your God.’” Again, the devil took him to an exceedingly high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. He said to him, “I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me.” Then Jesus said to him, “Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.’” Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and served him.

Key verses.

2 Corinthians, chapter 10, verses 4 to 5. for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ,

The Context.

Just before being tempted in the wilderness, Jesus has just been baptized. The heavens opened, the Spirit descended on him, and the Father spoke: "and the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form like a dove upon Him. And a voice came from heaven which said, 'You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.'" (Luke, chapter 3, verse 22)

And what does the devil do, right after? "Then the tempter came to Him and said, 'If You are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.'" (Matthew, chapter 4, verse 3)

What Scripture Says.

Did you notice? The devil's first attack is not about food, it's about identity. "If You are the Son of God…" The Father just said "You are My Son," and the enemy replies: "Prove it." That's always his strategy: to sow doubt about what God has said. Just like in the Garden of Eden: "Did God really say…?"

Jesus makes it clear: "You are of your father the devil, and the desires of your father you want to do. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, for he is a liar and the father of it." (John, chapter 8, verse 44) The enemy really has no other weapon than the lie. He can't tear you from the Father's hand, so he tries to make you believe you're not in it.

His lies often sound like our own thoughts: "God can't love you after what you've done." "You'll never change." "You're alone." "You have no value." They sometimes settle in from childhood, like strongholds in our minds.

Paul gives us the strategy: "For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty in God for pulling down strongholds, casting down arguments and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ." (2 Corinthians, chapter 10, verses 4 to 5) Pulling down strongholds, bringing every thought into captivity. That means you're not obligated to accept every thought that comes into your head. You can examine it, confront it with Scripture, and if it's a lie, reject it.
