And notice how Jesus responds: not with arguments, not with emotions, but with Scripture. Three times: "It is written."

You don't drive out the lie by fighting it in the dark; you turn on the light of truth.

Put it into practice.

One. The Two Columns. Write three lies you believe about yourself on the left, and on the right three truths from Scripture with their references. Keep the paper with you this week.

Two. Respond Out Loud. Each time a lie returns, respond like Jesus: "It is written…" and proclaim the truth. Do it even if you don't feel it yet: the truth eventually sinks into the heart.

Three. If a Lie Comes from a Wound. Some lies were born from a hurtful word ("you'll never amount to anything"). Forgive the person who said it, and ask God to heal the wound.

To reflect on. What are the three lies about myself that I have believed the longest, and what truth from Scripture answers each one?

Prayer. Lord, I thank you for calling me your beloved child. I refuse the enemy's lies about my identity. I pull down strongholds in my mind, and I bring every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ. It is written… and I believe what you say. Amen.

Key takeaway. You don't drive out the lie by fighting it in the dark; you turn on the light of truth.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 18
texte:
Day 18. Renew My Mind, Align My Words.

Today's reading : Romans, chapter 12, verses 1 to 2.

Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service. Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.

Key verses.

Proverbs, chapter 18, verse 21. Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.

The Context.

Yesterday, we unmasked the lies. Today, we go deeper: filling the empty space. Because an empty mind doesn't stay empty for long. Paul writes: "Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, that you may prove what is that good and acceptable and perfect will of God." (Romans, chapter 12, verse 2)

What Scripture Says.

The word "transformed" translates the Greek verb that gave us the word "metamorphosis." The same transformation as a caterpillar becoming a butterfly. And Paul says it happens through the "renewing of your mind," that is, your way of thinking.

Imagine a field of tall grass. The first time you cross it, it's hard. But if you always pass through the same spot, a path forms, and soon you walk it without thinking. Our thoughts work a bit like that. Old thoughts of fear, shame, or anger have worn deep paths. Renewal is tracing new paths with God's truth, day after day, until they become natural.

Paul also tells us where to direct our thoughts: "Finally, brethren, whatever things are true, whatever things are noble, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report, if there is any virtue and if there is anything praiseworthy—meditate on these things." (Philippians, chapter 4, verse 8)

And what fills the heart eventually comes out of the mouth. The book of Proverbs affirms it: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue, And those who love it will eat its fruits." (Proverbs, chapter 18, verse 21) Your words are not neutral. They build or they destroy, you and others. "I'm worthless," "it will never work," "my children are disasters": these sentences, repeated, become prophecies over our lives.

God gave Joshua a key to succeeding in his mission: "This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate in it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success." (Joshua, chapter 1, verse 8) "This Book shall not depart from your mouth." To meditate on Scripture is not only to read it, but to whisper it, repeat it, declare it.

Change your thoughts, and you will change your words; change your words, and you will change your direction.

Put it into practice.

One. Do an Inventory. Note for one day what you feed your mind (social media, shows, conversations, news). Choose one thing to reduce this week and replace that time with Scripture, praise, or a good book.

Two. The 24-Hour Challenge. For 24 hours, monitor your words. Every negative word about yourself or someone else—catch yourself and replace it with a word of faith or blessing.

Three. At Home or Work. Choose someone you tend to speak negatively about, and decide to speak at least one positive and true word about them today.

To reflect on. What negative words do I speak most often about myself or others, and what word of life will I replace them with?

Prayer. Lord, transform me by the renewing of my mind. Fill my thoughts with what is true, pure, and worthy of praise. Guard my lips: let my words give life, not death. Let Your word not depart from my mouth. Amen.

Key takeaway. Change your thoughts, and you will change your words; change your words, and you will change your direction.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 19
texte:
Day 19. My Value Is Neither My Performance Nor Others' Gaze.

Today's reading : 1 Samuel, chapter 16, verses 1 to 13.

The LORD said to Samuel, “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for I have provided a king for myself among his sons.” Samuel said, “How can I go? If Saul hears it, he will kill me.” The LORD said, “Take a heifer with you, and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.’ Call Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you shall do. You shall anoint to me him whom I name to you.” Samuel did that which the LORD spoke, and came to Bethlehem. The elders of the city came to meet him trembling, and said, “Do you come peaceably?” He said, “Peaceably; I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Sanctify yourselves, and come with me to the sacrifice.” He sanctified Jesse and his sons, and called them to the sacrifice. When they had come, he looked at Eliab, and said, “Surely the LORD’s anointed is before him.” But the LORD said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.” Then Jesse called Abinadab, and made him pass before Samuel. He said, “The LORD has not chosen this one, either.” Then Jesse made Shammah to pass by. He said, “The LORD has not chosen this one, either.” Jesse made seven of his sons to pass before Samuel. Samuel said to Jesse, “The LORD has not chosen these.” Samuel said to Jesse, “Are all your children here?” He said, “There remains yet the youngest. Behold, he is keeping the sheep.” Samuel said to Jesse, “Send and get him, for we will not sit down until he comes here.” He sent, and brought him in. Now he was ruddy, with a handsome face and good appearance. The LORD said, “Arise! Anoint him, for this is he.” Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the middle of his brothers. Then the LORD’s Spirit came mightily on David from that day forward. So Samuel rose up and went to Ramah.

Key verses.

Galatians, chapter 1, verse 10. For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ.

The Context.

God sends the prophet Samuel to Jesse in Bethlehem to anoint the future king of Israel. Jesse has his sons pass by. The first, Eliab, is tall and impressive; Samuel immediately thinks: "It must be him." But God stops him: "And the Lord said to Samuel, 'Do not look at his appearance or at the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the Lord does not see as man sees; for man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart.'" (1 Samuel, chapter 16, verse 7)

Seven sons pass by, and God chooses none of them. There remains one, the youngest, whom they hadn't even thought it necessary to call: David, who was tending the sheep. The one his own family had forgotten—he was the one God had chosen.

What Scripture Says.

We live in a culture that measures your worth by two things: what you produce and what others think of you. Degrees, salary, followers, "likes," appearance. And many Christians bring this system into their relationship with God: I'm worth something if I pray a lot, if I serve a lot, if people notice me at church.

Look at Jesus's baptism. The Father declares: "You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased." At that moment, Jesus had not yet performed any miracle, preached any sermon, healed any sick person. The Father loves him before any performance. He doesn't serve to be loved; he serves because he is loved.

Paul, who had been a very ambitious and highly recognized man, had to choose: "For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? Or am I trying to please men? If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ." (Galatians, chapter 1, verse 10) You cannot serve two masters, and the regard of others is a demanding master. It changes its mind every day, it's never satisfied, and it makes you a slave.

Jesus put his finger on the root of the problem: "How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?"

When you live for the approval of men, their criticism kills you and their compliments puff you up; when you live for God's approval, you are free.

For Your Life.

Ask yourself honest questions. Does my mood depend on what people think of me? Do I post, speak, serve to be seen? Do I feel worthless when I fail or when I rest?

Today, do something good in secret, that no one will see: an act of help, a gift, a prayer for someone. And say to God: "This is for you." Then receive, as Jesus did at the Jordan, the Father's word over your life, before any performance: you are his beloved child.

Put it into practice.

One. The Mirror Test. Ask yourself: does my mood depend on what people think of me? Write down a recent situation where others' regard took up too much space, and give it to God.

Two. Do Something in Secret. Perform an act of kindness today that no one will see, and tell God: "This is for you." Do it again this week without posting about it.

Three. Rest Without Guilt. If you feel worthless when you produce nothing, take real time to rest this week and thank God for being loved even when you do nothing.

To reflect on. Does my sense of worth depend more on my performance and others' regard, or on what God says about me?

Prayer. Father, you look not at appearance but at the heart. Free me from the slavery of others' regard and the race for performance. I receive your word over my life: I am your beloved child, before anything I could ever do. Amen.

Key takeaway. I don't serve God to be loved; I serve him because I am loved.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 20
texte:
Day 20. Called and Sent.

Today's reading : Judges, chapter 6, verses 11 to 16.

The LORD’s angel came and sat under the oak which was in Ophrah, that belonged to Joash the Abiezrite. His son Gideon was beating out wheat in the wine press, to hide it from the Midianites. The LORD’s angel appeared to him, and said to him, “The LORD is with you, you mighty man of valor!” Gideon said to him, “Oh, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us? Where are all his wondrous works which our fathers told us of, saying, ‘Didn’t the LORD bring us up from Egypt?’ But now the LORD has cast us off, and delivered us into the hand of Midian.” The LORD looked at him, and said, “Go in this your might, and save Israel from the hand of Midian. Haven’t I sent you?” He said to him, “O Lord, how shall I save Israel? Behold, my family is the poorest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.” The LORD said to him, “Surely I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man.”

Key verses.

John, chapter 20, verse 21. Jesus therefore said to them again, “Peace be to you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.”

The Context.

Gideon is hiding in a winepress, threshing wheat in secret so that the Midianite enemies won't steal it from him. He is a frightened man in a humiliated people. And it is there that the Angel of the Lord appears to him and says: "And the Angel of the Lord appeared to him, and said to him, 'The Lord is with you, O mighty man of valor!'" (Judges, chapter 6, verse 12)

Mighty man of valor? Gideon must have looked behind him. He answers: "Gideon said to Him, 'O my lord, if the Lord is with us, why then has all this happened to us? And where are all His miracles which our fathers told us about, saying, "Did not the Lord bring us up from Egypt?" But now the Lord has abandoned us and delivered us into the hands of the Midianites.'" (Judges, chapter 6, verse 15)

What Scripture Says.

God doesn't call Gideon for who he is, but for who he will become with him. "The Lord is with you"—that's the key. It's not Gideon's strength that will make him a hero; it's God's presence.

You are not only saved to go to heaven one day. You are called and sent right now. Paul says: "For we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them." (Ephesians, chapter 2, verse 10) God has prepared good works for you in advance. There are people only you can reach, places only you have access to.

After his resurrection, Jesus said to his disciples: "Jesus said to them again, 'Peace to you! As the Father has sent Me, I also send you.'" (John, chapter 20, verse 21) As the Father sent him—with the same mission, the same presence of the Spirit, the same authority. And he made this staggering promise: "Most assuredly, I say to you, he who believes in Me, the works that I do he will do also; and greater works than these he will do, because I go to My Father." (John, chapter 14, verse 12)

The greatest works don't come from great talents, but from ordinary people who say yes to an extraordinary God. Moses stammered, Jeremiah thought he was too young, Peter was impulsive, Gideon was afraid. God doesn't look for capable people; he makes capable those who make themselves available.

God doesn't call you for what you see in the mirror, but for what he sees in you.

For Your Life.

What is your "Midian"? The area where you hide, where you feel too small, too weak, not qualified enough? Maybe God has been speaking to you for a while about a calling: to witness to a coworker, to start a prayer group, to serve in the church, to go on a mission, to write, to sing, to build something for the kingdom.

Today, listen to what God says about you: "The Lord is with you, O mighty man of valor." Then take one step, just one, even if small, in the direction of your calling. Share your faith with a person this week. Dare to say: "May I pray for you?" You are a messenger of Jesus where you live, and he promised: "Lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the age."

Put it into practice.

One. Name Your Midian. Write down the area where you hide or feel too small. Then read Judges 6:12 putting your name in it: "The Lord is with you, O mighty [your name]."

Two. One Step. Choose a concrete step toward your calling this week: offer your help at church, talk about Jesus to a coworker, start a project God has put on your heart, ask advice from a leader.

Three. Pray for Someone Where You Are. At work, school, or in your neighborhood, dare to ask a person: "May I pray for you?" You are a messenger of Jesus where you live.

To reflect on. In what area do I feel "the smallest," when God calls me "mighty man of valor"? What concrete step will I take this week?

Prayer. Lord, like Gideon, I sometimes feel the smallest. But you are with me. I receive your calling: as the Father sent you, you send me. I make myself available. Use me to do the works you have prepared beforehand for me. Amen.

Key takeaway. God doesn't call me for what I see in the mirror, but for what he sees in me.

titre: I Am Not Just Anybody — Day 21
texte:
Day 21. Abiding in Him.

Today's reading : John, chapter 15, verses 1 to 17.

“I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer. Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away. Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit. You are already pruned clean because of the word which I have spoken to you. Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me. I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If a man doesn’t remain in me, he is thrown out as a branch and is withered; and they gather them, throw them into the fire, and they are burned. If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you. “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples. Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, even as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love. I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full. “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do whatever I command you. No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you. You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain; that whatever you will ask of the Father in my name, he may give it to you. “I command these things to you, that you may love one another.

Key verses.

Colossians, chapter 2, verses 6 to 7. As therefore you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, even as you were taught, abounding in it in thanksgiving.

The Context.

We've reached the last day of this journey. In 21 days, you've discovered your identity: created in God's image, redeemed, born again, adopted as a child, forgiven, declared righteous, a new creation. You've opened the treasure chest of all you have in Christ: the Spirit who dwells in you, access to the Father, freedom, victory, authority, the baptism of the Holy Spirit, his gifts. And you've begun living from this identity: praying for the sick, driving out oppression in Jesus's name, overturning lies, aligning your thoughts and words, serving without seeking approval, answering your calling.

But how can you keep all this just weeks from now? Jesus gives the answer in one word: abide.

What Scripture Says.

"As the Father loved Me, I also have loved you; abide in My love." (John, chapter 15, verse 9)

Identity is not a teaching you learn once and for all; it's a relationship in which you remain. Everything you are, you are "in Christ." Not outside of him, not beside him: in him.

Paul expresses it this way: "As you therefore have received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in Him, rooted and built up in Him and established in the faith, as you have been taught, abounding in it with thanksgiving." (Colossians, chapter 2, verses 6 to 7) As you received Jesus, through faith, through grace, walk in him the same way. Don't start with grace and continue by your own efforts.

And he sums up the entire Christian life in one magnificent verse: "I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me; and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself for me." (Galatians, chapter 2, verse 20)

A tree doesn't work hard to develop deep roots. It develops them day after day, reaching down deep to find water. Trees whose roots are shallow fall at the first storm. Those who are deeply rooted hold firm, even when the wind blows hard.

What defines a Christian is not having met Jesus one day, but abiding in him every day.

For Your Life.

To finish this journey, I invite you to do three things.

Reread your list. Go back to the sheet you made on day seven, with the crossed-out labels and God's truths. Add everything you've discovered since. Keep it somewhere you'll see it often.

Choose your rhythm. Abiding in Jesus comes through simple habits: a daily time in Scripture and prayer, fellowship in a local church, worship, service. Concretely choose what you'll keep after this plan.

Declare your identity. Read aloud, in conclusion: "I am created in God's image, redeemed by the blood of Jesus, born again, adopted child of the Father, forgiven and declared righteous, a new creation, temple of the Holy Spirit, free, more than a conqueror. I have the authority of Jesus's name, I am filled with the Spirit and equipped with his gifts. I am called and sent. And I abide in him."

This is not the end of the road; it's the beginning of a life lived out of who you truly are.

Put it into practice.

One. Reread Your Sheet. Go back to your sheet from day seven (crossed-out labels and God's truths). Add what you've discovered since, and post it somewhere you'll see it often.

Two. Choose Your Rhythm. Decide concretely what you'll keep after this plan: a daily time in Scripture, a local church, a home group, a service. Write it down and share it with someone who will encourage you.

Three. Pass It On. Think of someone who needs to discover who they are in Christ. Invite them to do this plan, or do it together as a "two-person plan" in the app.

To reflect on. What concrete habits will I keep after this plan to continue abiding in Jesus every day?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for these 21 days. Thank you for revealing to me who I am in you. I choose to abide in your love, rooted and founded in you. It is no longer I who live, but you who live in me. May my entire life flow from my identity in you from now on. Amen.

Key takeaway. What defines a Christian is not having met Jesus one day, but abiding in him every day.

Day 1. Sent as He Is.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 9, verses 1 to 6.

He called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons, and to cure diseases. He sent them out to preach God’s Kingdom and to heal the sick. He said to them, “Take nothing for your journey—no staffs, nor wallet, nor bread, nor money. Don’t have two tunics each. Into whatever house you enter, stay there, and depart from there. As many as don’t receive you, when you depart from that city, shake off even the dust from your feet for a testimony against them.” They departed and went throughout the villages, preaching the Good News and healing everywhere.

Key verses.

John, chapter 20, verse 21. Jesus therefore said to them again, “Peace be to you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.”

Part 1: The Mandate.

For 21 days, we're going to look closely at a mission. Not a mission invented by a church or organization, but one that Jesus himself entrusted to his disciples. It comes down to three verbs: announce, heal, free.

What the Word Says.

Jesus gathers the twelve. They are neither priests nor theologians nor public figures. Fishermen, a tax collector, a political activist. Ordinary people. And here's what he does: "Jesus called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases. He sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick." (Luke, chapter 9, verses 1 to 2)

Notice the order. First, Jesus gives: power, authority, strength. Only then does he send. He never sends anyone empty-handed. And the mission is clear: proclaim the kingdom of God, heal the sick, and authority over demons to free those who are tormented. Three mandates, one mission: to show that the reign of God has come.

To announce is to speak the good news. To heal and free is to demonstrate it. The message and the signs go together. A word without demonstration can seem theoretical; a demonstration without a word can seem like magic. Jesus unites the two.

And this mandate didn't stay on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. After his resurrection, Jesus says to his disciples: "Jesus said to them again, 'Peace be with you! As the Father has sent me, I also send you.'" (John, chapter 20, verse 21)

Ambassadors.

An ambassador is not at home. He lives in a foreign country, but he represents his own. When he speaks officially, it's not his personal opinion: it's the voice of his country. And behind him stands all the authority of his government. Paul uses exactly this image: "We are therefore Christ's ambassadors, as though God were making his appeal through us" (2 Corinthians, chapter 5, verse 20).

Jesus didn't just send a message: he sent messengers.

For Your Life.

Maybe you've always thought these things were for pastors, evangelists, missionaries. But look at who Jesus entrusted them to first: ordinary people, who weren't finished with their training, who often made mistakes, who even argued about who was the greatest.

You don't need to be perfect to be sent. You need to be with Jesus and receive what he gives. During these three weeks, let him show you how these three mandates can take shape in your life: in your home, at work, in your neighborhood, in your church.

Put it into practice.

One. Write Down Your Fears. Honestly note what scares you or troubles you about these three words: announce, heal, free. Present this list to Jesus; he doesn't send you without equipping you.

Two. Say Yes to Him. Pray simply: "Lord, as the Father sent you, send me. Give me what I need for this mission." Date this prayer in your Bible or journal.

Three. Do It With Someone. Jesus sent his disciples two by two (Luke, chapter 10, verse 1). Invite someone to do this plan with you and pray together once a week during these 21 days.

To reflect on. What makes me think these three mandates aren't "for me"? What does Jesus answer to that?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for entrusting your mission to ordinary people like me. As the Father sent you, send me. Give me your power and authority, and teach me during these 21 days to announce, to lay hands on the sick, and to see lives set free in your name. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus didn't just send a message: he sent messengers.

Day 2. Moved With Compassion.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 9, verses 35 to 38.

Jesus went about all the cities and the villages, teaching in their synagogues and preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people. But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd. Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore that the Lord of the harvest will send out laborers into his harvest.”

Key verses.

Acts, chapter 10, verse 38. how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.

What Jesus Did.

Before sending his disciples, Jesus showed them the model. Matthew sums up his entire ministry in one sentence: "Jesus went through all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom and healing every disease and sickness." (Matthew, chapter 9, verse 35)

Teaching, proclaiming, healing. And, as we see throughout the Gospels, freeing those who were tormented. Peter will summarize it later to a Roman official: "How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power, and how he went around doing good and healing all who were under the power of the devil, for God was with him." (Acts, chapter 10, verse 38)

The Engine: Compassion.

But what strikes most is the reason for all of this: "When he saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd." (Matthew, chapter 9, verse 36)

The Greek word translated "compassion" refers to the viscera, the gut. It's not a polite emotion, it's something that grabs you from the inside. Jesus sees a crowd that is tired, lost, sick, and beaten down, and it hurts him inside.

Jesus' miracles were never demonstrations of power to impress. When the devil offered him to throw himself from the top of the temple to make a sensation, he refused. But before a leper, a widow burying her son, a hungry crowd, he would stop. Compassion was the engine; power was the means.

Compassion without action remains an emotion; action without compassion becomes a performance.

Prayer Before Sending.

Then Jesus says something astonishing: "Then he said to his disciples, 'The harvest is plentiful but the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into his harvest field.'" (Matthew, chapter 9, verses 37 to 38)

He doesn't say "go" first, but "pray." And a few verses later, in chapter 10, those he asked to pray for workers... become themselves the workers sent out. Often, when you really pray for a need, God ends up saying to you: "And you?".

For Your Life.

Before asking God for his power, ask him for his heart. Many people would like to see miracles, but few accept to see the suffering of others up close. The two go together.

Look around you with the eyes of Jesus. In your apartment building, at your work, in your family, on your social feed, there are "sheep without a shepherd": people who are tired, lost, sick, alone. The harvest is not just in Africa or Asia. It's often two meters away from you.

The first step to announce, heal, and free is to let God break your heart for what breaks his.

Put it into practice.

One. Ask Him for His Heart. Pray today: "Lord, give me your compassion for the people around me." Then stay attentive all day: who do you notice that you didn't notice before?

Two. Make Your Harvest List. Write down five names of people in your circle who are tired, sick, lost, or far from God. Pray for them every day during this plan.

Three. A Gesture of Compassion. Choose one of these people and take a concrete action this week: a phone call, a visit, a meal, help. Compassion becomes real when it moves.

To reflect on. Who makes my heart "move with compassion" today? And for whom should it move even more?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you were moved with compassion for the crowds. Give me your heart. Break my heart for what breaks yours. I prayed for workers in your harvest; here I am, send me too. Amen.

Key takeaway. Compassion without action remains an emotion; action without compassion becomes a performance.

Day 3. For Today Still.

Today's reading : Mark, chapter 16, verses 14 to 20.

Afterward he was revealed to the eleven themselves as they sat at the table; and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they didn’t believe those who had seen him after he had risen. He said to them, “Go into all the world and preach the Good News to the whole creation. He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who disbelieves will be condemned. These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak with new languages; they will take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it will in no way hurt them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover.” So then the Lord, after he had spoken to them, was received up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. They went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed. Amen.

The Last Mandate.

Before ascending into heaven, Jesus gives his final instructions. And he doesn't limit them to the twelve: "Then he said to them, 'Go into all the world and preach the gospel to all creation.'" (Mark, chapter 16, verse 15)

Then he adds a promise that concerns "those who have believed," that is, all those who would believe through the testimony of the apostles—so you and me: "These signs will accompany those who have believed: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents, and if they drink anything deadly, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover." (Mark, chapter 16, verses 17 to 18)

Announce, free, heal: the three mandates are there, for the whole Church.

What History Says.

Some think miracles stopped with the apostles. But history tells a different story. Around the year 180, Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, wrote that in the Church of his time, some still cast out demons, others healed the sick by laying hands on them. More than a hundred years after the death of the apostles, in Lyon, in France, the Church was still living these mandates.

And these days, in many countries of Africa, Latin America, and Asia, the rapid growth of the Church is often accompanied by healings and deliverance. What Jesus began has never stopped.

Jesus had announced it: "Very truly I tell you, whoever believes in me will do the works I have been doing, and they will do even greater things than these, because I am going to the Father;" (John, chapter 14, verse 12)

A Relay.

Think of a relay race. The first runner doesn't run the whole race. He carries the baton, then passes it on. The second doesn't start over: he continues the same race. Jesus ran the first part; he passed the baton to the apostles, who passed it to others, generation after generation, until you.

A mandate doesn't expire with the one who received it first.

For Your Life.

Notice the end of the chapter: "Then the disciples went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked with them and confirmed his word by the signs that accompanied it." (Mark, chapter 16, verse 20) The disciples go out, and the Lord works with them. They preach; he confirms. It's not you who heals or you who frees. You, you obey: you announce, you lay on hands, you command in the name of Jesus. He does the miracle.

That takes away a lot of pressure. You don't have to produce results. You have to be faithful. The results belong to God.

Today, the question is not: "Am I spiritual enough for this?" But: "Do I believe that Jesus told the truth?"

Put it into practice.

One. Read the Promise for You. Reread Mark 16:17-18 replacing "those who have believed" with "I who believe." Note what that does in you: faith, fear, doubt, joy? Tell God about it.

Two. Collect the Testimonies. Ask Christians in your church if they've ever seen God heal or free someone. Listen to their stories: faith grows by hearing what God does.

Three. If You've Been Disappointed. If you prayed for someone who wasn't healed, or if you've seen abuse in this area, tell God about it honestly. Ask him to heal your disappointment without quenching your faith.

To reflect on. Do I really believe that the promises of Mark 16 are for today, and for me? What makes me hesitate?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, I believe you told the truth. I receive the baton you passed on to your Church. I don't want to produce results; I want to obey you. Work with me, and confirm your word by the signs that accompany it. Amen.

Key takeaway. A mandate doesn't expire with the one who received it first.

Day 4. Good News, Not Good Advice.

Today's reading : 1 Corinthians, chapter 15, verses 1 to 11.

Now I declare to you, brothers, the Good News which I preached to you, which also you received, in which you also stand, by which also you are saved, if you hold firmly the word which I preached to you—unless you believed in vain. For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles, and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also. For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. Whether then it is I or they, so we preach, and so you believed.

Key verses.

Romans, chapter 1, verse 16. For I am not ashamed of the Good News of Christ, because it is the power of God for salvation for everyone who believes, for the Jew first, and also for the Greek.

Part 2: Announce.

The first mandate is to announce. But announce what, exactly? Many Christians are afraid to talk about their faith because they don't know where to start. So let's begin with the heart of the message.

What the Word Says.

Paul writes to the Corinthians to remind them of what is essential, what he taught "first and foremost": "For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that He was buried, and that He rose again the third day according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians, chapter 15, verses 3 to 4)

There's the Gospel in four statements: Christ died, for our sins, He was buried, He rose again. Not a philosophy, not a list of rules, not a method to be happy: facts. Something that happened in history, with witnesses. Paul even mentions over five hundred people who saw the risen Jesus, most of whom were still alive when he wrote (1 Corinthians, chapter 15, verse 6).

The word "gospel" means "good news." In the Roman Empire, this word was used to announce a military victory or the birth of an emperor: an event that changed everyone's life. The early Christians took it up to announce the greatest victory in history: death has been defeated.

The Gospel is not good advice; it's good news.

Advice tells you what you should do. News tells you what has been done. "Try harder, be better, and maybe God will accept you": that's advice, and it crushes. "Jesus paid for you, He's alive, and He offers you a new life": that's news, and it sets you free.

The Power.

Paul adds elsewhere: "For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God to salvation for everyone who believes, for the Jew first and also for the Greek" (Romans, chapter 1, verse 16)

The Gospel is not just information; it's power. When you announce it, even awkwardly, something happens in people's hearts, because God works through His Word.

For Your Life.

To announce, you don't need to know all theology. You need to know the news, and be able to say it simply. Try: can you explain the Gospel in one minute to a ten-year-old? God loves us; sin has separated us from Him; Jesus died in our place and rose again; if we put our trust in Him, we receive forgiveness and a new life.

And don't be ashamed. Paul, who was beaten, imprisoned, mocked for this message, says he is not ashamed of it. Sometimes we're afraid of bothering people. But if you had found a cure for a deadly disease, would you keep it secret out of politeness?

Put it into practice.

One. Your One-Minute Gospel. Write out the Gospel in five simple sentences, in your own words. Read it aloud until you can say it without notes in one minute.

Two. Practice With Someone Close. Explain it to a Christian friend or your child, and ask them what was clear and what wasn't. You learn to announce by announcing.

Three. A Door to Open. Think of someone who doesn't know Jesus. Pray each day this week for an opportunity to open up and talk to them, and for you to recognize it when it comes.

To reflect on. If someone asked me tomorrow "what is the Gospel?", what would I say in one minute?

Prayer. Lord, thank you for the good news: You died for my sins, You were buried, You rose again. I am not ashamed of the Gospel. Give me simple words to announce it, and the power of Your Spirit to touch hearts. Amen.

Key takeaway. The Gospel is not good advice; it's good news.

Day 5. Peter's Boldness.

Today's reading : Acts, chapter 2, verses 22 to 41.

“Men of Israel, hear these words! Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God to you by mighty works and wonders and signs which God did by him among you, even as you yourselves know, him, being delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you have taken by the hand of lawless men, crucified and killed; whom God raised up, having freed him from the agony of death, because it was not possible that he should be held by it. For David says concerning him, ‘I saw the Lord always before my face, for he is on my right hand, that I should not be moved. Therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced. Moreover my flesh also will dwell in hope, because you will not leave my soul in Hades, neither will you allow your Holy One to see decay. You made known to me the ways of life. You will make me full of gladness with your presence.’ “Brothers, I may tell you freely of the patriarch David, that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Therefore, being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that of the fruit of his body, according to the flesh, he would raise up the Christ to sit on his throne, he foreseeing this, spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that his soul wasn’t left in Hades, and his flesh didn’t see decay. This Jesus God raised up, to which we all are witnesses. Being therefore exalted by the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this which you now see and hear. For David didn’t ascend into the heavens, but he says himself, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit by my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’ “Let all the house of Israel therefore know certainly that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.” Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” Peter said to them, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is to you and to your children, and to all who are far off, even as many as the Lord our God will call to himself.” With many other words he testified and exhorted them, saying, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation!” Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls.

Key verses.

Acts, chapter 4, verse 13. Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus.

The Story.

Fifty days after Passover, the disciples are filled with the Holy Spirit. A crowd gathers. And Peter stands up to speak. Peter—the one who, just a few weeks earlier, had denied Jesus before a servant girl, by a fire. That same man now stands before thousands of people, in the very city where Jesus was crucified, and he boldly announces: this Jesus whom you crucified, God has raised Him.

What Changed.

What happened between the Peter who trembled before a servant girl and the one preaching to the crowd? Two things: he saw the risen Jesus, and he was filled with the Holy Spirit.

Boldness is not the absence of fear; it's the presence of the Spirit.

And the result is stunning: "Now when they heard this, they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the other apostles, 'Men and brethren, what shall we do?' Then Peter said to them, 'Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.'" (Acts, chapter 2, verses 37 to 38) That day, about three thousand people join the disciples.

Notice how Peter announces. He starts from what the people just saw and heard (the tongues, the sound). He quotes the Scriptures they know (Joel, the Psalms). He speaks about Jesus: His life, His death, His resurrection. And he calls them to respond: repent, be baptized, receive the Spirit. Announcing is not just informing; it's inviting.

Ordinary People.

Some time later, Peter and John are arrested for healing a crippled beggar and announcing Jesus. The religious leaders are amazed: "Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated and untrained men, they marveled. And they realized that they had been with Jesus." (Acts, chapter 4, verse 13)

"Uneducated": they had no formal religious training. But it was clear they had been with Jesus. Their strength didn't come from their degrees; it came from their relationship with Him.

For Your Life.

Maybe you feel like the Peter of before: you've already been ashamed of Jesus, you've stayed silent when you should have spoken, you've even denied your faith in one way or another. That's not the end of your story. The same Spirit who transformed Peter wants to fill you with boldness.

Boldness doesn't mean being aggressive or forcing people. It's daring to say what you believe, with love, when the opportunity comes. It's no longer hiding your faith as if it were something to be ashamed of.

And remember: you're not responsible for people's response. Peter spoke; it was the Spirit who touched hearts. Your part is to open your mouth. God's part is to open hearts.

Put it into practice.

One. Ask for Boldness. Pray each morning this week: "Holy Spirit, fill me with boldness today." Then stay alert for opportunities to talk about Jesus, even with just a small sentence.

Two. Dare a Single Sentence. When someone asks how your weekend was, simply mention church or what God is doing in your life. One sentence is enough to open a door.

Three. Invite a Response. If you have a chance to talk about Jesus with someone this week, don't forget the invitation: offer to pray with them, suggest they read a Gospel, or invite them to church.

To reflect on. In what situation do I struggle most to talk about my faith? What does Peter's story tell me about that situation?

Prayer. Holy Spirit, You transformed fearful Peter into bold Peter. Fill me with Your boldness. I don't want to hide my faith anymore. Open my mouth when I need to speak, and open the hearts of those who hear me. Amen.

Key takeaway. Boldness is not the absence of fear; it's the presence of the Spirit.

Day 6. Philip on the Desert Road.

Today's reading : Acts, chapter 8, verses 26 to 40.

Then an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, “Arise, and go toward the south to the way that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. This is a desert.” He arose and went; and behold, there was a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasure, who had come to Jerusalem to worship. He was returning and sitting in his chariot, and was reading the prophet Isaiah. The Spirit said to Philip, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot.” Philip ran to him, and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said, “Do you understand what you are reading?” He said, “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?” He begged Philip to come up and sit with him. Now the passage of the Scripture which he was reading was this, “He was led as a sheep to the slaughter. As a lamb before his shearer is silent, so he doesn’t open his mouth. In his humiliation, his judgment was taken away. Who will declare His generation? For his life is taken from the earth.” The eunuch answered Philip, “Who is the prophet talking about? About himself, or about someone else?” Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him about Jesus. As they went on the way, they came to some water; and the eunuch said, “Behold, here is water. What is keeping me from being baptized?” He commanded the chariot to stand still, and they both went down into the water, both Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the eunuch didn’t see him any more, for he went on his way rejoicing. But Philip was found at Azotus. Passing through, he preached the Good News to all the cities until he came to Caesarea.

The Story.

Philip is in the midst of a revival. In Samaria, crowds are listening to him, the sick are healed, demons come out screaming, and there is great joy in the city. And it's precisely at this moment that an angel tells him: leave all this, go down the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza.

Why? For one person. A high-ranking Ethiopian official, minister of finance to the queen, sitting in his chariot, reading the prophet Isaiah without understanding.

For God, one person is worth a journey into the desert.

How Philip Announces.

"The Spirit said to Philip, 'Go near and overtake this chariot.' So Philip ran to him, and heard him reading the prophet Isaiah, and said, 'Do you understand what you are reading?'" (Acts, chapter 8, verses 29 to 30)

Notice first that Philip obeys the Spirit. He runs. He doesn't think about how to "place" the Gospel; he follows a direction.

Next, he starts with a question. He doesn't give a sermon: he asks the man what he's reading and if he understands it. He shows genuine interest in him. The man invites him to climb up into his chariot.

Finally, he starts from where the person is: "Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning at this Scripture, preached Jesus to him." (Acts, chapter 8, verse 35)

"Beginning at this Scripture." The Ethiopian was reading Isaiah 53, the lamb led to slaughter. Philip doesn't change the subject; he takes the man's question and brings him to Jesus. And a few miles down the road, the man asks to be baptized and continues on his way filled with joy.

For Your Life.

Evangelizing is not reciting a ready-made speech to just anyone. It's listening to the Spirit, taking genuine interest in the person, and starting from their question, their story, their pain, to bring them to Jesus.

The people around you are already "reading" something: a trial, a question about death, a search for meaning, a TV show that talks about redemption, a song. These are their "passages of Isaiah." Ask questions, listen carefully, and you'll often find a bridge to Jesus.

Peter writes: "But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts, and always be ready to give a defense to everyone who asks you a reason for the hope that is in you, with meekness and fear" (1 Peter, chapter 3, verse 15). With gentleness and respect. Not by crushing them, not by mocking them, not by trying to win a debate.

And perhaps God will sometimes ask you to leave the crowd for one person. One conversation on an ordinary road can change a life, and even a nation: tradition holds that the Church of Ethiopia traces its history to this man who returned home with the Gospel.

Put it into practice.

One. Ask a Real Question. This week, in a conversation with someone who doesn't know Jesus, ask a question about their life ("What gives you hope?" "How are you holding up through this trial?") and really listen.

Two. Spot Their "Passage". Note what concerns the people around you: grief, illness, the future, loneliness. Prepare a verse or a small testimony that could answer that particular question.

Three. Follow the Spirit. Ask each morning: "Holy Spirit, who do You want me to go to today?" If someone comes to mind, send them a message or give them a call.

To reflect on. What questions are the people around me asking right now? How could I start there to talk to them about Jesus?

Prayer. Holy Spirit, teach me to listen to Your voice like Philip. Send me to those who are searching. Give me genuine interest in them, help me ask the right questions, and help me start from their story to announce Jesus to them, with gentleness and respect. Amen.

Key takeaway. For God, one person is worth a journey into the desert.

Day 7. Paul in Athens.

Today's reading : Acts, chapter 17, verses 16 to 34.

Now while Paul waited for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw the city full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who met him. Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also were conversing with him. Some said, “What does this babbler want to say?” Others said, “He seems to be advocating foreign deities,” because he preached Jesus and the resurrection. They took hold of him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is, which you are speaking about? For you bring certain strange things to our ears. We want to know therefore what these things mean.” Now all the Athenians and the strangers living there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell or to hear some new thing. Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus and said, “You men of Athens, I perceive that you are very religious in all things. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I also found an altar with this inscription: ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What therefore you worship in ignorance, I announce to you. The God who made the world and all things in it, he, being Lord of heaven and earth, doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands. He isn’t served by men’s hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he himself gives to all life and breath and all things. He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwellings, that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us. ‘For in him we live, move, and have our being.’ As some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his offspring.’ Being then the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Divine Nature is like gold, or silver, or stone, engraved by art and design of man. The times of ignorance therefore God overlooked. But now he commands that all people everywhere should repent, because he has appointed a day in which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man whom he has ordained; of which he has given assurance to all men, in that he has raised him from the dead.” Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked; but others said, “We want to hear you again concerning this.” Thus Paul went out from among them. But certain men joined with him and believed, including Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

Key verses.

1 Corinthians, chapter 9, verse 22. To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some.

The Story.

Paul arrives in Athens, the intellectual capital of the ancient world. Philosophers, temples, statues at every corner. His spirit is "provoked" when he sees the city full of idols. But instead of shouting his anger, he reasons: in the synagogue, in the marketplace, with everyone he meets. Eventually he's brought to the Areopagus, where thinkers like to hear new ideas.

How Paul Announces.

"Then Paul stood in the midst of the Areopagus and said, 'Men of Athens, I perceive that in all things you are very religious; for as I was passing through and considering the objects of your worship, I even found an altar with this inscription: TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Therefore, the One whom you worship without knowing, Him I proclaim to you.'" (Acts, chapter 17, verses 22 to 23)

Paul doesn't start by condemning. He starts by observing and finding a point of contact: that altar "to an unknown god." He says in effect: "You're already seeking something. I've come to tell you who it is you're seeking."

Then he quotes their own poets: "We are also His offspring." He speaks their language, starts from their culture, uses their references. And he brings them to Jesus and His resurrection.

You don't change the message; you change the way you say it.

Paul explains it himself: "To the weak I became as weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I might by all means save some." (1 Corinthians, chapter 9, verse 22)

The Results.

And what are the reactions? Some mock. Others say: "We will hear you again on this matter." And a few believe, including a member of the Areopagus named Dionysius and a woman named Damaris.

Not a crowd of three thousand like at Pentecost. A few conversions, mockery, polite indifference. Yet Luke deems this story worth telling. Because obedience matters more than statistics.

For Your Life.

Your "Athens" might be your office, your university, your friend group, your social media. People who don't know the Bible, who have their idols (money, success, appearance, comfort), and yet are seeking something.

You don't need to start by condemning them. Find their "altar to an unknown god": the need for meaning, the longing for love, the fear of death, the desire for justice. Speak their language. Use examples from their lives, movies they watch, music they listen to.

And accept that not everyone will respond. Some will mock, others will say "later." That's not your failure. Your responsibility is to sow faithfully. God takes care of the harvest.

Put it into practice.

One. Find the Altar. Think of a person you know well who is not a believer. Write down what they're really searching for (meaning, love, peace, security). That's where you can begin to talk to them about Jesus.

Two. Speak Their Language. Prepare a way to explain your faith using words and images from their world (sports, work, music, family)—without church jargon like "sanctification" or "anointing".

Three. Accept the "Maybe Later". If someone mocks you or says "another time", don't get discouraged. Keep praying for them and loving them. Write their name on your prayer list.

To reflect on. What is my "Athens"? What are the "altars" of these people—what they're searching for without knowing it?

Prayer. Lord, give me a vision like Paul's: to see what people are really searching for without realizing it. Teach me to speak their language without changing your message. And when they mock me or put it off, keep me faithful and full of love. Amen.

Key takeaway. You don't change the message—you change the way you say it.

Day 8. I Know One Thing.

Today's reading : John, chapter 9, verses 1 to 25.

As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. His disciples asked him, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” Jesus answered, “This man didn’t sin, nor did his parents, but that the works of God might be revealed in him. I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. The night is coming, when no one can work. While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” When he had said this, he spat on the ground, made mud with the saliva, anointed the blind man’s eyes with the mud, and said to him, “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam” (which means “Sent”). So he went away, washed, and came back seeing. Therefore the neighbors and those who saw that he was blind before said, “Isn’t this he who sat and begged?” Others were saying, “It is he.” Still others were saying, “He looks like him.” He said, “I am he.” They therefore were asking him, “How were your eyes opened?” He answered, “A man called Jesus made mud, anointed my eyes, and said to me, ‘Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.’ So I went away and washed, and I received sight.” Then they asked him, “Where is he?” He said, “I don’t know.” They brought him who had been blind to the Pharisees. It was a Sabbath when Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes. Again therefore the Pharisees also asked him how he received his sight. He said to them, “He put mud on my eyes, I washed, and I see.” Some therefore of the Pharisees said, “This man is not from God, because he doesn’t keep the Sabbath.” Others said, “How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?” So there was division among them. Therefore they asked the blind man again, “What do you say about him, because he opened your eyes?” He said, “He is a prophet.” The Jews therefore didn’t believe concerning him, that he had been blind and had received his sight, until they called the parents of him who had received his sight, and asked them, “Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see?” His parents answered them, “We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind; but how he now sees, we don’t know; or who opened his eyes, we don’t know. He is of age. Ask him. He will speak for himself.” His parents said these things because they feared the Jews; for the Jews had already agreed that if any man would confess him as Christ, he would be put out of the synagogue. Therefore his parents said, “He is of age. Ask him.” So they called the man who was blind a second time, and said to him, “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.” He therefore answered, “I don’t know if he is a sinner. One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.”

Key verses.

Revelation, chapter 12, verse 11. They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.

The Story.

Jesus meets a man who has been blind from birth. He spits on the ground, makes mud, applies it to the man's eyes, and tells him to go wash at the Pool of Siloam. The man goes, washes, and comes back seeing.

Everyone should rejoice. Instead, an investigation begins. The neighbors question him, the Pharisees question him, then his parents, then the man again. They want him to say that Jesus is a sinner, because he healed on the Sabbath.

The man doesn't know theology. He can't answer all their questions. But he says one sentence that no one can dispute: "He answered, 'Whether he is a sinner I don't know. One thing I do know—that though I was blind, now I see.'" (John, chapter 9, verse 25)

The Power of Testimony.

The Pharisees have degrees, arguments, authority. The man has only one thing: what Jesus did for him. And it's unstoppable. You can debate a doctrine; you can't debate a blind man who now sees.

No one can dispute what Jesus has done in your life.

Revelation shows how believers overcame the accuser: "And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they loved not their lives even unto death." (Revelation, chapter 12, verse 11) The blood of the Lamb, and the word of their testimony. Your story with Jesus is a weapon.

Notice also that the man's understanding grows as he testifies. First, he talks about "the man they call Jesus." Then he says, "He is a prophet." Then he defends Jesus before the authorities. And at the end of the chapter, he bows down before him, saying, "I believe, Lord." Testifying strengthens your own faith too.

For Your Life.

You may have never been born blind. But if you know Jesus, you have a story. Maybe he brought you out of depression, restored your family, freed you from addiction, gave you peace through grief, or simply gave your life meaning.

A simple testimony has three parts: what my life was like before I knew Jesus (or before he intervened); how I met him (or how he stepped in); what has changed since. No need to exaggerate or tell every detail. The truth is enough.

And don't be afraid of questions you can't answer. You can say, like this man: "I don't know that. But I know one thing."

Put it into practice.

One. Write Your Testimony. In three short paragraphs: before, the encounter, after. No more than a page. Read it over, remove the jargon, and keep what matters most.

Two. Practice Saying It in Two Minutes. Tell it out loud, with a timer. Then tell it to a Christian friend and ask them what touched them most.

Three. Share It Once This Week. Choose one person and tell them what Jesus did for you, in the course of a conversation. If they ask hard questions, simply say: "I don't know everything, but I know one thing."

To reflect on. What is "the one thing I know"—what Jesus has done in my life that no one can dispute?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for what you have done in my life. I was blind, and now I see. Give me the courage to tell my story simply, without shame, and let my testimony lead others to you. Amen.

Key takeaway. No one can dispute what Jesus has done in your life.
