And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken; and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness." (Acts, chapter 4, verses 29 to 31)

They don't ask for persecution to stop. They don't ask to be protected, or for the leaders to be punished. They ask for boldness to keep speaking, and for God to stretch out his hand to heal and perform miracles in the name of Jesus. All three mandates are in their prayer.

The early church didn't pray for persecution to end—it prayed for boldness to increase.

And God answers immediately: the place shakes, they are all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they speak God's word with boldness.

Prayer, the Engine of Mission.

Throughout the history of the church, great missionary movements have almost always been born in prayer. In 1727, in a small village in Germany called Herrnhut, a community of Moravian Christians began a continuous prayer chain, day and night. It lasted about a hundred years. And from that village went missionaries to the Caribbean, Greenland, Africa, and America—ordinary men and women, often craftspeople, who went to live among the poorest to announce Jesus to them.

Before going to the people, they went to God.

For Your Life.

Paul asks a series of questions that show what's at stake: "How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!'" (Romans, chapter 10, verses 14 to 15)

If no one speaks, how will people hear? And if no one prays, where will the boldness to speak come from?

Today, pray like the church in Acts. Not just "Lord, protect me," but "Lord, give me boldness, and stretch out your hand." Pray for the five people on your list. Pray for your church, that it would be a community that speaks, heals, and sets free.

And if you can, pray with others. That day, it wasn't one believer alone who prayed, but a whole community, "with one accord." There's a special power when brothers and sisters pray together for the mission.

Put it into practice.

One. Pray the Prayer from Acts. Copy Acts 4:29-30 and pray it every day this week, adding the names of the people on your list and the name of your city.

Two. Join or Start a Prayer Time. Attend a prayer meeting at your church this week. If there isn't one, invite two or three people to pray together for 20 minutes about the mission, even by phone.

Three. If You Face Mockery for Your Faith. Don't just pray that it stops—ask God for boldness and love for those who mock you, and pray for them by name.

To reflect on. When I pray, do I mainly ask for comfort, or also for boldness for the mission?

Prayer. Lord, see the difficulties around us, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness. Stretch out your hand so that healings, signs and wonders may be performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus. Fill us with your Spirit. Amen.

Key takeaway. Before you go to the people, go to God.

Day 10. The God Who Heals.

Today's reading : Exodus, chapter 15, verses 22 to 27.

Moses led Israel onward from the Red Sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur; and they went three days in the wilderness, and found no water. When they came to Marah, they couldn’t drink from the waters of Marah, for they were bitter. Therefore its name was called Marah. The people murmured against Moses, saying, “What shall we drink?” Then he cried to the LORD. The LORD showed him a tree, and he threw it into the waters, and the waters were made sweet. There he made a statute and an ordinance for them, and there he tested them. He said, “If you will diligently listen to the LORD your God’s voice, and will do that which is right in his eyes, and will pay attention to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of the diseases on you which I have put on the Egyptians; for I am the LORD who heals you.” They came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees. They encamped there by the waters.

Key verses.

Psalms, chapter 103, verses 2 to 3. Praise the LORD, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits, who forgives all your sins, who heals all your diseases,

Part 3: Heal.

The second mandate is to heal the sick. Over the next six days, you'll discover that this mandate isn't reserved for a few pastors or famous evangelists. It's given to every disciple of Jesus. To you too. And each day, you'll have a concrete challenge to put it into action. But before we talk about what we do, let's look at who God is.

The Story.

The people of Israel have just crossed the Red Sea. Less than three days later, joy has given way to thirst. They arrive at Marah, but the water is bitter. The people complain. Moses cries out to God, and here is the answer: "Then Moses cried out to the Lord, and the Lord showed him a log; he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There the Lord issued a ruling and instruction for them and put them to the test. He said, 'If you listen carefully to the Lord your God and do what is right in his eyes, if you pay attention to his commands and keep all his decrees, I will not bring on you any of the diseases I brought on the Egyptians, for I am the Lord, who heals you.'" (Exodus, chapter 15, verses 25 to 26)

"I am the Lord, who heals you." In Hebrew, Yahweh Rapha. God doesn't say "I can heal" or "I heal sometimes," but "I am the one who heals you." Healing is part of his identity, like love, holiness, or faithfulness.

God doesn't just heal—healing is part of who he is.

And notice how the water becomes sweet: God shows Moses a log, which he throws into the water. Many Christians have seen in this an image of the cross, the log thrown into the midst of our bitterness to make it sweet. It is through the cross that God heals the heart, soul, and body.

This God Lives in You.

David sang: "Praise the Lord, my soul, and forget not all his benefits—who forgives all your sins and heals all your diseases;" (Psalm, chapter 103, verses 2 to 3) Forgiveness and healing, side by side. The God who forgives all your iniquities is the one who heals all your diseases.

And here's the good news that changes everything for the rest of this journey: this Yahweh Rapha no longer just speaks to Moses from a cloud. Through Jesus, he came to dwell in those who believe. The God who heals is not far from you, waiting for you to convince him—he lives in you through his Spirit. When you lay your hand on a sick person, you are not alone—it is the one whose name is "I am the one who heals."

For Your Life.

Maybe you're going through your own "Marah"—an illness, chronic pain, depression. Don't stop crying out to God like Moses did: he is still Yahweh Rapha. And start looking at those around you with a new conviction: the God who heals wants to show himself through you.

God sometimes also uses means: a doctor, treatment, rest. Healing that comes through medicine comes from him too; prayer and medical care go together. But never forget that behind all means, there is a God whose name is "the one who heals."

Put it into practice.

One. Healing Challenge, Day 1: Start at Home. Pray today for yourself if you have pain or illness, then for someone in your home or family. A short prayer: "In the name of Jesus, the Lord who heals, I ask for healing for…"

Two. Proclaim His Name. Write "Yahweh Rapha: the Lord who heals" on a note or as your phone wallpaper. Every time you see it this week, thank him for being the one who heals and for living in you.

Three. Pray and Take Care of Yourself. Continue following your treatments and medical appointments, and pray for your doctors. Always encourage those you pray for in the same way: faith and medical care don't conflict.

To reflect on. Do I believe that healing is part of who God is, and that this God lives in me?

Prayer. Lord, you are the one who heals. I do not forget any of your benefits: you forgive all my sins, you heal all my diseases. Thank you for dwelling in me through your Spirit. Show your healing power in my life, and through me, in the lives of others. Amen.

Key takeaway. God doesn't just heal—healing is part of who he is.

Day 11. By His Wounds.

Today's reading : Isaiah, chapter 53, verses 1 to 12.

Who has believed our message? To whom has the LORD’s arm been revealed? For he grew up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of dry ground. He has no good looks or majesty. When we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he didn’t open his mouth. He was taken away by oppression and judgment. As for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people? They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death, although he had done no violence, nor was any deceit in his mouth. Yet it pleased the LORD to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he will see his offspring. He will prolong his days and the LORD’s pleasure will prosper in his hand. After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore I will give him a portion with the great. He will divide the plunder with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death and was counted with the transgressors; yet he bore the sins of many and made intercession for the transgressors.

Key verses.

Matthew, chapter 8, verses 16 to 17. When evening came, they brought to him many possessed with demons. He cast out the spirits with a word, and healed all who were sick, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying, “He took our infirmities and bore our diseases.”

What the Word Says.

Seven centuries before Jesus, the prophet Isaiah describes a suffering servant who bears upon himself what belonged to us: "Yet it was our infirmities that he bore, and our sorrows that he carried; but we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his stripes we are healed." (Isaiah, chapter 53, verses 4 to 5)

He bore our sins and our iniquities, yes. But also our sorrows and our suffering. And the result: peace, and healing.

Matthew, recounting an evening when Jesus was healing the sick, quotes this very passage: "When evening had come, they brought to him many who were demon-possessed. And he cast out the spirits with a word, and healed all who were sick, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaiah the prophet, saying: 'He himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses.'" (Matthew, chapter 8, verses 16 to 17)

Healing Is Part of the Gospel.

For Matthew, Jesus's healings fulfill Isaiah 53. Healing is therefore not an optional bonus to the Gospel, reserved for a few "specialized" Christians: it is part of the work of the cross. Jesus came to save the whole human being—soul and body.

This changes how you pray. When you pray for someone who is sick, you are not praying on shaky ground, hoping God might be in a good mood today. You are praying on the basis of a price already paid. Imagine someone going to pick up a package that has already been paid for: they don't beg the shopkeeper, they present the receipt. The cross is your receipt.

Paul says that the Holy Spirit is "the guarantee of our inheritance" (Ephesians, chapter 1, verse 14), like a down payment given right now on what is promised to us. Every healing today is a down payment on the world to come, where there will be no more sickness or pain. And God wants to distribute this down payment through the hands of his children.

For Your Life.

It is not your holiness, your experience, or your title that gives weight to your prayer: it is what Jesus bore. A new convert who prays on the basis of the cross has the same basis as a pastor with thirty years of ministry.

So pray with confidence. Not "Lord, if it's your will, maybe…" as if the cross had settled nothing. But: "Jesus, you bore this sickness. By your stripes, I declare healing on this person."

And if healing doesn't appear right away, don't question the cross, and never make the sick person feel guilty. Keep praying, loving, walking with them. The receipt remains valid.

Put it into practice.

One. Healing Challenge, Day 2: Make a Call. Call someone sick today (family, friend, church member). Check in with them, then offer: "Can I pray for you right now, over the phone?" Pray for a minute, with confidence, on the basis of Isaiah 53:5.

Two. Learn Your "Receipt". Memorize Isaiah 53:5 today. It's the foundation you will pray from for the sick throughout this journey.

Three. Change How You Pray. Replace "if it's your will, maybe" with a prayer that relies on the cross: "Jesus, you bore this pain; in Jesus's name, be healed." Practice praying for yourself this evening.

To reflect on. Am I praying for the sick on the basis of what Jesus bore on the cross, or on the basis of my impressions?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, thank you for bearing our sins and our sufferings. By your stripes, we are healed. I no longer want to pray timidly, as if the cross had settled nothing. Teach me to pray with the confidence of one who knows what you paid. Amen.

Key takeaway. The cross is your receipt: don't plead, present it.

Day 12. Greater Works.

Today's reading : John, chapter 14, verses 10 to 17.

Don’t you believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? The words that I tell you, I speak not from myself; but the Father who lives in me does his works. Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me; or else believe me for the very works’ sake. Most certainly I tell you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father. Whatever you will ask in my name, I will do it, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you will ask anything in my name, I will do it. If you love me, keep my commandments. I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive, for it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him. You know him, for he lives with you and will be in you.

Key verses.

Colossians, chapter 1, verse 27. to whom God was pleased to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.

What the Word Says.

On the evening of his last meal, Jesus makes to his disciples a promise that seems almost too great: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father;" (John, chapter 14, verse 12)

"Whoever believes in me." Not "whoever is an apostle," not "whoever is a pastor," not "whoever has a special gift." Whoever believes. If you believe in Jesus, this promise is for you.

And what are "the works that I do"? The disciples had just spent three years watching Jesus heal the sick, open the eyes of the blind, raise up the paralyzed, cast out demons. Jesus tells them: you will do these works. And even greater ones.

Why "Greater" Ones?.

"Because I am going to the Father." While Jesus was on the earth, he was in one place at a time, in one body. In rising to the Father, he sends the Holy Spirit, who comes to live in every believer. Jesus says this just after: the Spirit "dwells with you and will be in you" (John, chapter 14, verse 17). From now on, it is not two hands healing in Galilee, but millions of hands, in every city of the world.

Paul sums up this mystery in three words: "God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory." (Colossians, chapter 1, verse 27) "Christ in you." The same Jesus who touched the lepers lives in you. The same Spirit that raised Jesus from the dead lives in you (Romans, chapter 8, verse 11).

You do not carry a religion: you carry a Person. And that Person heals.

Not an Exclusive Club.

Healing has sometimes been made the business of a select few: the great evangelists, the pastors, the elders, those who have "the gift." It is true that Paul speaks of gifts of healings that the Spirit gives to some in a particular way (1 Corinthians, chapter 12, verse 9). But the mandate is given to all: "those who believe will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover" (Mark, chapter 16, verse 18). The particular gift does not cancel the general call.

For Your Life.

Today, stop looking at yourself: your weaknesses, your lack of experience, your doubts. Look at who lives in you. You don't need to become someone else to pray for the sick: you need to believe that Christ is in you.

And start. The disciples didn't become disciples who heal by reading books about healing, but by obeying: by laying on hands, one person at a time.

Put it into practice.

One. Healing Challenge, Day 3: Pray Face to Face. Choose someone sick in your circle today and pray for them face to face (at home, at work, at church). Ask their permission, pray briefly in Jesus's name, then ask how they feel.

Two. Declare Who Lives in You. Each morning this week, before you start your day, say aloud: "Christ is in me. He who believes in Jesus will do the works he did. I believe." (John, chapter 14, verse 12,Colossians, chapter 1, verse 27)

Three. If You Feel Unworthy. Write down what makes you think this "isn't for you" (your past, sin, lack of training). Opposite it, write: "Whoever believes in me." The promise doesn't rest on your background, but on your faith in Jesus.

To reflect on. What changes in how I see the sick around me if I truly believe that Christ lives in me?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you said: whoever believes in me will do the works that I do. I believe in you. Thank you for living in me by your Spirit. I no longer want to look at myself, but at you, who are in me. Use my hands to heal the sick around me. Amen.

Key takeaway. You do not carry a religion: you carry a Person. And that Person heals.

Day 13. I Am Willing.

Today's reading : Mark, chapter 1, verses 35 to 45.

Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there. Simon and those who were with him searched for him. They found him and told him, “Everyone is looking for you.” He said to them, “Let’s go elsewhere into the next towns, that I may preach there also, because I came out for this reason.” He went into their synagogues throughout all Galilee, preaching and casting out demons. A leper came to him, begging him, kneeling down to him, and saying to him, “If you want to, you can make me clean.” Being moved with compassion, he stretched out his hand, and touched him, and said to him, “I want to. Be made clean.” When he had said this, immediately the leprosy departed from him and he was made clean. He strictly warned him and immediately sent him out, and said to him, “See that you say nothing to anybody, but go show yourself to the priest and offer for your cleansing the things which Moses commanded, for a testimony to them.” But he went out, and began to proclaim it much, and to spread about the matter, so that Jesus could no more openly enter into a city, but was outside in desert places. People came to him from everywhere.

Key verses.

Matthew, chapter 14, verse 14. Jesus went out, and he saw a great multitude. He had compassion on them and healed their sick.

The Story.

A leper comes to Jesus. In those days, leprosy was a sentence of exile: living apart, wearing torn clothes, crying out "Unclean!" when anyone approached. Years without a hand touching you.

He falls to his knees and says: "A leper came to him, begging him on his knees and saying, 'If you are willing, you can make me clean.' Moved with compassion, Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, and said to him, 'I am willing; be clean.'" (Mark, chapter 1, verses 40 to 41)

What This Reveals About Jesus.

The leper doesn't doubt that Jesus can heal him. His question is: does he want to? That's often our question too. And Jesus's answer is unambiguous: "I am willing."

Three actions: he is "moved with compassion," he stretches out his hand and touches him, he speaks. Jesus could have healed with a word, from a distance. But this man needed to be touched. Jesus touched the one no one else touched.

Matthew says it again elsewhere: "When he stepped ashore, he saw a large crowd, and out of compassion for them he healed their sick." (Matthew, chapter 14, verse 14) With Jesus, compassion always ends in action.

The Hands of Jesus Today.

In the nineteenth century, a Belgian priest, Father Damien, volunteered to live on the island of Molokai, in Hawaii, where lepers were exiled. He cared for them, he built houses, he buried the dead, until he contracted the disease himself. He then began one of his sermons with these words: "We lepers…"

Jesus no longer has physical hands on the earth except ours. When you place your hand on a sick person's shoulder and pray, it is Jesus's hand reaching out still, and it is his voice saying still: "I am willing."

Also notice the beginning of the passage: before this healing, Jesus rose early to pray in a solitary place (Mark, chapter 1, verse 35). His compassion and power came from his intimacy with the Father. It's the same for you.

For Your Life.

When you pray for someone who is sick, start with this certainty: Jesus loves this person, and he wants them healed. You don't come to convince a reluctant God; you come to bring the will of a God who has already said "I am willing."

And look around you: who are the "lepers" of today? The elderly living in isolation, the chronically ill whom we no longer visit, those suffering from mental illness, the homeless. Praying for them is good. Drawing near them, sitting with them, touching them with respect and praying with them—that's even better.

Put it into practice.

One. Healing Challenge, Day 4: "Can I Pray for You?". Ask this question today of someone in pain (a coworker with a sore back, a neighbor, a family member). If they agree, place your hand on their shoulder and pray in one sentence: "In Jesus's name, I command this pain to leave."

Two. Visit an "Untouchable". Visit this week someone sick, elderly, or isolated whom people often forget. Sit down, listen to them, and pray with them.

Three. Your Solitary Place. Rise a little earlier one day this week to pray alone, as Jesus did. Ask the Father for his compassion for the sick you will encounter.

To reflect on. Do I doubt Jesus's willingness to heal? Who are the "untouchables" around me whom Jesus wants to touch through my hands?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you said to the leper: I am willing. Give me this certainty when I pray for the sick, and your compassion to draw near those others avoid. Let my hands become yours, and my voice, yours. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus touched the one no one else touched. Today he does it through your hands.

Day 14. Ananias, an Ordinary Disciple.

Today's reading : Acts, chapter 9, verses 10 to 19.

Now there was a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias!” He said, “Behold, it’s me, Lord.” The Lord said to him, “Arise and go to the street which is called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judah for one named Saul, a man of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying, and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias coming in and laying his hands on him, that he might receive his sight.” But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem. Here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.” But the Lord said to him, “Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel. For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.” Ananias departed and entered into the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me that you may receive your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized. He took food and was strengthened. Saul stayed several days with the disciples who were at Damascus.

Key verses.

Mark, chapter 8, verses 24 to 25. He looked up, and said, “I see men, but I see them like walking trees.” Then again he laid his hands on his eyes. He looked intently, and was restored, and saw everyone clearly.

The Story.

In Damascus, there is a man about whom we know almost nothing. Not an apostle, not an elder, not a pastor. Luke simply introduces him: "a disciple named Ananias." And to him, Jesus entrusts an impressive mission: to lay hands on Saul of Tarsus, the persecutor of Christians, who has become blind on the road to Damascus.

Ananias is afraid, and he says so: "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much harm he has done to your saints." But he obeys: "Ananias went away and entered the house. Placing his hands on Saul, he said, 'Brother Saul, the Lord—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.' Immediately, something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized" (Acts, chapter 9, verses 17 to 18)

What It Reveals.

The greatest apostle in history, Paul, was healed and filled with the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands by an anonymous disciple. No one knows about Ananias's ministry before that day, or after. He simply obeyed, with his fear, at a specific moment.

God is not looking for celebrities: he is looking for available disciples.

Also notice that Ananias doesn't perform a long ceremony. He lays on hands, he says why he is there, in the name of the Lord Jesus, and healing comes.

What If It's Not Complete Right Away?.

Mark's Gospel tells a precious detail. Jesus laid his hands on a blind man at Bethsaida, then asked him if he could see anything. The man answered: "He looked up and said, 'I see people; they look like trees walking around.' Once more Jesus put his hands on the man's eyes. Then his eyes were opened, his sight was restored, and he saw everything clearly." (Mark, chapter 8, verses 24 to 25)

Even Jesus prayed twice! He laid on hands, asked a question, noticed progress, and did it again until complete healing came. This is a very liberating lesson: praying a second time is not a lack of faith, it is following Jesus's example.

When you pray for someone, ask them afterward: "What are you feeling? Is there any change?" If it's better but not complete, thank God and pray again. If nothing changes, don't get discouraged and never make the person feel guilty: thank them, and keep praying in the days ahead.

For Your Life.

Maybe you feel like Ananias: unknown, without title, and a little afraid. That's exactly the profile of people God loves to use. Your obedience today could change someone's life, maybe even that of a future "Paul."

Dare to step outside your circle of close friends. Jesus's disciples prayed for people they didn't know: in streets, in marketplaces, in homes where they were welcomed.

Put it into practice.

One. Healing Challenge, Day 5: Beyond Your Close Circle. Pray today for someone you know less well (coworker, neighbor, shopkeeper, classmate). Ask permission, pray briefly in Jesus's name, then ask the question: "What are you feeling?"

Two. Pray a Second Time. If the person says there's an improvement but it's not complete, do as Jesus did at Bethsaida: thank God and pray again. Write down what happens in your journal.

Three. Obey With Your Fear. If God puts a person on your heart and you're afraid, tell him: "Lord, I'm afraid, but I'm going." Like Ananias, obedience doesn't wait for fear to disappear.

To reflect on. Am I waiting to have a title or to stop being afraid before I pray for the sick? What does Ananias's example tell me?

Prayer. Lord, thank you for using simple disciples like Ananias. Here I am, Lord. Even with my fear, I want to obey you. Send me to those who need you, give me the grace to lay on hands in your name, and teach me Jesus's perseverance—to keep praying until complete healing comes. Amen.

Key takeaway. God is not looking for celebrities: he is looking for available disciples.

The Story.

We often talk about the twelve apostles. But Luke tells of another sending, much less known: "After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them two by two ahead of him to every town and place where he was about to go." (Luke, chapter 10, verse 1)

Seventy disciples whose names we don't even know. Anonymities. And here is their mission: "When you enter a town and are welcomed, eat what is offered to you. Heal the sick who are there and tell them, 'The kingdom of God has come near to you.'" (Luke, chapter 10, verses 8 to 9)

Heal the sick and announce the kingdom. Exactly the same mission as the twelve. The mandate to heal was not already reserved for Jesus's apostles of that time. And when they return, they are full of joy: "The seventy-two returned with joy and said, 'Lord, even the demons submit to us in your name'" (Luke, chapter 10, verse 17).

All Called.

James, in his letter, asks the sick person to call the church elders so they can pray for him. That's a beautiful practice. But he adds right away, for the whole church: "Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed" (James, chapter 5, verse 16). Pray for each other: everyone.

Praying for the sick is not the work of the pastoral team, it is the normal breath of the whole body of Christ.

How to Pray for a Sick Person.

Here is a simple way to do it, which you can use everywhere, at work as at home.

First, ask: "Can I pray for you?" Then listen: "Where does it hurt? How long have you had this?" Next, pray briefly, with authority, in the name of Jesus: one or two sentences are enough, eyes open, one hand on the shoulder if the person agrees. For example: "In Jesus's name, I command this pain to leave. Be healed." Then check: "What are you feeling?" If it's better but not complete, pray again. Finally, whatever the result, bless the person, and tell them in one sentence why you believe in Jesus.

No need to shout, make a long speech, or make the person uncomfortable. The power is not in the form, it is in the name of Jesus.

For Your Life.

Jesus sent his disciples two by two. Why not do the same this week? With a friend, a brother, a sister, go out with the intention to pray for sick people: in your neighborhood, at the hospital (respecting the establishment's rules), in the home of an elderly person, at work.

You have had six days of challenges. This is not the end, it is a beginning: praying for the sick can become a reflex of your disciple life.

Put it into practice.

One. Healing Challenge, Day 6: Go Out Two by Two. Organize a time this week with a brother or sister to pray for at least three sick people (visits, neighborhood, work, calls). Use the method: ask, listen, pray briefly, check, pray again, bless.

Two. Tell What God Has Done. Write down everything that happened during these six days of challenges: the prayers, the changes, even small ones. Share a testimony with your church or a friend: testimonies build the faith of others.

Three. Make It a Reflex. Make a simple commitment for what comes next: for example, offering to pray for at least one sick person each week. Write it down, and ask someone to remind you of it.

To reflect on. What is still keeping me from praying for the sick around me? With whom could I go out "two by two" this week?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you sent seventy anonymous disciples to heal the sick and announce your kingdom. Send me too. Make praying for the sick a reflex of my life, and make my church a family where everyone prays for one another. May many be healed and come to know you. Amen.

Key takeaway. Praying for the sick is not the work of a few: it is the normal breath of the whole body of Christ.

Day 16. Come to Destroy the Works of the Devil.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 4, verses 31 to 41.

He came down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. He was teaching them on the Sabbath day, and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word was with authority. In the synagogue there was a man who had a spirit of an unclean demon; and he cried out with a loud voice, saying, “Ah! what have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God!” Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent and come out of him!” When the demon had thrown him down in the middle of them, he came out of him, having done him no harm. Amazement came on all and they spoke together, one with another, saying, “What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!” News about him went out into every place of the surrounding region. He rose up from the synagogue and entered into Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was afflicted with a great fever, and they begged him to help her. He stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her. Immediately she rose up and served them. When the sun was setting, all those who had any sick with various diseases brought them to him; and he laid his hands on every one of them, and healed them. Demons also came out of many, crying out and saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of God!” Rebuking them, he didn’t allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.

Key verses.

1 John, chapter 3, verse 8. He who sins is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. To this end the Son of God was revealed: that he might destroy the works of the devil.

Part 4: Setting Free.

The third mandate is to set captives free: to cast out demons and deliver those who are bound. This is perhaps the most forgotten mandate in our Western churches, and yet it occupies an enormous place in Jesus's ministry.

The Story.

Jesus is teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum. And in the assembly, a man possessed by a demon begins to cry out. Notice: he was in the synagogue. The place of worship didn't prevent his captivity. Jesus rebuked him: "Be quiet!" he said sharply. "Come out of him!" The demon threw the man down before them all and came out without injuring him.

The crowd's reaction: "All the people were amazed and said to each other, 'What is this teaching? With authority and power he gives orders to impure spirits and they come out!'" (Luke, chapter 4, verse 36)

When evening came, the people brought to Jesus all who had various kinds of sickness, and laying his hands on each one, he healed them. Moreover, demons came out of many people, shouting, "You are the Son of God!" But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak.

What It Reveals.

Jesus never negotiated with demons; he silenced them.

He does not argue, he does not have long conversations, he gives them no platform. He commands, and they obey. Why? Because he came precisely for this: "The one who does what is sinful is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the devil's work." (1 John, chapter 3, verse 8)

A Necessary Balance.

There are two errors to avoid, as writer C. S. Lewis showed well in the preface to his book "The Screwtape Letters": one is not believing in the existence of demons; the other is believing in them and showing excessive and unhealthy interest in them.

The Bible does not see a demon behind every problem. It distinguishes sickness and possession. Jesus healed some sick people simply, and delivered others. Depression can have medical, psychological, relational causes. But the Bible also does not deny the reality of a hostile spiritual world that can oppress, torment, bind.

For Your Life.

Do not live in fear. The one in you is greater than the one in the world (1 John, chapter 4, verse 4). Demons trembled before Jesus; they still tremble before his name.

And do not live in naivety either. If you observe in your life or that of someone close to you unexplainable torments, paralyzing fears without cause, occult practices in the family, thoughts of death that return with force, do not stay alone. Talk to mature church leaders. In prayer, with calmness and authority, the name of Jesus sets free.

Put it into practice.

One. Replace Fear With Truth. If the subject of demons frightens you, learn 1 John 4:4 by heart today and say it aloud. You are on the side of the Victor.

Two. Discern With Wisdom. Don't see a demon everywhere. For a physical or psychological health problem, also see a doctor. Prayer and care go together, and discernment is made with mature leaders.

Three. If a Torment Returns. If you experience repeated torments (nightmares, unexplainable fears, thoughts of death), pray with calmness: "In Jesus's name, I command you to be quiet and depart." Then talk about it this week with a leader in your church.

To reflect on. Do I tend to ignore the reality of spiritual warfare, or do I see it everywhere? How can I find Jesus's balance?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, you came to destroy the works of the devil, and you defeated them at the cross. I do not want to live in fear or in naivety. Give me your discernment and your authority, to be free and to help others be set free. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus never negotiated with demons; he silenced them.

He took them the same hour of the night and washed their stripes, and was immediately baptized, he and all his household. He brought them up into his house and set food before them, and rejoiced greatly with all his household, having believed in God.

Key verses.

Philippians, chapter 2, verses 9 to 10. Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth,

The Story.

In Philippi, Paul and his companions encounter a young slave girl possessed by a spirit of divination. She predicts the future, and her masters make much money through her. She follows Paul for several days, crying out: "These men are servants of the Most High God, and they proclaim to you the way of salvation."

What she says is true. But the source is evil. And finally: "She did this for many days. But Paul, greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.' And it came out that very hour." (Acts, chapter 16, verse 18)

What It Reveals.

Paul doesn't perform long rituals. He doesn't shout for hours. He speaks to the spirit—one sentence, in the name of Jesus Christ. And the spirit comes out that very hour.

It's not the volume of your voice that casts out demons; it's the name you speak.

Paul explains elsewhere why this name has such authority: "Therefore God also has highly exalted Him and given Him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, and of those on earth, and of those under the earth," (Philippians, chapter 2, verses 9 to 10)

Also notice that Paul doesn't accept the spirit's "advertising," even when it seems favorable. Not everything that speaks of God is necessarily from God. Discernment is essential.

The Price of Freedom.

This young girl's deliverance comes at a cost. Her masters, seeing their source of income disappear, drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates. They are beaten with rods and thrown into prison, with their feet in stocks.

And at midnight, instead of complaining, they pray and sing praises to God. The other prisoners hear them. An earthquake shakes the prison—the doors fly open, and everyone's chains fall off. The jailer, terrified, asks: "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" And that night, he and his whole household believe and are baptized.

One deliverance led to another, and praise opened prisons.

For Your Life.

Freeing someone sometimes disturbs interests: those who profit from the occult, from addictions, from exploitation. Don't be surprised if you face opposition.

But remember this above all: your authority doesn't depend on your strength, your experience, or your eloquence. It rests on the name of Jesus, which is above every name. When you pray for someone who is bound, speak with calm and confidence, in the name of Jesus.

And in your nights of prison, when everything seems locked, do as Paul and Silas did: praise God. Praise isn't only a response to victory; it's often a weapon that precedes it.

Put it into practice.

One. Use the Name with Faith. When you pray against oppression (fear, torment, confusion), do it in one clear, calm sentence: "In the name of Jesus Christ, I command you to leave." No need to shout or repeat for hours.

Two. Discern the Voices. Not everything that speaks of God is from God. If you follow "prophets," seers, or spiritual influencers, verify their message in the light of Scripture and ask advice from mature leaders.

Three. Praise in Your Night. If you're going through a "prison" right now, choose a moment this week to praise God aloud, even if you don't feel like it: a song, a psalm, a list of thanksgivings.

To reflect on. Am I relying on the name of Jesus, or on my own spiritual strength, when facing spiritual warfare?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, Your name is above every name. Before it, every knee bends. Teach me to speak it with faith and calm to free those who are bound. Give me discernment, and in my nights, teach me to praise You until the doors open. Amen.

Key takeaway. It's not the volume of your voice that casts out demons; it's the name you speak.

Day 18. Closing the Doors.

Today's reading : Acts, chapter 19, verses 11 to 20.

God worked special miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons were carried away from his body to the sick, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out. But some of the itinerant Jews, exorcists, took on themselves to invoke over those who had the evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, “We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.” There were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, who did this. The evil spirit answered, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?” The man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, overpowered them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. This became known to all, both Jews and Greeks, who lived at Ephesus. Fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified. Many also of those who had believed came, confessing and declaring their deeds. Many of those who practiced magical arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. They counted their price, and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord was growing and becoming mighty.

The Story.

In Ephesus, a city famous for its magic and sorcerers, God works extraordinary miracles through Paul's hands: the sick are healed, evil spirits come out.

Then some Jewish exorcists, the seven sons of a man named Sceva, try to imitate Paul. They say to the demons: "I adjure you by Jesus whom Paul proclaims!" And here is the reply of the evil spirit: "The evil spirit answered and said, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?'" (Acts, chapter 19, verse 15)

The man possessed jumps on them, overpowers them, and puts them to flight, naked and wounded.

What It Reveals.

The name of Jesus is not a magic formula. The sons of Sceva knew the name, but they didn't know the person. They spoke of "Jesus whom Paul proclaims," not "Jesus my Lord."

You don't cast out demons with a formula; you cast them out with a relationship.

Spiritual authority comes from belonging. It's because you are God's child, submitted to Jesus, filled with His Spirit, that you can use His name.

The Great Housecleaning of Ephesus.

And the story doesn't end there: "Many of those who had believed came confessing and telling their deeds. And many of those who had practiced magic brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted up the value of them, and it totaled fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord grew mightily and prevailed." (Acts, chapter 19, verses 18 to 20)

Believers, not pagans, come to confess their practices. They had believed in Jesus, but they had kept their magic books at home. And they burn them publicly. Fifty thousand pieces of silver: an enormous sum, years of wages. They don't try to resell them. They destroy them.

The result: the word of the Lord grows mighty and prevails.

For Your Life.

Many Christians today have believed in Jesus but still keep "magic books": horoscopes consulted "for fun," tarot cards, past visits to a fortune teller or witch doctor, amulets and lucky charms, spiritist practices, objects tied to rituals, certain practices presented as "wellness" but linked to spirits. The Bible is clear on this (Deuteronomy, chapter 18, verses 10 to 12).

These things are open doors. You can pray for a long time to be free, but if you leave the doors open, freedom won't last.

Today, do as the believers in Ephesus did: confess, renounce, and get rid of what's connected to it. This isn't superstition in reverse: it's an act of loyalty to Jesus alone.

Put it into practice.

One. Make an Inventory. Ask the Holy Spirit to remind you of any occult practice in your life or your family (fortune-telling, horoscopes, tarot, witch doctor, spiritism, amulets). Write them down honestly.

Two. Renounce and Destroy. For each one, pray aloud: "In the name of Jesus, I renounce… and I close this door." Then get rid of the related objects—don't sell or give them away.

Three. Have Someone Walk with You. If these practices were significant (rituals, pacts, repeated consultations), ask church leaders to pray with you. You shouldn't do this housecleaning alone.

To reflect on. Do I still have, in my life or my home, "magic books" that I've never burned? Do I know Jesus personally, or only "the Jesus that others proclaim"?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, I don't want to know You by name only, but personally. I renounce any occult practice from my past and my family, and I close all the doors I've opened. I belong to You alone. May Your word grow mighty in my life. Amen.

Key takeaway. You don't cast out demons with a formula; you cast them out with a relationship.

Day 19. What Bends You.

Today's reading : Luke, chapter 13, verses 10 to 17.

When Jesus saw her, he called her and said to her, “Woman, you are freed from your infirmity.” He laid his hands on her, and immediately she stood up straight and glorified God. Doesn’t each one of you free his ox or his donkey from the stall on the Sabbath and lead him away to water? Ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound eighteen long years, be freed from this bondage on the Sabbath day?” As he said these things, all his adversaries were disappointed; and all the multitude rejoiced for all the glorious things that were done by him.

The Story.

One Sabbath day, Jesus is teaching in a synagogue. There is a woman bent over for eighteen years. Eighteen years looking at the ground. Eighteen years without seeing people's faces, without seeing the sky. "And behold, there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years, and was bent over and could in no way raise herself up. But when Jesus saw her, He called her to Him and said to her, 'Woman, you are loosed from your infirmity.' And He laid His hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and glorified God." (Luke, chapter 13, verses 11 to 13)

The synagogue leader objects: healing is not done on the Sabbath! And Jesus answers him: "So ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound—think of it—for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath?" (Luke, chapter 13, verse 16)

What It Reveals.

First, notice that Jesus sees her. She's not crying out, she's not asking anything. She's there, invisible, as she probably has been for years in this synagogue. Jesus sees her, calls her, speaks to her, and lays His hands on her.

Second, Jesus names the cause: "Satan bound this woman." It wasn't just a back problem; there was a spiritual chain. And Jesus frees her by laying His hands on her: healing and deliverance are intertwined.

Finally, He calls her "a daughter of Abraham." He restores her dignity and her place among God's people, before all those who may have looked down on her.

Jesus doesn't ask you to straighten up by yourself: He lays His hand on what bends you.

The Invisible Chains.

Not all chains are visible. Some people walk straight, but their soul has been bent for years: shame that makes them lower their eyes, childhood trauma, abuse never spoken of, bitterness that gnaws, a hidden addiction, a curse word that returns ("you're worthless," "you'll end up like your father").

Freeing means more than casting out demons spectacularly. It means helping people be freed from what holds them bent: through prayer, forgiveness, the truth of God's Word, companionship, and sometimes professional help.

For Your Life.

What bends you? How long has it been? Eighteen years, maybe longer. You may have become so used to it that you believe it's your normal posture. Jesus doesn't see you as a hopeless case. He sees you as a son or daughter of Abraham, who has the right to freedom.

And around you, who is bent, invisible, in the back of the room? Jesus noticed this woman. Ask Him for eyes to see those no one sees.

Put it into practice.

One. Name What Bends You. Write what has weighed on you for a long time: shame, fear, trauma, bitterness, addiction, negative words. Present it to Jesus and ask Him to lay His hand on that specific place.

Two. Break Negative Words. If a curse has been spoken over you ("you're worthless," "you'll never succeed"), pray: "In the name of Jesus, I reject this word and I receive what God says about me." Then read Ephesians 2:10.

Three. Don't Walk Alone. For trauma or abuse, seek companionship: a trained pastor, a support group, and if necessary a healthcare professional. God also frees through skilled people.

To reflect on. What has held me "bent" for so long that I've become used to it? Who around me is bent and invisible?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, You see what bends me for so many years. Lay Your hand on me. I receive Your word: I am freed. Straighten me so I glorify You. And open my eyes to those bent around me, that I might bring them Your freedom. Amen.

Key takeaway. Jesus doesn't ask you to straighten up by yourself: He lays His hand on what bends you.

Day 20. Staying Free.

Today's reading : John, chapter 8, verses 31 to 36.

Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” They answered him, “We are Abraham’s offspring, and have never been in bondage to anyone. How do you say, ‘You will be made free’?” Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, everyone who commits sin is the bondservant of sin. A bondservant doesn’t live in the house forever. A son remains forever. If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.

Key verses.

Galatians, chapter 5, verse 1. Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage.

What the Word Says.

Jesus speaks to Jews who have just believed in him. And he tells them the secret of a freedom that lasts: "Jesus said to the Jews who had believed in him, 'If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.'" (John, chapter 8, verses 31 to 32)

Then he adds: "So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed." (John, chapter 8, verse 36)

Free Without Knowing It.

On January 1, 1863, in the middle of the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln signs the Emancipation Proclamation: enslaved people in the rebellious Confederate States are declared free. But in Texas, far from the fighting, the news doesn't circulate, or it's hidden. It isn't until June 19, 1865, more than two years later, that soldiers arrive in Galveston and publicly announce freedom to the enslaved people. For two and a half years, hundreds of thousands of people were free on paper, and lived still in chains, because no one had announced the news to them.

You can be free on paper and still live in chains, if no one has announced it to you.

That's why the three mandates go together. Freedom was purchased at the cross, but it must be announced, and it must be applied in lives.

Staying Free.

Paul writes to the Galatians, who were falling back into old slavery: "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not let yourselves be burdened again by a yoke of slavery." (Galatians, chapter 5, verse 1)

Being set free is a moment. Staying free is a journey. Jesus told a troubling story: an unclean spirit comes out of a person, then returns and finds the house "empty, swept, and put in order." It returns with seven other spirits worse than itself (Matthew, chapter 12, verses 43 to 45). An empty house is a vulnerable house.

The secret, according to Jesus, is to "abide in his word." Fill the house. After a deliverance, it's not enough to drive out what was evil; you must let Jesus, his Word, and his Spirit occupy the whole place.

For Your Life.

If you have been set free from something (an addiction, an oppression, a fear, a habit), protect your freedom. Fill your life with the Word, with praise, with fellowship, with service. Close the doors you had opened. Surround yourself with people who help you stand firm.

And remember the enslaved people of Texas. Around you, people are free on paper, because Jesus paid for them, but they don't know it yet. Someone must announce the news to them. Why not you?

Put it into practice.

One. Fill the House. If you have been set free from something, choose three habits to fill your life this week: a daily time in the Word, a time of praise, a moment with brothers and sisters.

Two. Abide in the Word. Choose a verse about freedom (John, chapter 8, verse 36,Galatians, chapter 5, verse 1,Romans, chapter 8, verse 2) and memorize it. Say it out loud each time the old chains try to come back.

Three. Announce Freedom. Think of someone who still lives "in chains" without knowing that Jesus can set them free. Pray for them, then find an opportunity to tell them, in your own words, that there is true freedom in Jesus.

To reflect on. What have I been set free from, and how am I protecting that freedom? Is my "house" filled, or empty and swept?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, if you set me free, I am truly free. I want to abide in your word, and let you fill my whole house. Keep me from returning under the yoke. And send me to announce freedom to those who don't yet know it's for them. Amen.

Key takeaway. Being set free is a moment. Staying free is a journey.

Day 21. You Have Received Freely.

Today's reading : Matthew, chapter 10, verses 5 to 16.

As you go, preach, saying, ‘The Kingdom of Heaven is at hand!’ Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, and cast out demons. Freely you received, so freely give. Don’t take any gold, silver, or brass in your money belts. Take no bag for your journey, neither two coats, nor sandals, nor staff: for the laborer is worthy of his food. Into whatever city or village you enter, find out who in it is worthy, and stay there until you go on. As you enter into the household, greet it. If the household is worthy, let your peace come on it, but if it isn’t worthy, let your peace return to you. Whoever doesn’t receive you or hear your words, as you go out of that house or that city, shake the dust off your feet. Most certainly I tell you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah in the day of judgment than for that city. “Behold, I send you out as sheep among wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and harmless as doves.

Part 5: Sent Out.

Here we are on the last day. We started with Jesus sending out the twelve in Luke 9. We finish with the same commission, told by Matthew, in more detail.

What the Word Says.

"Go and say: 'The kingdom of heaven is near.' Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse those who have leprosy, drive out demons. Freely you have received; freely give." (Matthew, chapter 10, verses 7 to 8)

Announce: "The kingdom of heaven is near." Heal: "Heal the sick, cleanse those who have leprosy." Set free: "Drive out demons." And even "raise the dead": nothing is too great for the kingdom.

Then this phrase that sums it all up: "Freely you have received; freely give."

Freely.

Everything you have received from God, you received freely: forgiveness, peace, healing, freedom, the Spirit, the gifts. You paid nothing, deserved nothing. And Jesus asks you to give it the same way.

That means two things. First, no commerce: you don't charge for a prayer, a deliverance, a healing. Second, no pride: what you give is not yours. You're just a distributor of what you've received.

Sheep Among Wolves.

Jesus doesn't hide the reality: "I am sending you out like sheep among wolves. Therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves." (Matthew, chapter 10, verse 16)

Shrewdly as snakes: with wisdom, discernment, intelligence. Don't be naive, know the terrain, respect people, choose your words. Innocent as doves: with purity, without ulterior motives, without manipulation, without seeking your own interest.

The mission isn't always easy. There will be refusals, mockery, sometimes opposition. But Jesus sends, and he goes with you.

For Your Life.

Announce, heal, set free: this isn't the job of a few, it's the DNA of all.

For 21 days, you've seen Jesus do it, then the apostles, then the Church. Now it's your turn. Not necessarily on a stage or in a distant country. Where you live: in your family, in your neighborhood, at your work, in your school, in your church, on your networks.

Announcing is telling what Jesus did for you, and inviting. Healing is daring to say "Can I pray for you?" to someone who is sick, and walking alongside them. Setting free is helping someone close the doors and abide in the truth.

You have received freely. Now go, and give freely.

Put it into practice.

One. Your Plan for the Next 30 Days. Write one concrete step for each mandate: a person to announce Jesus to, a sick person to pray for, a person to walk with toward freedom. Put a date next to each name.

Two. Shrewd and Innocent. Before each action, ask yourself: Am I acting with wisdom (respect, discernment, right timing) and with purity (without manipulation, without seeking my glory)?

Three. Don't Keep This Plan to Yourself. Invite one or two people to do this plan with you, or to live these three mandates together: pray once a week, go out in pairs to visit the sick, share your testimonies.

To reflect on. Concretely, how will I live these three mandates (announce, heal, set free) in the next 30 days?

Prayer. Lord Jesus, I have received freely your forgiveness, peace, healing, freedom, and your Spirit. I want to give freely. Send me to announce your kingdom, heal the sick, and set the captives free, where you have placed me. Make me shrewd as a snake and innocent as a dove. Here I am, send me. Amen.

Key takeaway. Announce, heal, set free: this isn't the job of a few, it's the DNA of all.

titre: Who Is God? — Who Is God
texte:
Who God Is

We believe in one true God, the Creator of all things: the heavens, the earth, humanity, and the universe. God is Spirit, one in essence yet existing in three distinct persons. His attributes can be divided into two categories:

— Communicable Attributes: characteristics He has shared with us, such as love, will, and intelligence.

— Incommunicable Attributes: attributes belonging to God alone, such as His omnipotence or His omnipresence.

Before going further, let's ask the question that changes everything: why study who God is? Jeremiah 9:23-24 answers powerfully: let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the rich man in his riches — “but let him who glories glory in this, that he understands and knows Me.” And Jesus goes even further: “This is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God” (John 17:3). Notice carefully: He doesn't say “that they may know things about You,” but “that they may know You.” Eternal life is not first a destination; it is a relationship.

There is a huge difference between knowing things about God and knowing God. You can read the biography of a famous person and know everything about them without ever having met them; but the day you share a meal with someone, you no longer know them the same way. Look at Moses: this man had seen the burning bush, the ten plagues, the sea split in two, the pillar of fire. And yet, on top of Sinai, what does he ask? “Please, show me Your glory!” (Exodus 33:18). After all he had seen, he still wanted more of God Himself. That is the heart this lesson wants to teach you: never be satisfied with what you know about God, but long for Him.

A word of advice before we continue: don't read this lesson like a course to review. Pause right now and simply tell Him: “Lord, I don't just want to learn things about You — I want to meet You in this lesson.” Every attribute we are about to discover answers a real question in your life: Can I trust Him? Does He see me? Does He change His mind about me?

titre: Who Is God? — Here Are Some of His Attributes
texte:
Here Are Some of His Attributes

— Eternal: God was never created. He has always existed and is not limited by time. (Isaiah 40:28; 2 Peter 3:8)

— Sovereign: He rules and reigns over everything and everyone. (Daniel 4:35; Psalms 99:1)

— Almighty: Nothing can defeat God, and nothing is impossible for Him. (Revelation 11:16-17; Jeremiah 32:27; Luke 1:37)

— Omniscient: He knows everything, and nothing can be hidden from His eyes. (Hebrews 4:13; 1 John 3:20)

— Omnipresent: He is everywhere at the same time and fills the whole universe. (Psalms 139:7-8; Jeremiah 23:23-24)

— Immutable: God does not change. He is constant and unchanging. (Hebrews 13:8; James 1:17)

— Holy: God is pure and free from all imperfection or evil. (Revelation 4:8; Isaiah 57:15; 1 Samuel 2:2)

— Love: His very essence is love. He is merciful, good, and patient. (1 John 4:8; Ephesians 2:4; Psalms 34:8; Exodus 34:6)

— Just and perfect: God never makes a mistake and remains faithful in all things. (Zephaniah 3:5; Psalms 7:11; Romans 1:20)

These attributes are not abstract ideas: the Bible shows them to us in action in real lives. Let's take time to look closely at a few of them.

His sovereignty: the story of Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4). The king of Babylon, the most powerful man in the world, is walking on the roof of his palace, boasting: “Is not this great Babylon, that I have built by my mighty power?” At that very moment, a word falls from heaven: the kingdom is taken from him. For seven times, this proud king lives like a beast of the field, until he lifts his eyes and acknowledges “that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men” (Daniel 4:32). When his reason returns, his first words are worship. Lesson for us: thrones, economies, crises, and our own plans all remain under God's rule. You can go through the darkest news without panicking — no event escapes His hand.

His omniscience: the God who sees me. In Genesis 16, Hagar, a pregnant and mistreated servant, flees into the desert — a woman alone, without status, without a future. It is there that the Angel of the Lord finds her, calls her by name, and speaks to her about her unborn son. Overwhelmed, she gives God this magnificent name: “El Roi,” the God who sees me (Genesis 16:13). Centuries later, Jesus would tell an astonished Nathanael: “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1:48). God saw you before you knew Him. Direct application: since God already knows everything — our doubts, our anger, our shame — prayer can finally become honest. There's no need to put on an act before Him; David prayed without a mask, and that is why the Psalms still touch us today.

His omnipresence: on both sides of running away. Jonah tried to flee “from the presence of the Lord” — he discovered that the ship, the storm, and even the belly of the fish were still before that presence. But omnipresence has a gentler side: in Daniel 3, when the three young men are thrown into the furnace, the king jumps up, astonished: “Did we not cast three men bound…? Look! I see four men walking in the midst of the fire” (Daniel 3:24-25). God had not stayed outside the furnace: He was inside, with them. In a hospital room at three in the morning, in an exam room, in grief — there is no “dead zone” with God, no place where the signal is lost. And in the furnace, He is right beside you.

His immutability: “God is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should repent. Has He said, and will He not do?” (Numbers 23:19). We all know people whose affection changes from day to day; God, however, is exactly the same today as on the day He made His promises. That is what makes faith possible: we build on a rock, not on shifting sand.

titre: Who Is God? — Here Are Some of His Attributes (continued)
texte:
His holiness: when Isaiah sees the Lord in the temple, the seraphim themselves cover their faces, crying “Holy, holy, holy!”, and the prophet collapses: “Woe is me, for I am undone! Because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). But look at what follows: God's holiness does not destroy Isaiah — a seraph touches his lips with a live coal from the altar, and his sin is taken away. God's holiness is not a distance that crushes: it is a fire that purifies those who draw near.

Finally, His love: God's love is not a changing feeling; it is His very essence — and it has a visible definition: “In this the love of God was manifested toward us, that God has sent His only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through Him” (1 John 4:9). To know whether God loves you, don't look at your circumstances: look at the cross.

The Trinity

The triune nature of God is revealed primarily in the New Testament. Although God manifests Himself in three persons — the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit — He is indivisible. These three persons share the same divine essence and power.

“Then God said, Let Us make man in Our image, according to Our likeness…” (Genesis 1:26)

“For there is one God and one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus.” (1 Timothy 2:5)

“When He had been baptized, Jesus came up immediately from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to Him, and He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and alighting upon Him. And suddenly a voice came from heaven, saying, This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” (Matthew 3:16-17)

The Trinity is a mystery that goes beyond our human understanding, yet it contains no contradiction. God exists eternally in three distinct persons, perfectly united.

Let's first make one important thing clear: the Trinity was not invented by the Church centuries later — it is woven throughout all of Scripture. From the very first page: “Let Us make man in Our image” (Genesis 1:26) — a mysterious plural at the heart of the one God. And in Jesus' Great Commission, there is a beautiful grammatical detail: baptize “in the NAME of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19) — in the name, singular, not “in the names.” Three persons, one Name, one God.

People have often looked for images to explain the Trinity: water existing as ice, liquid, and steam; the three-leaf clover; the sun with its light and heat. These images may help for a moment, but we need to know their limits. Water is never ice, liquid, and steam at the same time — yet the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit exist together, eternally, in perfect communion. At Jesus' baptism, all three are present at the same moment: the Son in the water, the Spirit descending, the voice of the Father speaking.

Why is this truth so precious, beyond the mystery? For two reasons that touch your life. First: it alone explains that “God is love” (1 John 4:8). Love requires a relationship — you can't love all by yourself. Even before creation, from all eternity, the Father loved the Son in the communion of the Spirit: God did not create the world out of a need to be loved, but out of the overflow of a love that already existed. You weren't born out of a lack, but out of an abundance.

Second: your entire salvation is Trinitarian. Ephesians 1 unfolds it: the Father chose you before the foundation of the world, the Son redeemed you by His blood, the Holy Spirit sealed you for the day of redemption. All three divine persons committed themselves to save you. And that's why Christian prayer has the movement described in Ephesians 2:18: through Jesus, we have access to the Father by one Spirit. When you pray, all of heaven is involved: you speak to the Father, on the basis of the Son's work, carried by the power of the Spirit. The Trinity isn't a theologian's puzzle: it's the house in which you pray.

titre: Who Is God? — God the Father
texte:
God the Father

God the Father is the person of the Trinity who sits enthroned in heaven, sovereign over all creation. He acts as a loving Father toward His children.

“Yet for us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we for Him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and through whom we live.” (1 Corinthians 8:6)

Let's pause here, because for many people everything hinges on this one word: “Father.” Some of us had fathers who were absent, harsh, unpredictable, or hurtful, and this word stirs up more pain than trust. So we need to answer a crucial question: why is our heavenly Father so different from our earthly fathers?

First, because God didn't become a Father — He has been one from all eternity. A man becomes a father when his child is born, and he learns that role by trial and error, carrying his own wounds. God, however, has always been Father: before creation, He already loved the Son (John 17:24). Fatherhood isn't a role He takes on; it is His very being. Paul says it in a breathtaking phrase: it is from Him that “the whole family in heaven and earth is named” (Ephesians 3:14-15). In other words, God doesn't resemble human fathers — human fathers are called to resemble Him. The best of them are only a pale reflection; the worst are a betrayal of Him. But the original is perfect.

Next, because Scripture takes care to distinguish Him, point by point, from our wounded fathers. Our fathers can abandon us — David writes: “When my father and my mother forsake me, then the Lord will take care of me” (Psalms 27:10). Our fathers can be harsh or fickle — “As a father pities his children, so the Lord pities those who fear Him. For He knows our frame; He remembers that we are dust” (Psalms 103:13-14). Our fathers can give poorly — Jesus Himself makes the argument: “If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!” (Matthew 7:11). Even a mother's love, the strongest we know, is surpassed: “Can a woman forget her nursing child?… Surely they may forget, yet I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15).

And when God trains, He doesn't crush: He raises up. In Hosea 11:3-4, God describes Himself as a parent teaching a little one to walk: “I taught Ephraim to walk, taking them by their arms… I drew them with gentle cords, with bands of love.” Picture the scene: a toddler wobbling, two hands reaching out so he won't fall. That's how God taught you to walk in faith — and He hasn't changed His method. Even His discipline is proof of His love: “For whom the Lord loves He chastens, as a father the son in whom he delights” (Hebrews 12:6) — not to punish, but to shape.

Jesus portrayed all of this in the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15). Take time to look at it in detail. The son demands his share of the inheritance while his father is still alive — in that culture, it meant saying: “You're already dead to me.” The father, incredibly, lets him go. Then comes the famine, the pigs — the ultimate humiliation for a son of Israel — and the speech the son rehearses: “Make me like one of your hired servants.” He hopes for an employee's status; he has lost the very idea of being a son. But the text says: “When he was still a great way off, his father saw him” — so the father had been scanning the horizon, every single day. And he runs — a patriarch never ran; it was beneath his dignity. This one hikes up his robe and runs. Then three gestures, before the son even finishes his confession: the best robe (dignity restored), the ring (the family's authority, like a credit card on his finger), the sandals (slaves went barefoot — sons wear shoes). No probation period, no employee status: a son, fully, immediately.

That's exactly what God does for you in Christ: “As many as received Him, to them He gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). And the Spirit you received is not “the spirit of bondage again to fear, but the Spirit of adoption by whom we cry out, Abba, Father!” (Romans 8:15). “Abba” is the word little Aramaic children used — our “Daddy.” A slave doesn't walk into the king's chamber; a little child climbs onto his lap.

titre: Who Is God? — God the Father (continued)
texte: How can you apply this if the word “father” hurts you? Here's a concrete path. First, name the wound before God — He already knows, but saying it sets you free. Second, refuse the transfer: every time you catch yourself thinking, “God must be like my father — disappointed, distant, unpredictable,” answer that thought with a verse; read Psalm 103 slowly every morning for a week. Third, pray out loud starting with “Abba, Father” — not as a formula, but because saying the words heals the mouth that could never say them. Fourth, begin the journey of forgiveness toward your earthly father: forgiving isn't excusing or forgetting; it's handing the debt over to God so you no longer carry it yourself. And fifth, let the Church be a family to you: God often heals the image of the father through spiritual fathers and mothers in whom His heart becomes visible.

titre: Who Is God? — God the Son: Jesus Christ
texte:
God the Son: Jesus Christ

Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. He is fully God and fully man, who came to earth to save us.

“Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but made Himself of no reputation, taking the form of a bondservant, and coming in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:6-7)

— Present from the beginning: (John 1:1-3)

— Creator of the universe: (Colossians 1:16)

— Promised from Genesis: (Genesis 3:15)

— His coming prophesied: (Isaiah 53; Micah 5:1; Zechariah 9:9)

— God incarnate: (Isaiah 7:14; John 1:1; Luke 19:10)

— Died for our sins and raised for our justification: (1 Corinthians 15:1-5)

— The only Savior and Mediator: (Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5)

— Almighty and eternal: (Revelation 22:12-13; Matthew 28:18)

Let's take a close look at these two statements, because the entire Christian faith rests on their union: fully God, fully man.

Fully God: this is not an honorary title. John opens his Gospel the way Genesis opens: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Jesus does what only God can do: He forgives sins — and the scribes don't miss it: “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:7); He commands the storm, and it falls silent; He receives worship without ever refusing it, whereas angels and apostles refuse it in alarm. And when Thomas, eight days after the resurrection, touches His wounds and cries out, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28), Jesus doesn't correct him — He commends him for believing.

Fully man: He was hungry in the wilderness, thirsty at noon by a well (John 4:6-7), He slept from exhaustion in a boat in the middle of a storm, He wept at the tomb of His friend Lazarus (John 11:35), He knew such anguish in Gethsemane that His sweat became like great drops of blood. He “was in all points tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). His humanity wasn't a disguise: it was real flesh, real fatigue, real tears.

Why must He absolutely be both? Follow the reasoning closely, because its logic is brilliantly clear. The debt of sin is a human debt: man sinned, so man must pay. But no man can: each one is already bankrupt from his own debt. Only God has the means to pay — but God owed nothing. So it took someone who had to pay as a man and who could pay as God: Jesus, and Him alone. That's why “there is one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). Imagine a mediator tasked with reconciling two peoples who don't speak the same language: he must speak both perfectly. Jesus places one hand on God and one hand on us, and He brings us together.

And consider how far down He agreed to come. Philippians 2:6-7 describes this willing descent: though He was in the form of God, He didn't cling to His rank — He emptied Himself. From the glory of heaven to a stable's manger; from the worship of angels to the spit of a judgment hall; from the throne to the cross. No one took His life from Him: He laid it down (John 10:18). When you wonder what you're worth in God's eyes, look at the price He agreed to pay.

Here's a very practical consequence for your prayer life: because your advocate with the Father knows hardship from the inside, you can “come boldly to the throne of grace, that you may obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16). When you pray in your suffering, you're not talking to someone watching from a distance — you're talking to someone who has been there.

titre: Who Is God? — God the Holy Spirit
texte:
God the Holy Spirit

The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God. He is a divine person, not merely a force or an influence. He is the One who convicts hearts, teaches believers, and transforms them into the image of Christ. He is the person of God who dwells within us.

— He speaks (Hebrews 3:7),

— He leads (Galatians 5:18),
